Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:37:56.799+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later
3. Initially,
the Prince of Liáng, seeing that all the military governors of Héběi had submitted,
except for Yōu and Cāng, which remained unconquered,
launched a major campaign against them,
intending to strengthen the allegiance of the various governors.
Subsequently, Lùzhōu rebelled internally,
and the prince burned his camp and returned.
These events are recorded in the third year of the Tiānyòu era in the previous scroll.
Regarding the pronunciation of "return" (還),
it follows the Xuān reading,
and also the usual reading.
Fearing that both the court and the provinces would become disloyal because of this,
he wished to quickly accept the abdication in order to stabilize them.
On Dīnghài,
the prince entered and lodged in Wèi,
fell ill,
and lay in his residence.
Luó Shàowēi, fearing the prince would attack him,
went in to see the prince and said:
"Now, all those in the four directions who raise troops and cause trouble for you, my prince,
do so under the pretext of supporting and upholding the Táng court.
It would be better for you, my prince, to quickly destroy the Táng to cut off people's hopes."
Although the prince did not agree, he was inwardly grateful to him,
and thus hurried back.
On Rényín,
he reached Dàliáng.
On Jiǎchén,
Táng Emperor Zhāoxuān dispatched the Censor-in-chief Xuē Yíjǔ to Dàliáng to convey greetings to the prince.
Yíjǔ requested to see him with the etiquette of a subject,
and the prince, bowing, invited him to ascend the steps.
Yíjǔ said:
"Your Highness's merits and virtues reside among the people;
the Three Numinous Ones have changed their divination.
(The Three Numinous Ones are
the spirits of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
This means that the hearts of Heaven, Earth, and Man have all already abandoned the Táng house,
changing the divination of the ruler and bestowing the mandate [on another].)
How dare I, your subject, oppose this!"
He then faced north and performed the ceremonial bow and dance in the courtyard.
The prince turned sideways to avoid it.
Yíjǔ returned
and said to the emperor:
"The marshal has the intention to accept the abdication!"
The emperor then issued an edict.
(The emperor
refers to Táng Emperor Zhāoxuān.
The marshal
refers to the Prince of Liáng.)
He also dispatched the chief ministers with a letter to inform the prince;
the prince declined.
4. Hé dōng troops were still stationed in Zhǎngzǐ,
intending to spy on Zézhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Zhǎngzǐ,
it is 140 lǐ southwest to Zézhōu.
In the first year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era of Emperor Tàizōng of Sòng, the Bǎoyì Army was changed to the Bǎopíng Army,
to avoid the old name of the imperial residence.
This is recorded because the historian-official avoided the temple name.
However, observing that Kāng Huáizhēn was ordered to dispatch troops from Jīngzhào and Tónghuá to station in Jìnzhōu,
it seems likely that troops from the two garrisons east of Fūzhōu were sent to station in Jìnzhōu.
For if Huáizhēn dispatched troops from Jīngzhào and Tónghuá from Xíngzhōu,
the route would be separated and difficult,
and Xíngzhōu is close to Lùzhōu,
so it should also be prepared for the arrival of Hé dōng troops.
There was no reason for Huáizhēn to leave Xíngzhōu and station in Jìnzhōu.
I humbly believe
that "Bǎopíng"
should also be written as
"Bǎodà".
According to the biography of Huáiyīng in the Ouyáng History, it also records
"Bǎoyì".
This is likely because he was appointed as the Bǎoyì military governor due to the victory at Měiyuán.
Zhū Quánzhōng was eager to usurp the Táng,
and had no time to raise troops to attack Lùzhōu,
merely defending himself.
Therefore, Lùzhōu was increasingly able to strengthen its defenses.
5. In the second month,
the great ministers of Táng jointly petitioned Emperor Zhāoxuān to abdicate.
On Rénzǐ,
an edict ordered the chief ministers to lead the hundred officials to the Marshal's Office to urge the prince to ascend the throne;
the Prince of Liáng had established the Marshal's Office in Dàliáng.
Regarding "leading" (相帥),
it is read as "to lead" (率).
Thereafter, court officials, military governors, and even those from Húnán and Lǐngnán submitted memorials urging the prince to ascend the throne, one after another.
6. In the third month,
on Guǐwèi,
the prince appointed Lǐ Sī'ān, the prefect of Bózhōu, as Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Route Army,
to lead troops to attack Yōuzhōu.
(To attack Liú Réngōng.)
7. On Gēngyín,
Táng Emperor Zhāoxuān issued an edict ordering Xuē Yíjǔ to go again to Dàliáng to convey the intention of abdication,
and also ordered Sū Xún, the Minister of Rites, to take the memorial of the hundred officials to Dàliáng.
8. Qián Liú, the Prince of Wú and military governor of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, sent his sons Chuán Liǎo and Chuán Guàn to attack Lú Jí in Wēnzhōu.
9. On Jiǎchén,
Táng Emperor Zhāoxuān issued an imperial rescript abdicating in favor of Liáng.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records, Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties, and the Supplementary Records of Táng all state it was in the fourth month,
that the Táng emperor issued an imperial rescript ordering the chief minister Zhāng Wénwèi and others to prepare the imperial carriage to welcome the Liáng court,
but without a specific day.
The Comprehensive Records of the Five Dynasties states it was on Dīngwèi of the fourth month.
Dīngwèi
is the first day of the fourth month.
The Old History of Táng states it was on Jiǎchén of the third month.
Jiǎchén
is the 27th day of the third month.
The Supplementary Annals of Táng: On the 27th day of the third month, Jiǎzǐ, this imperial rescript was issued,
and on Wùchén of the fourth month, Zhū Quánzhōng ascended the throne.
This is particularly erroneous.
According to the calendar, the first day of the third month this year was Wùyín,
and the first day of the fourth month was Dīngwèi.
Now, we follow the Old History of Táng.
Sū Xún, the Minister of Rites, served as his deputy;
the Envoy of the Investiture Ceremony,
responsible for presenting the abdication edict and imperial seals,
and commanding the Imperial Guard, the Grand Ceremonial Guard, and others.
Táng possessed the Eight Imperial Seals.
Empress Wǔ detested the character "seal" (璽),
and changed it to "treasure" (寶),
so the Eight Mandate-receiving and State-transmitting Seals were all re-engraved with the character "treasure".
Xuē Yíjǔ, the Censor-in-chief, served as the Envoy in Charge of the Golden Treasures.
The Six Statutes of Táng states: The Son of Heaven has eight treasures,
made of jade,
and sealed with clay.
The seals of the empress and crown prince are called "treasures",
made of gold.
They led the hundred officials, prepared the imperial carriage, and went to Dàliáng.
The Six Statutes of Táng: The Grand Carriage is equipped with the five chariots,
each of the five chariots has a secondary carriage;

also the south-pointing chariot, the mileage-drum chariot, the white egret chariot, the phoenix banner chariot, the evil-warding chariot, the leather-canopied chariot, the plowing-root chariot, the comfort chariot, the four-view chariot, the sheep chariot, the yellow battle-axe chariot, the leopard-tail chariot,
and twelve auxiliary chariots.
For the Ceremonial Carriage, the five secondary chariots are reduced,
as well as the white egret, evil-warding, comfort, and four-view chariots,
and one-fourth of the auxiliary chariots.
Regarding "led" (帥),
it is read as "to lead" (率).
Yáng Shè's son, Níngshì, who served in the Historiography Institute,
(In the third year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the Historiography Institute was established under the Chancellery,
with other officials concurrently holding positions.
Those of lower rank but with talent were also called "Directors of the Institute",
with chief ministers overseeing the compilation.
After the Tiānbǎo era,
other officials concurrently holding historiographical positions were called "Compilers of the Historiography Institute",
and those newly appointed were called "Directors of the Institute".
In the first year of the Yuánhé era,
Chief Minister Péi Jì proposed,
that court officials holding historiographical positions be called "Compilers",
with high-ranking officials overseeing the institute's affairs,
and those not yet at court rank be called "Directors of the Institute".)
said to his father: "You, father, are a chief minister of Táng,
and yet the state has come to this.
It cannot be said that you are without fault.
Moreover, you are personally handing over the Son of Heaven's seal and ribbons to another.
Even if you preserve wealth and honor,
what about a thousand years from now?
Why not decline it!"
Shè was greatly alarmed and said:
"You will destroy our clan!"
For several days, his spirit and expression were unsettled because of this.
Cè
was from Dūnhuáng.
Guāngféng
was the son of Yǐn.
(Zhào Yǐn appears in the 13th year of the Xiántōng era of Emperor Yìzōng, in scroll 252.)
10. Liú Réngōng, the military governor of Lúlóng,
was arrogant, extravagant, greedy, and cruel.
He often worried that the city of Yōuzhōu was not secure,
so he built a residence on Dà'ān Mountain.
(The Old History of the Five Dynasties states: West of Yōuzhōu there is a famous mountain called Dà'ān Mountain.
"This mountain is steep and isolated on all sides,
allowing a few to control many.")
Its buildings were magnificent and grand,
comparable to those of an emperor.
He selected beautiful women to fill it.
Together with alchemists, he refined elixirs,
seeking immortality.
He collected all the money within his territory
and buried it on the mountain peak;
he ordered the people to use clay mixed with artemisia to make coins.
He also prohibited tea merchants from Jiāngnán from entering his territory,
instead picking plants and trees from the mountains to make tea himself,
and selling it.
Rén Gōng had a beloved concubine named Luó Shì,
whom his son Shǒu Guāng had an affair with.
Rén Gōng caned Shǒu Guāng and expelled him,
no longer considering him a son.
He did not count him among his other sons.
Everywhere they passed, they burned and plundered, leaving nothing behind.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
they advanced directly to the walls of Yōu Zhōu.
Rén Gōng was still at Dà'ān Shān,
and the city was unprepared,
nearly falling.
Shǒu Guāng led troops in from outside,
ascended the walls to defend them;
he also sent troops out to engage Sī'ān in battle,
and Sī'ān was defeated and retreated.
Shǒu Guāng then declared himself military governor,
ordering his generals Lǐ Xiǎoxǐ and Yuán Xíngqín to lead troops to attack Dà'ān Shān.
Rén Gōng sent troops to resist,
but was defeated by Xiǎoxǐ.
They captured Rén Gōng and brought him back,
imprisoning him in a separate room.
Rén Gōng's officers, aides, and attendants,
all those whom Shǒu Guāng had long disliked, were killed.
The Silver Húlù Commander-in-Chief Wáng Sītóng led his three thousand troops,
and the Shānhòu Eight Armies Patrol and Inspection Commissioner Lǐ Chéngyuē led his two thousand troops
(in Lúlóng, the four prefectures of Guī, Tán, Xīn, and Wǔ constituted Shānhòu).
and fled to Lǐ Kèyòng.
Not long after,
they also fled to Hédōng.
The Hédōng military governor, Prince of Jìn Kèyòng, appointed Chéngyuē as the Kuāngbà Commander and
Sītóng as the Fēiténg Commander.
Sītóng's mother
was Rén Gōng's daughter.
Kuāngbà and Fēiténg
were both names of army units established by the Prince of Jìn.
11. The Prince of Liáng
first held court in the Jīnxiáng Hall.
Wáng Pǔ's Wǔdài Huìyào states: After receiving the abdication and establishing the capital at Dàliáng,
the main audience hall was renamed Chóngyuán Hall,
the eastern hall Xuándé Hall,
the inner hall Jīnxiáng Hall,
the Wànsuì Hall was renamed Wànsuì Hall,
and the gates were named accordingly.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says: The Liáng claimed to rule by virtue of the Metal phase,
and also because Fújiàn presented a parrot as tribute,
and various prefectures successively presented white crows, white rabbits, and white lotuses with joined stems,
which were taken as omens that the Metal phase's mandate was in effect,
hence the hall was named Jīnxiáng (Metal Auspice).
These were the officials appointed by the Liáng themselves.
He referred to himself as "the solitary one."
On the day Xīnhài,
he ordered that all memorials, reports, registers, and records omit the Táng era name,
referring only to the month and day.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Zhāng Wénwèi and others arrived at Dàliáng.
12. Lú Jí heard that Qián Chuánliǔ and others were approaching,
and led a naval force to resist them at Qīng'ào.
Qīng'ào is in the sea northeast of Wēnzhōu,
commonly called Qīng'ào Gate.
Proceeding by boat through Qīng'ào Gate leads into Wēnzhōu,
beyond which lies the open ocean.
Ào
is pronounced wū dào fān.
A coastal inlet is called an ào.
"Jí's elite troops are all here,
we cannot engage them in battle."
So they abandoned their ships at Āngù,
and took a side road to attack Wēnzhōu.
Āngù
was Zhāng'ān in the Later Hàn.
Jiàn
is pronounced gǔ xiàn fān.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Wēnzhōu collapsed,
and Jí was captured and executed.
In the second year of Tiānyòu,
Lú Jí captured Wēnzhōu,
and by now was defeated and destroyed.
They ordered Chuánliǔ and others to move troops to attack Lú Yuē at Chùzhōu.
13. On the day Rénxū,
the Prince of Liáng changed his name to Huǎng.
The Prince's elder brother Quányù heard that the Prince was about to ascend the throne,
and said to the Prince:
"Zhū Sān,
how can you become the Son of Heaven!"
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Zhāng Wénwèi and Yáng Shè rode in a carriage from Shàngyuán Station following the imperial seal and regalia,
various offices each prepared ceremonial guards and processional insignia to lead the way,
and the officials followed behind them,
these were the officials of the Táng.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
The Prince donned the imperial robe and crown,
and ascended the throne as emperor.
Zhāng Wénwèi and Sū Xún presented the edict, ascended the hall, and read it aloud,
Yáng Shè, Zhāng Cè, Xuē Yíjǔ, and Zhào Guāngféng in turn presented the imperial seal and ascended the hall,
and after the reading was finished,
yǐ means
completed.
They led the officials in performing the ceremonial dance and offering congratulations.
The Emperor then feasted with Wénwèi and others in the Xuándé Hall.
The Emperor raised his wine cup and said:
"I have assisted in governance for only a short time,
this is all due to the support and endorsement of you gentlemen."
Wénwèi and others were ashamed and fearful,
prostrating themselves and unable to reply,
only Sū Xún, Xuē Yíjǔ, and the Minister of Justice Zhāng Yī
lavishly praised the Emperor's virtue and merit, saying he should comply with Heaven and accord with the people.
The Emperor again drank and gambled with his clan relatives in the palace,
zōng
refers to those of the same surname;
qī
refers to relatives of different surnames.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
Zhū Quányù suddenly threw the dice, hitting the basin and scattering them,
Bào Hóng's Bójīng says: In the Chǔcí, kūn bì xiàng qí refers to liù bó.
Kūn bì
are jade rods,
each player throws six rods,
moves six pieces,
hence it is called liù bó.
Using twelve pieces,
six white,
six black,
the die thrown is called a qióng.
The qióng has five colors,
one mark carved is called a sāi,
two marks carved is called a bái,
three marks carved is called a hēi.
Uncarved,
between the five sāi,
is called the wǔ sāi.
According to the New History of the Five Dynasties,
this so-called tóu qióng
refers to dice.
Bèng
is pronounced běi mèng fān.
The Textual Analysis states: Wáng Rényù's Yùtáng Xiánhuà says:
"After the dice had been thrown several rounds,
Prince Guǎng Quányù suddenly stopped and did not throw,
turned and addressed Liáng Zǔ,
calling out twice 'Zhū Sān,'
Liáng Zǔ's expression changed.
Prince Guǎng said: 'You love such high office,
but will your clan be secure for long?'
Then, greatly angered,
he threw the gaming pieces down the steps,
striking the basin and shattering it,
gnashing his teeth and glaring fiercely,
and did not stop for several days."
Now we follow Wáng Yǔchēng's Wǔdài Shǐ Quēwén.
"Zhū Sān,
you were originally a commoner from Dàngshān,
followed Huáng Cháo as a bandit,
the Son of Heaven appointed you as military governor of four towns,
(the Prince of Liáng first held four towns concurrently,
see the 262nd volume, Táng Emperor Zhāozōng's first year of Tiānfù).
How could you suddenly destroy the three-hundred-year state of the Táng house,
(the Táng received the abdication in the first year of Wǔdé,
the year being wù yín,
and abdicated to the Liáng,
the year being dīng mǎo,
enjoying the state for 290 years).
Your clan will soon be exterminated,
what is the point of gambling!"
The Emperor was displeased and ended the gathering.
The Khitan sent their minister Páohù Méilǎo to establish friendly relations,
and the Emperor dispatched the Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Gāo Qí, to reciprocate.
In the beginning, the Khitan had eight tribes.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Khitan chieftain was called the Dàhè clan.
Later, it divided into eight tribes: the first was called the Dànlìjiē tribe,
the second was the Yǐshìhuó tribe,
the third was the Shíhuó tribe,
the fourth was the Nàwěi tribe,
the fifth was the Pínmò tribe,
the sixth was the Nèihuìjī tribe,
the seventh was the Jíjiě tribe,
and the eighth was the Xīwà tribe.
The leader of a tribe was called the "Great Man."
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔguózhì* states: The Khitan
were originally of the ancient Xiōngnú stock.
For generations, they lived in the Liáo marshes,
on the southern bank of the Huángshuǐ River.
To the south, it was 1,100 *lǐ* from Yúguān,
and from Yúguān, it was 700 *lǐ* south to Yōuzhōu.
*Kǎoyì* (Investigation of Discrepancies) says: Sū Féngjí's *Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù* (Veritable Records of Emperor Gaozu of Han) states:
"The Khitan originally had the surname Dàhè.
Later, they divided into eight clans: the first was called Lìjiēdǐ,
the second was Yǐshīhuódǐ,
the third was Shíhuódǐ,
the fourth was Nàwěidǐ,
the fifth was Pínmòdǐ,
the sixth was Nèihuìjīdǐ,
the seventh was Jíjiědǐ,
and the eighth was Xīwàdǐ.
They administered forty-one counties,
each county had a magistrate.
The leaders of the eight clans
were all called 'Great Men,'
styled as Cìshǐ (Regional Inspectors).
They often elected one person as king,
establishing banners and drums to honor him.
Every three years,
they would rank their names to take turns succeeding him."
*Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* (Biography of Emperor Zhuangzong) says:
"At the end of the Xiántōng era (860-874),
their king was called Xí'ěr.
His territory gradually expanded,
and he frequently came to pay tribute.
During the Guāngqǐ era (885-888),
their king was called Qīndé.
Taking advantage of the many troubles in the Central Plains
and the lack of preparedness on the northern border,
he gradually encroached upon the various tribes.
Tribes such as the Dá dá, Xī, and Shìwéi
were all driven into servitude."
Both *Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù* and *Táng Yúlù* (Remaining Records of the Tang) state:
"During the reigns of Emperors Xī and Zhāo (873-904),
their king, Yēlǜ Ābǎojī, relying on his strength and courage,
resisted the other clans and refused to be replaced.
He proclaimed himself the Heavenly King.
Later, the other clans confronted him,
requesting the use of the old system.
Bǎojī had no choice
but to hand over the banners and drums.
He then said: 'I have been the leader for nine years,
and I have gathered many Han Chinese.
I wish to lead my own clan with the ancient Hànchéng,
commanding the Han Chinese to guard it,
forming my own tribe.'
The other clans agreed.
Soon, he devised a plan and re-annexed the other clans,
arrogantly declaring himself emperor.
His territory grew daily.
During the Dàshùn era (890-891),
the Later Táng Wǔhuáng (Emperor Taizu of Later Tang) sent an envoy to form an alliance with him.
They held a grand meeting in the eastern city of Yúnzhōu,
invited him into the tent,
and swore brotherhood."
*Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn* also says:
"When Qīndé's governance declined,
Ābǎojī's clan became powerful.
He proclaimed himself king.
In the second year of Tiānyòu (905),
he launched a major invasion of our Yúnzhōng.
Tàizǔ (Emperor Taizu of Later Liang) sent an envoy to form an alliance,
and thus met him face-to-face in the eastern city of Yúnzhōu.
He was invited into the tent,
and they swore brotherhood.
Tàizǔ said to him: 'The Táng house has been usurped by treacherous ministers.
I will launch a major campaign this winter.
Brother, lend me 20,000 elite cavalry
to jointly capture Biàn and Luò.'
Bǎojī agreed.
After Bǎojī returned,
Qīndé handed over state affairs to him."
Jiǎ Wěi's *Bèishǐ* (Supplementary History) states:
"Wǔhuáng met Bǎojī at the old Yúnzhōu city,
forming a brotherly bond.
At the time, their troops were arrayed five *lǐ* apart.
Messengers rode back and forth on horseback with cups
to perform the rituals of toasting.
Bǎojī was pleased
and said to Wǔhuáng: 'Among our barbarian chieftains,
the old rule is to step down after three years.
If I see you another day,
will you still treat me with the same courtesy?'
Wǔhuáng said: 'I have received a court appointment to govern Tàiyuán.
There is also a system of transfer,
but as long as one is not replaced, it is fine.
Why worry about stepping down?'
From then on, Bǎojī followed his advice
and refused to be replaced by the other clans."
Zhào Zhìzhōng's *Lǔtíng Zájì* (Miscellaneous Records of the Barbarian Court) states:
"Tàizǔ's personal name was Yì,
his barbarian name was Ābǎojǐn,
and he was also called Wòlǐ.
Tàizǔ was born intelligent.
The leaders of the eight tribes admired his bravery and prowess,
so they dismissed the old leader Āniǎnshì and sent him back to his own tribe,
establishing Tàizǔ as king."
It also says:
"Whenever a king was to be established,
the chieftains of all the tribes would gather for a meeting.
They would choose someone with virtue and achievements.
If no disasters occurred,
if animal husbandry flourished,
and if the people lived in peace,
then the king would not be replaced.
If not,
the various chieftains would gather the tribes to select another person as king.
Therefore, according to barbarian law,
the king would willingly step down
and not be harmed by the multitude."
It also says:
"There were Hán Zhīgǔ, Hán Yǐng, Kāng Méi, Wáng Zòushì, and Wáng Yù,
all of whom were Chinese,
who together urged Tàizǔ not to accept replacement."
The *Xīn Tángshū* (New Book of Tang) records the names of the eight Khitan tribes, which differ significantly from those in *Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù*.
This is likely due to the great distance in time
and the inconsistency of the barbarian language,
but they are essentially the same.
Ābǎojī said,
"I have been the leader for nine years,"
indicating that he had long refused replacement in his state,
not because of Wǔhuáng's advice.
I now follow *Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù*.
Also, *Táng Yúlù* earlier states:
"During the Qiánníng era (894-898),
Liú Réngōng governed Yōuzhōu.
Bǎojī invaded,
and Réngōng captured his brother-in-law Shùlǜ Ābō.
As a result, for over ten years, he could not raid the border."
Later, it says:
"During the Dàshùn era (890-891), he met with Wǔhuáng in Yúnzhōng."
Note: Dàshùn was before Qiánníng.
Liú Réngōng only became the military governor of Yōuzhōu in the second year of Qiánníng (895),
not during Dàshùn.
Also, Wǔhuáng said:
"The Táng house has been usurped by treacherous ministers.
I will launch a major campaign this winter."
This was not an event of the Dàshùn era;
*Táng Yúlù* is mistaken.
Also, *Biānyílù* (Compiled Omitted Records) states:
"In the fifth month of the second year of Kāipíng (908),
the Khitan king Ābǎojī and the former king Qīndé presented local products as tribute."
This shows that at that time, the seven tribes still existed.
They made an agreement
to elect one person as king,
establishing banners and drums to command the various tribes.
Every three years, they would take turns succeeding him.
At the end of the Xiántōng era (860-874),
there was a king named Xí'ěr,
and the territory began to expand.
Later, Qīndé became king.
Taking advantage of the many troubles in the Central Plains,
he frequently raided the border.
When Ābǎojī became king,
he was especially brave and powerful.
The five surnames of the Xī
(The five surnames of the Xī:
first, the Āhuì tribe;
second, the Chǔhé tribe;
third, the Àoshī tribe;
fourth, the Dùjī tribe;
fifth, the Yuánsìzhé tribe.
Each had a Rǔgēzhǔ as its chieftain.)
Ōuyáng Xiū said: At the end of the Táng, the Xī lived in Yīnliángchuān,
west of Yíngfǔ
and northwest of Yōuzhōu,
both several hundred *lǐ* away.
They were divided into five tribes: the first was called the Āhuì tribe,
the second was the Yòumǐ tribe,
the third was the Yuèzhì tribe,
the fourth was the Nùjiē tribe,
and the fifth was the Hēigēzhī tribe.
Later, they moved to live several hundred *lǐ* northeast of Yōuzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: The Xī lived in Yīnliángchuān,
500 *lǐ* east of Yíngfǔ,
900 *lǐ* southwest of Yōuzhōu,
connecting to the sea in the southeast,
with mountains and rivers spanning 3,000 *lǐ*.
Later, they moved to Pípáchuān.
The Shìwéi originally had over twenty tribes,
of which seven surnames were close to the Khitan.
Ābǎojī's surname was Yēlǜ.
The *Ōu Shǐ Sìyí Fùlù* (Ōuyáng's History, Appendix on the Four Barbarians) says: Ābǎojī took the name of the Héngzhàngdì where he lived as his surname.
It was called Shìlǐ.
Shìlǐ,
translators called it Yélǜ.
He refused to accept being replaced.
After a long time,
Ābǎojī returned from attacking the Huángtóu Shìwéi,
and the seven tribes intercepted him at the border,
demanding that he abide by the agreement.
That is, the agreement to rotate leadership every three years.
They passed on the banners and drums,
and he said:
"I have been king for nine years,
and have acquired many Han people.
I request to lead my tribe
to settle in the ancient Hànchéng,
guard it together with the Han people,
and form a separate tribe."
The seven tribes agreed.
Hànchéng
was the former Huáyán County of the Later Wei.
According to the Hànshū,
Huáyán County belonged to the Yúyáng Commandery.
Emperor Ming of the Later Han changed its name to Yántián.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Dàyú River flows southeast from south of the Mìyún city walls,
passing south of Huáyán County, which was part of the old Yúyáng Commandery of the Later Wei's Ānzhōu.
Huáyán
was commonly called Húyánchéng.
It was two hundred li northwest of the Yùyí Garrison.
Ōuyáng Xiū said: Hànchéng was on the Luán River southeast of Tànshān.
Sòng Bái said: The Qìdān lived within the Liáo marshes,
on the southern bank of the Huángshuǐ.
The Liáo marshes were 1,130 li from Yúguān,
and Yúguān was 174 li from Yōuzhōu.
Their territory extended southeast to the sea,
east to the Liáo River,
west encompassing Lěngxíng,
and north bounded by the Sōngxíng Mountains.
It stretched three thousand li east to west,
the land was rich in pine and willow trees,
and the marshes were full of cattails and reeds.
Ābǎojī resided at Hànchéng,
which was 550 li northwest of Tánzhōu.
North of the city was Lóngménshān,
north of the mountain was Tànshān,
and west of Tànshān was the area where the Qìdān and Shìwéi territories connected.
This area was at the headwaters of the Luán River,
with salt marshes to the west,
which was the Later Wei's Huáyán County.
It had the benefit of salt ponds.
Later, Ābǎojī gradually used his troops to attack and destroy the seven tribes,
reuniting them into a single state.
He also invaded northward against the Shìwéi and Nǚzhēn.
The Nǚzhēn
were descendants of the Sùshèn clan.
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé occupied that territory.
Those registered within Liáodōng were called Shú Nǚzhēn,
those living wild beyond the borders were called Shēng Nǚzhēn,
and those at the extreme distant frontiers were called Huángtóu Nǚzhēn.
He attacked the Xī,
destroyed them,
then reinstated a Xī king but placed a Qìdān overseer to supervise their troops.
All the various tribes in the northeast feared and submitted to him.
In that year,
Ābǎojī led a force of three hundred thousand to invade Yúnzhōu.
The Prince of Jìn formed an alliance with him,
meeting face-to-face at the eastern city,
swearing brotherhood,
inviting him into his tent,
drinking freely,
clasping hands in great joy,
and agreeing to jointly attack Liáng that winter.
Textual Analysis says: The Táng Tàizǔ Jìnián Lù states:
"Tàizǔ, because Ābǎojī's clan and faction had grown somewhat powerful,
summoned him.
In the fifth month of the second year of Tiānyòu,
Ābǎojī led his tribe of three hundred thousand to the eastern city of Yúnzhōu.
They discussed matters in the tent,
clasped hands in great joy,
swore brotherhood,
and he left after ten days.
He left behind his son Gǔdū Shělì and the chief Jǔbǐng Méi as hostages,
agreeing to launch a major campaign early in winter to cross the river and restore order,
but it was halted when Emperor Zhāozōng met with bandits."
Ōuyáng's History says:
"When Liáng was about to usurp Táng,
the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng, sent an envoy to engage with the Qìdān.
Ābǎojī met Kèyòng at the eastern city of Yúnzhōu with three hundred thousand troops,
clasped hands and swore brotherhood,
planning to jointly raise troops to attack Liáng."
Regarding the meeting at Yúnzhōu,
the Zhuāngzōng Biographies and the Old History of the Five Dynasties both place it in the fourth year of Tiānyòu,
while the Jìnián Lù alone places it in the second year of Tiānyòu;
it also says
"they agreed to capture Biàn and Luò together this winter,
but it was halted when Emperor Zhāozōng met with bandits."
If so, then it should have been before the death of Emperor Zhāozōng in the first year of Tiānyòu,
not in the second year.
Moreover, if Emperor Zhāozōng met with bandits, it would be even more reason to raise troops to punish them,
why would they stop!
According to Wǔhuáng's statement
"the Táng house was usurped by treacherous ministers,"
this was spoken in the fourth year;
that winter Wǔhuáng fell ill,
probably because of this the planned military expedition did not materialize.
I follow this now.
"Taking advantage of his coming,
we could capture him,"
the Prince said:
"With enemies not yet destroyed, to break faith with barbarians
is the path to self-destruction."
Ābǎojī stayed for ten days before leaving.
The Prince of Jìn gifted him tens of thousands in gold and silk.
Ābǎojī left three thousand horses
and tens of thousands of various livestock in return.
Ābǎojī returned and betrayed the alliance,
instead attaching himself to Liáng.
The Prince of Jìn therefore hated him.
The Comprehensive Mirror, in the Táng annals, writes
"Lǐ Kèyòng,"
reflecting the relationship of ruler and minister;
in the Liáng annals, it writes
"the Prince of Jìn,"
reflecting the status of a rival state.
The same principle applies to Wú and Shǔ.
On the 22nd, Jǐmǎo,
Zhāng Quányì, the Governor of Hénán concurrently holding the position of Héyáng military commissioner, was appointed Prince of Wèi;
the military commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, Prince of Wú Qián Liú, was appointed Prince of Wúyuè;
Qīnghǎi military commissioner Liú Yǐn and Wǔwēi military commissioner Wáng Shěnzhī were additionally appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng,
"Wǔwēi military commissioner"
should have
"commissioner"
below it.
Since Emperor Wǔ of Sòng, a descendant of Péngchéng, rose in Jiāngnán,
later many considered the Liú of Péngchéng a prominent clan.
Liú Yǐn was enfeoffed as Prince of Dàpéng,
the intent likely deriving from this.
On Guǐwèi,
Gāo Jìchāng, acting as interim governor of Jīngnán, was appointed military commissioner.
Jīngnán originally governed eight prefectures:
Jīng, Guī, Xiá, Kuí, Zhōng, Wàn, Lǐ, and Lǎng,
eight prefectures in total.
Due to successive bandit disturbances,
all the prefectures were seized by neighboring circuits,
leaving only Jiānglíng.
When Jìchāng took office,
the city walls were ruined and destroyed,
and the population was depleted.
Jìchāng pacified and resettled the scattered people,
and the people all returned to their livelihoods.
On the 23rd, Yǐyǒu,
his elder brother Quányù was established as Prince of Guǎng,
his son Yǒuwén as Prince of Bó,
Yǒuguī as Prince of Yǐng,
Yǒuzhāng as Prince of Fú,
Yǒuzhēn as Prince of Jūn,
Yǒuyōng as Prince of Hè,
and Yǒuhuī as Prince of Jiàn.
Yǒuwén, as an adopted son, was placed above the other sons.
Yǒuguī's regicide and rebellion
had its origins here.
On the 24th, Xīnmǎo,
the old residence in the Eastern Capital was made the Jiànchāng Palace,
and the position of Supervisor of the Jiànchāng Bureau was changed to Commissioner of the Jiànchāng Palace.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says: Initially,
when the Emperor was founding his enterprise,
because the military provisions and storehouse registers of the four garrisons were numerous and complex,
he established the Jiànchāng Bureau to oversee them.
At this time it was changed to a palace,
likely to emphasize its importance.
Sòng Bái says: This year, the Secretariat-Chancellery memorialized to change the Supervisor of the Jiànchāng Bureau to Commissioner of the Jiànchāng Palace,
and requested that the old mansion in the capital be used as the Jiànchāng Palace.
On the 25th, Rénchén,
Bǎopíng military commissioner Kāng Huáizhēn was ordered to lead eighty thousand troops to join the Wèibó army in attacking Lùzhōu.
This was an attack on the Jìn general Lǐ Sìzhāo.
On the 26th, Jiǎwǔ,
an edict abolished the Bureau of Military Affairs,
its duties all transferred to the Chóngzhèng Institute,
with the Administrator of the Institute, Jìng Xiáng, appointed as its Commissioner.
Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records state:
"On the fourth month, Xīnwèi,
Xiáng was appointed Administrator of the Chóngzhèng Institute.
On the fifth month, Jiǎwǔ,
an edict stated that the Bureau of Military Affairs should be changed to the Chóngzhèng Institute,
and Xiáng was first appointed as its Commissioner."
It seems the name Chóngzhèng Institute already existed earlier,
and at this time the duties of the Bureau of Military Affairs were all merged into the Chóngzhèng Institute.
27 The Minister of Rites Sū Xún and his son, the Gentleman of the Daily Records Sū Kǎi, considered themselves to have rendered meritorious service to the Liang.
In the second year of the Tiānyòu era of Emperor Zhāoxuān of Táng, Sū Xún had instigated the matter of the abdication and succession,
and therefore believed himself to have rendered merit.
Xún hoped day and night to become Chancellor.
The Emperor despised his character.
The Old Táng History, Annals of Emperors: In the second year of Tiānyòu of Emperor Zhāoxuān,
Sū Kǎi submitted a memorial refuting the posthumous title of Emperor Zhāozōng.
Quánzhōng was suspicious and discerning in judging men.
After Kǎi refuted the posthumous title, he deeply despised him.
After the succession was completed,
both father and son were expelled,
not permitted to remain at court.
Jìngxiáng spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"Sū Xún,
the owl of the Táng,
sold out the state for profit.
He cannot be allowed to stand in a court that is making a fresh start."
On the Wùxū day,
an edict ordered Xún and the Minister of Justice Zhāng Yī, among fifteen others, all to be compelled to retire from office.
Kǎi was dismissed and sent back to his native fields.
The father and son Xún then went to Hézōng to rely on Zhū Yǒuqiān.
This laid the groundwork for Sū Xún's flattery of Táng Zhuāngzōng at the beginning of the Tóngguāng era.
28 Lǜ Yuē surrendered Chùzhōu to Wúyuè.
In the first year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng,
Lǜ Yuē occupied Chùzhōu.
By this time, it was lost.
To surrender,
pronunciation: hù jiāng fān.
29 The Prince of Hóngnóng appointed the Surveillance Commissioner of Èyuè, Liú Cún, as the Commander-in-Chief of the Southwest Front;
the Prefect of Yuèzhōu, Chén Zhīxīn, as the Tuanlian Commissioner of Yuèzhōu;
the Surveillance Commissioner of Lúzhōu, Liú Wēi, as the Relief Commissioner;
and the Assistant General Xǔ Xuányīng as the Army Supervisor;
leading a naval force of thirty thousand to attack Chǔ.
The Prince of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, was very fearful.
The Military Commissioner of Jìngjiāng, Yáng Dìngzhēn, congratulated him, saying:
"Our army will be victorious!"
Yīn asked the reason.
Dìngzhēn said:
"In warfare, fear leads to victory,
arrogance leads to defeat.
Now the Huáinán troops are advancing directly towards our city;
this is arrogance and underestimation of the enemy.
Yet Your Majesty shows a fearful countenance.
I therefore know we are certain to be victorious."
Yīn ordered the Capital Commandant of the City, Qín Yànhuī,
the Capital Commandant of the City,
to take overall command of all troops within Tánzhōu city.
The Deputy Naval Commander Huáng Fán led three hundred warships to station at Liúyángkǒu.
Wú established Liúyáng County from part of Chángshā;
Suí abolished it;
in the second year of the Jǐnglóng era, it was re-established at the old city site,
belonging to Tánzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: The county is 160 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Xiāng River flows north past the west of the Hàn-era Línxiāng County.
The Liú River flows from the northwest of the county and empties into it.
There was a Liúkǒu garrison.
Fán,
pronunciation: fú yuán fān.
Liú,
pronunciation: lì zhōu fān.
Cún and others encountered heavy rain.
They led their troops back to the north of the Yuè Dīke.
Yànhuī pursued them.
Cún fought several battles unsuccessfully.
He then sent a letter to Yīn feigning surrender.
Yànhuī sent a message to Yīn, saying:
"This is certainly a trick.
Do not accept it!"
Cún and Yànhuī formed battle lines separated by water.
Cún shouted from afar:
"It is inauspicious to kill those who surrender!
Do you, sir, not consider your descendants?"
Yànhuī replied:
"When bandits enter our territory and we do not attack them,
what consideration for descendants is there then?"
He advanced with loud shouts and drums.
Cún and others fled.
Huáng Fán from Liúyáng
crossed the river,
and joined Yànhuī in a combined attack,
inflicting a major defeat.
They captured Cún and Zhīxīn.
Examination of Discrepancies: The Biān Yí Lù records:
"In the fourth month of the fourth year of Tiānyòu,
the Húnán army's Chén Shào reported victory.
The Huáinán and Lángzhōu forces combined by land and water to charge into their territory.
Mǎ Yīn sent out his naval force at Liúyángjiāngkǒu and heavily defeated the rebel faction,
capturing the false Èzhōu Military Commissioner Liú Cún alive."
According to the Liáng Annals in the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
Mǎ Yīn's memorial reporting the defeat of the Huái bandits was in the sixth month;
the Wú History in the Ten States Chronicle,
records Liú Cún attacking Chǔ in the fifth month,
and being defeated in the sixth month;
the Chǔ History is the same;
the Biān Yí Lù is in error.
The number of soldiers killed reached tens of thousands.
Eight hundred warships were captured.
Wēi escaped back with the remaining troops.
Yànhuī then captured Yuèzhōu.
Chén Zhīxīn's capture of Yuèzhōu is mentioned in the previous scroll, last year.
Warship,
pronunciation: hù àn fān.
Vessel,
pronunciation: sū zāo fān.
They were comforted and admonished.
Both men cursed, saying:
"A true man repays his lord with death.
How could he serve a rebel?"
They were then beheaded.
The history records that Liú Cún and Chén Zhīxīn were loyal and brave.
They were trusted confidants of the Prince of Hóngnóng,
often participating in government affairs.
Zhāng Hào and Xú Wēn, taking advantage of their defeat,
arrested and executed them.
30 The Prince of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, sent troops to join the Prefect of Jízhōu, Péng Gān, in attacking Hóngzhōu,
but they did not succeed.
Péng Gān's allegiance to Chǔ is mentioned in the previous scroll, third year of Tiānyòu of Emperor Zhāoxuān of Táng.
31 Kāng Huáizhēn arrived at Lùzhōu.
The Jìn Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, Lǐ Sìzhāo, and his Deputy, Lǐ Sìbì, closed the city gates and resisted.
Huáizhēn attacked day and night.
After half a month without success,
he then built fortifications, dug winding trenches, and held his position,
cutting off all communication inside and out.
The Prince of Jìn appointed the Commander-in-Chief of the Fan and Han Troops, Zhōu Déwēi, as the Field Army Commander-in-Chief.
Zhōu Déwēi commanded all Fan and Han troops;
he was a great general of Hédōng.
In the era of the Five Dynasties,
each military district had its own Commander-in-Chief,
but the official duties assigned could differ.
For example, Zhōu Déwēi as Commander-in-Chief of Fan and Han Troops
meant all Fan and Han troops were under his command;
as Field Army Commander-in-Chief,
then all field army troops were under his command;
the Iron Forest Commander-in-Chief Ān Yuánxìn
was merely the commander of one Iron Forest Army unit.
Those reading history should understand each according to its category.
The history states that Jìn mobilized the entire country to rescue Lùzhōu.
To lead,
read as "shuài".
The son of Kèxiū;
Kèxiū
was the younger brother of the Prince of Jìn,
mentioned in the annals of Emperors Xīzōng and Zhāozōng of Táng.
Originally surnamed Zhāng;
Jiàntáng,
was the son of Jìngsī;
Shǐ Jìngsī is mentioned in scroll 255, fourth year of Zhōnghé of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng.
He was from Dàiběi.
32 Jìn troops attacked Zézhōu.
They attacked Zézhōu to threaten Kāng Huáizhēn's rear.
33 On the Jiǎyǐn day,
the Military Commissioner of Pínglú, Hán Jiàn, was appointed Guardian Minister and Tongzhōngshūménxià Píngzhāngshì.

The Military Commissioner of Jīngnán, Gāo Jìchāng, led troops to station at Gōng'ān.
Gōng'ān
was the Hàn-era Chánlíng County.
At the end of the Hàn,
Liú Bèi stationed there
and renamed it Gōng'ān.
In Táng times, it belonged to the Jiānglíng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 90 lǐ south of the prefecture.
Yángōng was defeated.
The Chǔ troops also withdrew.
35 Liú Shǒuguāng, having imprisoned his father
(the matter is seen in the fourth month above),
sent an envoy to request an appointment.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
Shǒuguāng was appointed Military Commissioner of Lúlóng and Tongzhōngshūménxià Píngzhāngshì.
36 The Military Commissioner of Jìnghǎi, Qū Yù, died.
Qū Yù is Qū Chéngyù.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
his son, who was temporarily in charge as Acting Commissioner, Qū Hào, was appointed Military Commissioner.
Examination of Discrepancies: The various books do not show what relation Hào was to Yù.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties:
"In the sixth month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
Yù died.
In the seventh month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,

Since it says

"Field Army Headquarters"
should be
"Field Army".
37 Léi Yángōng attacked Yuèzhōu,
but did not succeed.
Léi Yángōng, having joined Chǔ to attack Jīngnán,
soon after attacked Chǔ's Yuèzhōu.
This shows his fickleness.
38 On the Bǐng
wǔ day,
the Governor of Hénán, Zhāng Quányì, was granted the name Zōngshì.
The Emperor's original name was Quánzhōng,
therefore he changed Quányì's name to Zōngshì.
On the 39th day, Xīnhài,
Wúyuè King Qián Liú was appointed concurrently as Military Commissioner of Huáinán,
and Chǔ King Mǎ Yīn concurrently as Military Commissioner of Wǔchāng,
each serving as Campaign Commander and Military Commissioner of their respective circuits.
The intention was to have Liǎngzhè and Húnán attack Hóngnóng King Yáng Wò,
first granting them the two garrisons previously controlled by the Yáng family.
40 Jìn general Zhōu Déwēi encamped at Gāohé,
located southeast of Túnliú County in Lùzhōu.
Wǔ was defeated.
The Qīnqí,
Liáng's personal guard,
were cavalry troops.
On Dīngsì,
the Emperor replaced Huái Zhēn as Commander of the Lùzhōu Campaign Headquarters with Bózhōu Prefect Lǐ Sī'ān,
demoting Huái Zhēn to Deputy Commander of the Campaign Headquarters.
Sī'ān led Héběi troops westward,
as Shàngdǎng was high terrain,
west of the various Héběi garrisons,
hence "westward."
Shàng,
pronounced with rising tone.
They constructed a second wall,
internally to prevent breakouts,
externally to resist relief forces,
called the "Double Garrison."
They requisitioned supplies from Shāndōng civilians for the army,
but Déwēi daily harassed them with light cavalry,
so Sī'ān built a covered passageway from the southeastern mountain pass,
connecting to the Double Garrison.
Déwēi and his generals took turns attacking it,
demolishing walls and filling moats,
launching dozens of assaults day and night,
exhausting the Liáng troops.
When foragers emerged from the Double Garrison,
Déwēi would capture them,
so the Liáng troops remained behind their walls.
41 In the ninth month,
Léi Yángōng attacked Cényáng and Gōng'ān.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Jiānglíng Prefecture's Gōng'ān County had a Cényáng town.
Cén,
pronounced with rising tone.
Yángōng's greed and cruelty resembled his father's,
Léi Yángōng
was Léi Mǎn's son.
The Jīng and Hú regions often suffered from him;
he also allied with Huáinán.
On Bǐngshēn,
an edict stripped Yángōng of his offices and titles,
ordering Jì Chāng and Chǔ King Mǎ Yīn to attack him.
42 The Shǔ King consulted his officials about proclaiming himself emperor,
all saying:
"Although Your Highness is loyal to Táng,
Táng has already fallen,
this is what is called 'Heaven gives but you do not take'!"
Féng Juān alone proposed that the Shǔ King assume imperial authority without the title,
saying:
"If the dynasty revives, you will not have failed in your duty as a subject;
while rebels exist, you will not share in their evil."
The King did not listen,
and Juān secluded himself at home.
Féng Juān,
grandson of Féng Sù,
after the Táng house had perished,
remained loyal to his former lord,
was different from Wéi Zhuāng, Zhāng Gé and their ilk.
He led officials and people in mourning for three days;
on Jǐhài,
he ascended the imperial throne.
Wáng Jiàn, styled Guāngtú,
was from Wǔyáng, Xǔzhōu.
Kǎo Yì states: Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn:
"After Tàizǔ passed away,
Jiàn proclaimed himself emperor in Chéngdū,
era name Wǔchéng."
Xuē Shǐ, Táng Yú Lù:
"In the ninth month of the fifth year of Tiānyòu,
Jiàn proclaimed himself emperor in Chéngdū,
era name Wǔchéng."
Jiǔ Guó Zhì:
"In the seventh month of this year he ascended the throne,
changing the era name the following year."
Sòng Xiáng's Jìnián Tōngpǔ:

changing the era name the next year."
Ōuyáng Shǐ, Shí Guó Jìnián:
"In the ninth month of the seventh year of Tiānfù he ascended the throne,

We follow this.
On Xīnchǒu,
former Dōngchuān Military Commissioner and concurrently Palace Attendant Wáng Zōngjí was appointed Central Secretariat Director,
Wéi Zhuāng as Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Manager of Central Secretariat Affairs,
and Lángzhōu Defense Commissioner Táng Dàoxí as Palace Commissioner.
Zhuāng,

he led Zhōu Déwēi and others to depart from Jìnyáng.
19. Huáinán sent troops to raid Shíshǒu.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era of Táng, Shíshǒu County was established by dividing Huáróng County,
named after the Shíshǒu Mountain north of the county,

The Jiǔyù Zhì states it is 200 lǐ southeast of the prefectural seat.
Sūn Jiàn said: From Ānlù to Jìnglíng,
the two postal stages are all flat land.
To the south, reaching the great river,
there are no hills or ridges as obstacles.
Crossing the river to Shíshǒu,
one begins to encounter low hills.
It is called Jìnglíng,
meaning the ridges end here.
It is called Shíshǒu,
meaning the stones begin here.
They also sent their general Lǐ Hòu to lead a naval force of fifteen thousand towards Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng engaged them in battle,

Jīngnán administered Jiānglíng,
located north of the river.
The southern bank was called Mǎtóu'àn,

20. On the jǐsì day,
the Jìn Prince encamped his army at Huángniǎn,
forty-five lǐ from Shàngdǎng.
Huángniǎn Village is in Lùchéng County, Lùzhōu.
Niǎn
is pronounced niǔ shàn fān.
On the first day xīnwèi,
the Jìn Prince concealed troops at the foot of Sānchuígāng.
Sānchuígāng is southeast of Túnliú County.
He advanced his troops directly to Jiāzhài.
The Liáng army had no scouts,
and did not expect the arrival of the Jìn troops.
The officers and soldiers had not yet risen,

The Jìn Prince ordered Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Sìyuán to divide their troops into two columns.
Déwēi attacked the northwestern corner,
Sìyuán attacked the northeastern corner.
They filled in the moats, set fire to the stockade,
and charged in with loud shouts.
The Liáng troops suffered a great collapse,
fleeing southward.
The recruiting and campaigning commissioner Fú Dàozhāo fell from his horse,
and was killed by the Jìn men.
The loss of generals, officers, and soldiers numbered in the tens of thousands,
with abandoned supplies, grain, and equipment piled up like mountains.
Zhōu Déwēi and others arrived at the city walls,
calling out to Lǐ Sìzhāo:
"The former king has passed away,
and the current king has come personally,
breaking the enemy's encirclement at Jiázhài.
The enemy has already retreated,
you may open the gates!"
Sìzhāo did not believe it,
saying:
"This must be someone captured by the enemy,
sent here to deceive me."
He wanted to shoot them.
Those around him stopped him,
and Sìzhāo said:
"If the king has truly come,
can I see him?"
The king himself went forward and called out to him.
Sìzhāo saw the king dressed in white mourning clothes,
and was overcome with grief, nearly fainting,
his breath almost ceasing.
Jī,
pronounced jū yī fān.
He then opened the gates.
Earlier,
Déwēi and Sìzhāo had a rift between them,
and Jìn King Lǐ Kèyòng, on his deathbed, said to Jìn King Lǐ Cúnxù:

and I love him deeply.
Now he has not emerged from the heavy siege,
could it be that Déwēi has not forgotten their old grudge?
You must convey this meaning to him on my behalf.
If the siege of Lù is not lifted,
I will not close my eyes in death."
Jìntōng,
was Sìzhāo's childhood name.
Jìn King Lǐ Cúnxù told Déwēi this,
and Déwēi was moved to tears,
fighting with great effort at Jiázhài from then on;
after meeting with Sìzhāo,
they became friendly again as before.
Kāng Huáizhēn fled back with over a hundred cavalry from Tiānjǐng Pass.
The Emperor heard that Jiázhài had not been held,

then sighed:
"To have a son, one should have one like Lǐ Yàzǐ,
Kèyòng's line will not perish!
As for my own son,

He issued an edict to gather and reorganize the scattered troops wherever they were.
Zhōu Déwēi and Lǐ Cúnzhāng took advantage of the victory to advance towards Zézhōu,
where the prefect Wáng Bān had long lost the people's hearts,
and the masses would not serve him.
The Dragon-Tiger Commander Niú Cúnjié led troops from the Western Capital to respond to the defeated soldiers from Jiázhài,
the Dragon-Tiger Army was the same as the Táng Dynasty's Dragon-Guard Army designation.
Liáng received the Táng's abdication,
and changed
"Guard"
to

Wáng Pǔ's Wǔdài Huìyào says: In the first year of Kāipíng,
in the fourth month,
the Left and Right Longzhí were changed to the Left and Right Dragon-Tiger Armies.

He said to his troops:
"Zézhōu is a crucial location,

The troops were all unwilling,

Cúnjié said:

to fear the enemy's strength and avoid them,

He then raised his whip and led the troops forward.
Cè,
means horse whip.
The people in the city had already set fires and made noise,

Bān closed the inner city and defended himself,
when Cúnjié arrived,
order was restored.
Examination of discrepancies says: Ōuyáng Shǐ says:

If Cúnjié had fled back from the double-walled city,

Now follow Liáng Lièzhuàn and Xuē Shǐ.

They retreated to defend Gāopíng.
Gāopíng,
was the location of the Hàn Dynasty's Xuànshì County,

Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 83 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.

The Jìn King returned to Jìnyáng,
rested the troops and distributed rewards,

dismiss corrupt and cruel officials,
reduce taxes and levies,
care for orphans and the poor,

Because Hé'dōng was narrow in territory and had few troops,
he trained the soldiers,
ordering the cavalry not to mount their horses unless they saw the enemy;
once formations were set,
they were not to cross over each other,
or leave gaps to avoid danger;
advancing along separate routes,
they were to meet at the appointed time without the slightest delay.

according to military law.
Guǐ,
pronounced jū wěi fān,
means the shadow of the sun.
The appointed time was noon,
if the sun's shadow passed noon and they had not arrived, it was considered a delay;

Day and night are divided into one hundred marks.
Thus, they were able to conquer Shāndōng,
take Hénán,

Earlier,
when Jìn King Lǐ Kèyòng pacified Wáng Xíngyú,
see volume 260, Táng Zhāozōng Qiánníng second year.
At that time, many regional governors issued unauthorized appointments,
and the king was ashamed to be like them,
always reporting appointments to the court.
By this time,
Jìn King Lǐ Cúnxù began to make appointments by his own authority.
The Jìn King was grateful to Zhāng Chéngyè,
for his help in resolving Lǐ Kèníng's rebellion.
Whenever he visited his residence,
he would enter the hall and bow to his mother,
giving generous gifts.
The siege of Lùzhōu lasted for years,
with more than half of the scholars and commoners dying from cold and starvation,
and the markets and streets desolate.
Lǐ Sìzhāo encouraged farming and sericulture,

and within a few years,

The history records Lǐ Sìzhāo's achievements in governing Lù.
21 Jìngjiāng Military Commissioner and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Qióng died,

23 On Yǐhài,
Chǔ troops invaded Èzhōu,
and Qín Péi, appointed by Huáinán, defeated them.
The Left Yá Commander Zhāng Hào and Right Yá Commander Xú Wēn of Huáinán monopolized military and administrative power,
causing the Prince of Wēi of Hóngnóng great discontent.
(Yáng Wò was posthumously titled Prince of Wēi.)
The two men, feeling insecure,
conspired together to assassinate the prince,
intending to divide his territory and submit as vassals to Liáng.
On the wùyín day,
Hào sent his accomplice Jì Xiáng and others to murder the prince in his bedchamber.
(Examination of Discrepancies states: According to the Wú Lù:
"Hào ordered Jì Xiáng, Chén Huī, Lí Fán, Sūn Yīn, and others to seize Wò in his bedchamber,
and assassinate him."
It does not mention Xú Wēn,
likely because Xú Xuàn concealed it for Wēn's sake.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties follows this, while the Jiāngnán Biélù records matters concerning the exclusive use of the Left Yá troops.
The New History of the Five Dynasties states:
"Wēn and Hào together sent assassins to kill Wò,
agreeing to divide his territory and submit as vassals to Liáng."
Considering that Wēn and Hào separately commanded the Yá troops,
if Wēn were not part of the conspiracy,
Hào would certainly not have dared to assassinate Wò alone.
We now follow the Jiāngnán Biélù.
The Shíguó Jìnián states:
"Zhāng Hào wished to declare himself Liúhòu of Huáinán,
offering allegiance to Liáng,
in exchange for the Jiédùshǐ position of Càizhōu in return for Huáinán.
Xú Wēn said:
'Yángzhōu is only three thousand lǐ round trip from Biànzhōu;
if the military government lacks a ruler for over a month, it will certainly fall into chaos.
It would be better to establish someone first,
and then plan accordingly.'"
If Hào declared himself Liúhòu,
then there would be a ruler.
We do not adopt this account.)
He was twenty-three years old.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Hào assembled the generals and officials in the government hall,
lining both sides of the path and the hall itself with drawn blades,
ordering all generals to dismiss their guards and attendants before entering. (Note: "Dismiss" is pronounced qiě; "attendants" is pronounced zòng.)
"The heir apparent has passed away;
who should lead the military government?"
He asked three times,
but no one responded.
Hào's expression grew increasingly furious.
The advisor Yán Kěqiú stepped forward and secretly advised:
"The military government is vast,
and the borders face many troubles;
none but you, my lord, can lead it.
However, to do so today would likely be too hasty."
Hào asked:
"What do you mean by too hasty?"
Kěqiú replied:
"Liú Wēi, Táo Yǎ, Lǐ Yù, Lǐ Jiǎn—
(Liú Wēi was in Lúzhōu,
Táo Yǎ in Shèzhōu,
Lǐ Yù in Xuānzhōu,
Lǐ Jiǎn in Chángzhōu.)
If you, my lord, establish yourself now,
would these men be willing to be subordinate to you?
It would be better to install a young lord and assist him;
then which general would dare not to obey!"
Hào remained silent for a long time.
Kěqiú then dismissed the attendants,
hastily wrote a note and placed it in his sleeve,

and gestured for his colleagues to proceed to the commissioner's residence to offer congratulations. (The residence of the Jiédùshǐ is called the commissioner's residence. Those offering congratulations intended to congratulate the new ruler.)
Upon arrival, Kěqiú knelt and read it aloud;

it was an instruction from the Grand Dowager, Lady Shǐ. (According to Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì, Wò's mother, Lady Shǐ, was enfeoffed as Junjūn of Wǔchāng Commandery; it seems she was honored as Grand Dowager after Wò succeeded to the position.)
"The founding king established the enterprise with great difficulty;
(This passage: whenever 'the founding king' is mentioned, it refers to Yáng Xíngmì.)
Lóngyǎn is next in line for succession.
The generals must not betray the Yáng family,
and should guide him well."
The wording was clear and earnest.
Hào's expression turned dejected;
as the principle was righteous,
he dared not oppose it,

and thus they supported the Prince of Wēi's younger brother, Lóngyǎn, declaring him Liúhòu of Huáinán and Dūtǒng of the Eastern Front Various Circuits Field Headquarters. (Yáng Lóngyǎn, styled Hóngyuán, was the second son of Yáng Xíngmì. The Old History of the Five Dynasties and Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì both record "Lóngyǎn" as "Wèi".)
Deputy Dūtǒng Zhū Jǐn went to Kěqiú's residence and said:
"From the age of sixteen or seventeen, I have wielded spears and leapt onto horses,
charging against formidable enemies,
and never felt fear.
Yet today, facing Hào,
I could not help but sweat.
You, sir, refuted him to his face as if he were nobody;
now I realize my courage is merely that of a common man,
far inferior to yours, sir."
Thereafter, he treated Kěqiú as an elder brother.
Hào appointed Xú Wēn as Observation Commissioner of Zhèxī,
stationing him in Rùnzhōu.
Yán Kěqiú advised Wēn:
"By abandoning your Yá troops and going to an outer province,
Hào is certain to pin the crime of regicide on you."
Wēn exclaimed in alarm:
"What should I do then?"
Kěqiú said:
"Hào is stubborn and obtuse in handling affairs.
If you will listen to me,
allow me to devise a plan for you."
At the time, Deputy Commissioner Lǐ Chéngsì
(Lǐ Chéngsì was then Deputy Military Commissioner of Huáinán.)
Kěqiú also advised Chéngsì:
"Hào's tyranny is so severe.
Now he is sending Xú away;
his intentions are not without purpose,
and I fear it may not be in your interest either."
Chéngsì deeply agreed.
Kěqiú went to see Hào and said:
"By sending Lord Xú away,
people are saying that you intend to seize his military authority and kill him.
Public opinion can be fearsome."
Hào said:
"The Right Yá desired it,
(Referring to Xú Wēn by his official title as Right Yá.)
and it has already been carried out." (Once an action is completed, it is called yè.)
Kěqiú said:
"Stopping it is easy."
The next day,
Kěqiú invited Hào and Chéngsì together to see Wēn.
Kěqiú glared and reprimanded Wēn:

how much more so you, a veteran general of the Yáng family!

Wēn apologized:
"If you gentlemen will tolerate me,
how dare I act on my own authority!"
Thus, he did not leave.
Hào realized that Kěqiú secretly sided with Wēn.
That night,
he sent an assassin to stab him.
Knowing escape was impossible,
Kěqiú requested to write a letter bidding farewell to the lord of the government. (The lord of the government refers to Lóngyǎn.)
Kěqiú took up the brush without showing fear.
The assassin could read,
and seeing the letter's loyal and righteous content,
said:
"You, sir, are a noble man.
I cannot bear to kill you."
He plundered Kěqiú's belongings and returned to report,
saying:
"I could not capture him."
Hào angrily said:
"I wanted Kěqiú's head;
what use are belongings!"
Wēn and Kěqiú plotted to kill Hào.
Kěqiú said:
"None but Zhōng Tàizhāng can do it."
Tàizhāng was
a man from Héféi,
and at the time held the position of General of the Left Gate Guard.
Textual analysis note: The Wú Jì records it as
"Zhōng Zhāng."

Zhái Qián informed him.

they went straight in and beheaded Hào in the Yá Hall.
The Yá Hall was
the place where the Left and Right Yá Commanders conducted their affairs.

The Western Palace in Guǎnglíng was

Wēn said:

Please, Madam, set your mind at ease!"
Initially,
Wēn and Hào plotted to assassinate King Wēi.
Wēn said:
"If we employ both the Left and Right Yá troops,

It would be better to use only my troops."
Hào would not agree.
Wēn said:
"Then use only your troops."
Hào complied.
At this point,
when the rebellious faction was thoroughly investigated,
they were all from the Left Yá troops.
Because of this, people believed that Wēn truly had no knowledge of the plot.
Judging the circumstances and determining the crime,
Xú Wēn should have been in the same category as Zhāng Hào.
Yet Xú Wēn escaped the name of regicide,
and subsequently monopolized the governance of the state of Wú.
This was perhaps Heaven's will.
Zhì,
is pronounced zhí.
All matters of the military government were decided by him.
He appointed Yán Kěqiú as the Sīmǎ of Yángzhōu.
Wēn was by nature deep and resolute,
and personally maintained a simple and frugal life.

all fitting reason and circumstance.
Previously,
when Zhāng Hào was in power,
punishments were cruel and excessive,
and he allowed his personal troops to plunder the markets and neighborhoods.
Wēn said to Yán Kěqiú:

He then established laws and regulations,
prohibited violence,

"Even robbers have their principles."
However, those who steal goods are petty thieves,

Observing how Xú Wēn stole the state,

He entrusted financial and tax matters to the Zhījì official Luò Zhīxiáng.
The Zhījì official

"Yán and Luò."

The barbarians observe the state's strength to decide their coming and going.

on Rényín,

the seventh month,
