By this time, Líng and Yán were once again combined into a single military district.
22. The Emperor sent a close attendant to admonish Liú Zhījùn, saying:
"I have treated you very generously;
why have you suddenly betrayed me?"
He replied:
"I have not betrayed your virtue,
but I fear being exterminated along with my clan like Wáng Chóngshī."
The Emperor again sent someone to tell him:
"Liú Hàn said that Chóngshī secretly allied with Bīn and Qí;
I now regret it, but it is too late.
Hàn's death is insufficient to atone for his crime."
Zhījùn did not reply.
On Gēngxū,
an edict was issued stripping Zhījùn of his offices and ranks,
and appointing Yáng Shīhòu, military governor of Shānnán Dōngdào, as commander of the western front campaign to suppress him,
leading Liú Xún, the commander of the imperial guard cavalry and infantry, and others to attack him.
On Xīnhài,
the Emperor departed from Luòyáng.
Liú Xún arrived east of Tóngguān,
captured thirty of Liú Zhījùn's ambush soldiers, including Lìn Rúhǎi,
released them, and had them act as guides.
After Liú Zhījùn captured Tóngguān,
he placed ambush troops along the roads outside the pass to keep watch;
Liú Xún instead captured and used them as guides.
Shǐ Zhào said: Lìn
is a surname.
Their ancestor was Kāng, a great-great-grandson of the Hán nobleman Xiànzǐ,
who was enfeoffed at Lìn,
and thus took it as his surname.
After lingering for several days,
they finally reached the pass,
and the pass officials let them in.
Rúhǎi and the others followed,
and the pass officials, unaware they had been captured,
also let them in.
Xún's troops took advantage of the open gate and charged straight in,
thus capturing Tóngguān.
They pursued and caught up with Zhīhuàn,
and captured him.
On Guǐchǒu,
the Emperor arrived in Shǎn.
23. Wáng Xíngsī and others, the cavalry commanders of Dānzhōu, rebelled.
Prefect Sòng Zhīhuì fled and returned.
24. The Emperor sent Liú Zhījùn's nephew Sìyè with an edict to Tóngzhōu to summon and admonish Zhījùn.
Zhījùn wanted to go lightly mounted to the imperial presence to apologize for his crime,
but his younger brother Zhīyǎn stopped him.
When Yáng Shīhòu and others reached Huàzhōu,
Zhījùn's general Niè Shǎng opened the gates and surrendered.
When Zhījùn heard that Tóngguān was lost,
and the imperial army was approaching,
he panicked and lost his composure.
On Yǐmǎo,
he fled with his entire clan to Qí.
When Yáng Shīhòu reached Cháng'ān,
Qí troops were already occupying the city.
Shīhòu led a surprise force along the southern mountains and advanced rapidly,
entering through the west gate,
and thus captured the city.
On Gēngshēn,
Liú Xún was appointed acting military governor of Yòuguó.
The Prince of Qí treated Liú Zhījùn with great courtesy,
appointing him as Secretariat Director.
However, the territory was narrow,
and there was no military district to place him in,
so he was merely given a generous salary.
A hoofprint cannot hold a foot-long carp.
This laid the groundwork for Liú Zhījùn fleeing to Shǔ.
25. Liú Shǒuguāng sent an envoy to present a memorial reporting victory,
and also said:
"Once the matters of Cāng and Dé are concluded,
I will sweep away the bandits of Bìng for Your Majesty."
He also sent a letter to the Prince of Jìn,
saying he wished to join him in destroying the false Liáng.
Liú Shǒuguāng vacillated between Liáng and Jìn,
thinking himself clever,
not realizing this was precisely what would hasten his destruction.
The Military Governor of Fǔzhōu, Wēi Quánfèng, proclaimed himself the Jiedushi of Zhènnán,
leading troops from Fǔ, Xìn, Yuán, and Jí, claiming a force of one hundred thousand, to attack Hóngzhōu.
The Táng had established the Zhènnán Army in Hóngzhōu,
and Fǔ, Xìn, Yuán, and Jí were all under its jurisdiction.
Wēi Quánfèng proclaimed himself Jiedushi,
raised troops to attack Hóngzhōu,
intending to seize it for himself.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Fǔzhōu is 209 lǐ northwest to Hóngzhōu.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ".
The officials and officers were all afraid.
The Jiedushi Liú Wēi secretly sent an envoy to report the emergency to Guǎnglíng,
while daily summoning his subordinates for banquets and drinking.
Wēi Quánfèng heard of this,
encamped at Xiàngyá Tán,
and did not dare to advance.
Xiàngyá Tán is located northeast of Jīnxī County in Fǔzhōu.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, dispatched the Commander Yuàn Gōng
Yuàn is
a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn records
that in Qí there was a senior official named Yuàn Héjì.
Gōng,
is pronounced Mòbēi.
Gōng,
was from Càizhōu;
Yànzhāng,
was the elder brother of Gān
Péng Gān appears in scroll 265, in the third year of the Tiānyòu era of Emperor Zhāoxuān of Táng.
Xú Wēn asked Yán Kěqiú about generals,
and Kěqiú recommended Zhōu Běn.
He then appointed Zhōu Běn as the Commander of the Southwest Front Campaign to Subdue and Reinforce,
leading seven thousand troops to rescue Gāo'ān.
Zhōu Běn had previously attacked Sūzhōu without success,
as seen in the events of the fourth month above.
Yán Kěqiú went to his bedroom and forced him to get up.
Zhōu Běn said:
"In the Sūzhōu campaign,
the enemy could not defeat me,
but the commanding general lacked sufficient authority.
Now if I am to be employed,
I hope there will be no deputy appointed."
Yán Kěqiú agreed.
Zhōu Běn said:
"The men of Chǔ are merely providing support for Wēi Quánfèng,
they do not intend to capture Gāo'ān.
If I defeat Wēi Quánfèng,
the relief troops will certainly withdraw."
Relief troops,
refers to the troops besieging Gāo'ān.
Withdraw,
is pronounced according to Xuān.
Passing through Hóngzhōu,
Liú Wēi wanted to feast the army,
but Zhōu Běn refused to stay.
Someone said:
"Wēi Quánfèng's troops are strong,
you should observe the situation before advancing."
Zhōu Běn said:
"The enemy outnumbers us ten to one,
if our troops hear of this they will certainly be afraid,
it is better to take advantage of their sharp morale and use it."
27 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Liú Shǒuguāng was appointed King of Yān.
28 Liáng troops captured Dānzhōu,
and captured Wáng Xíngsī.
29 The Prefect of Shāngzhōu, Lǐ Chóu, drove the officials and people westward,
intending to flee to Shǔ.
Examination of discrepancies: The Xuē Shǐ states:
"Chóu abandoned the commandery and fled west,
the local officers and officials appointed the capital officer Liú Wén to temporarily administer the prefecture."
The Ōuyáng Shǐ states:
"There was a mutiny in Shāngzhōu,
they expelled their Prefect Lǐ Chóu,
Chóu fled to Qí."
The Shílù states:
"On the bǐngyín day,
Shǎnzhōu reported that the Prefect of Shāngzhōu, Lǐ Chóu, had abandoned the commandery and fled into the mountains."
It also states:
"The officers and officials of Shāngzhōu, because Chóu had driven and plundered the officials and commoners in his westward flight,
pursued and beheaded them all,
temporarily ordered the capital officer Liú Wén to administer the prefecture."
We now follow this.
30 On the gēngwǔ day,
the Yòuguó Army was renamed Yǒngpíng.
In the first year of Kāipíng, the Yòuguó Army was moved to Cháng'ān,
now it was renamed Yǒngpíng.
31 Hé dōng troops invaded Jìnzhōu,
plundering as far as Yáocí before withdrawing.
Yáo's capital was Píngyáng,
there is a shrine on the eastern plain ten lǐ east of Fénchéng.
Píngyáng,
in Táng times was Línfén County,
the seat of Jìnzhōu.
32 On the guǐyǒu day,
the Emperor departed from Shǎnzhōu;
on the yǐhài day,
he arrived at Luòyáng,
and fell ill.
33 Earlier,
the Emperor had summoned the Jiedushi of Shānnán Dōngdào, Yáng Shīhòu,
intending to have him supervise the generals in attacking Lùzhōu,
and appointed the former Liúhòu of Yǎnhǎi, Wáng Bān, as Liúhòu,
to guard Xiāngzhōu.
Examination of discrepancies: The Xuē Shǐ writes
"Wáng ⿰王玉",
now we follow the Shílù.
He should have been prepared,
but Wáng Bān, relying on having strong warriors around him,
did not take it seriously,
and often publicly humiliated them.
On the wùyín day,
they requested to be stationed on the western border,
that night,
they mutinied,
killed Wáng Bān,
and promoted the Commander Yōngqiū Liú ⿰王巳 as Liúhòu;
⿰王巳 pretended to comply,
the next day,
together with Commander Wáng Yánshùn, fled to where the Emperor was.
Examination of discrepancies: The Míngzōng Shílù by Yáo Yǐ and the Xuē Shǐ biography of ⿰王巳 both say:
"The next day he received congratulations,
held a feast for the troops in the yáting,
concealed armed men under the curtains,
and in the middle of the feast beheaded all the mutinous generals and reported it,
and for his merit was made Prefect of Fùzhōu."
According to the Liángzǔ Shílù:
"On the dīngyǒu day of the eighth month, ⿰王巳 and Wáng Yánshùn were granted gifts,
because they had escaped the rebels' calamity and come over."
The Biānyílù edict beheading Lǐ Hóng and others states:
"At first they supported Liú ⿰王巳,
but then fled and returned to the light."
If ⿰王巳 had beheaded the mutinous generals the next day,
how could it be that Xiāngzhōu was not recovered until the ninth month!
It seems ⿰王巳 escaped and returned to the court,
and after Liáng perished and he entered Táng,
falsely claimed to have beheaded the mutinous generals to boast,
and the historians, unable to investigate,
recorded it accordingly.
They submitted to Shǔ.
Not long after,
the Prefect of Fángzhōu, Yáng Qián, also rebelled and submitted to Shǔ.
34 Wēi Quánfèng was at Xiàngyá Tán,
with his camp fences bordering the stream,
stretching for several tens of lǐ.
On the gēngchén day,
Zhōu Běn deployed his formations across the stream,
first sending weak troops to test the enemy;
Wēi Quánfèng's troops forded the stream to pursue them,
Zhōu Běn attacked when they were halfway across,
unleashing his troops to strike,
Wēi Quánfèng's troops were utterly routed,
trampling each other,
many drowning in the water,
Zhōu Běn sent troops to cut off their retreat,
and captured Wēi Quánfèng and five thousand officers and soldiers.
Riding the victory, he captured Yuánzhōu,
seizing the Prefect Péng Yànzhāng,
and attacked Jízhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yuánzhōu is 315 lǐ south to Jízhōu.
The Prefect of Xìnzhōu, Wēi Zǎichàng, requested to surrender,
in the second year of the Zhōnghé era of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng,
Wēi Quánfèng occupied Fǔzhōu,
Zǎichàng occupied Xìnzhōu,
and by now both were gone.
The Campaign Commander Mǐ Zhìchéng and Commandant Lǚ Shīzào and others defeated Yuàn Gōng at Shànggāo.
The Prefect of Jízhōu, Péng Gān, led several thousand followers and fled to Chǔ.
In the third year of the Tiānyòu era of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng, Péng Gān submitted to Chǔ.
He married his daughter to Mǎ Xīfàn.
Huáinán appointed the Left Vanguard Commander Zhāng Jǐngsī to administer Xìnzhōu,
and dispatched the Campaign Deputy Commander Gǔ Yán with five thousand troops to escort him.
Gǔ,
is a surname.
In early Táng there was Gǔ Yí.
He fled to Wúyuè,
the King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, appointed Zǎichàng as Deputy Jiedushi of Huáinán,
and changed his surname to Yuán.
The Ōu Shǐ Shíguó Shìjiā states: Qián Liú disliked the surname Wēi,
and changed it to Yuán.
Change,
is pronounced Gōnghéng.
The Prince of Hóngnóng, because he had once shown kindness to Wǔzhōng Wáng,
released him,
and provided him with generous support.
Yáng Xíngmì was posthumously titled Wǔzhōng.
At that time, the Huáinán generals discussed:
"In the past, when the former king attacked Zhào Huáng,
Wēi Quánfèng repeatedly supplied our army."
So they released him.
The Prefect of Qiánzhōu, Lú Guāngchóu, submitted the prefecture to Huáinán.
Thus, the lands of Jiāngxī all entered the possession of the Yáng clan.
Lú Guāngchóu also sent an envoy to submit to Liáng.
On the Jia Yin day (the 35th day),
the Emperor's illness slightly improved,
and he began to resume holding court sessions.
He had been bedridden since the Yi Hai day in the seventh month,
making a total of forty days until now.
(Note: The character "朝" (cháo) is pronounced with the rising tone;
the same applies below.)
36. The Zhenguó Jiedushi Shǐ Kāng Huáizhēn was appointed as the Deputy Pacification Commissioner of the Western Route Campaign Headquarters.
37. The Shu ruler ordered the Crown Prince, Zōng Yì, to oversee the Six Armies,
established the Yǒnghé Prefecture,
and carefully selected court officials to serve as his subordinates.
38. On the Xīn Yǒu day,
Jūnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Jìngfāng reported the capture of Fángzhōu.
(Yáng Qián had previously surrendered Fángzhōu to Shu; see above.)
The Jiǔ Yù Zhì states: Jūnzhōu is 215 li south to Fángzhōu.
39. The King of Qí intended to send Liú Zhījùn to lead troops to attack Língzhōu and Xiàzhōu,
and also arranged with the King of Jìn to attack Jìnzhōu and Jiàngzhōu.
The King of Jìn led his troops southward,
first dispatching Zhōu Déwēi and others to lead troops out of Yīndì Pass to attack Jìnzhōu.
The Cìshǐ, Biān Jìwēi, defended with all his might.
The Jìn troops dug tunnels,
causing a section of the city wall over twenty paces long to collapse.
The defenders fought desperately to resist,
and by the next morning, the wall had been repaired.
An edict ordered Yáng Shīhòu to lead troops to rescue Jìnzhōu.
Zhōu Déwēi used cavalry to block the strategic pass at Méng Kēng.
(Méng Kēng is east of the Fén River,
stretching over 300 li from east to west,
with no accessible paths.)
Yáng Shīhòu advanced to Jìnzhōu,
and the Jìn troops lifted the siege and fled.
(Textual analysis: The Shílù states:
"They killed and captured enemy generals such as Xiāo Wàntōng,
and the enemy thus abandoned their camps and fled."
The Zhuāngzōng Shílù states:
"The Biàn army reached Méng Kēng,
Zhōu Déwēi engaged them in battle,
defeated them,
beheaded two hundred,
and Yáng Shīhòu retreated to Jiàngzhōu.
In this battle,
the minor general Xiāo Wàntōng died in combat,
Yáng Shīhòu advanced his camp to Píngyáng,
and Zhōu Déwēi withdrew his troops."
Each army claimed victory,
but since Xiāo Wàntōng was killed,
why would Yáng Shīhòu willingly retreat to Jiàngzhōu?
If he retreated after defeat,
how could he then advance his camp to Píngyáng?
If Zhōu Déwēi was victorious,
why would he simply withdraw his troops?
It is likely that the Jìn army was actually defeated and fled,
and the Zhuāngzōng Shílù falsely claimed otherwise.)
40. Lǐ Hóng raided Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng sent his general Ní Kěfú to defeat him.
An edict ordered the Infantry and Cavalry Commander-in-Chief Chén Huī to lead troops to join forces with the Jīngnán army to attack Lǐ Hóng.
41. The Shu ruler appointed the Censor-in-Chief Wáng Kǎi as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
42. Chén Huī's army reached Xiāngzhōu.
Lǐ Hóng engaged them in battle,
was severely defeated,
and Wáng Qiú died.
In the ninth month,
on the Dīng Yǒu day,
they captured the city,
beheaded a thousand rebel soldiers,
captured Lǐ Hóng and Yáng Qián, and sent them to Luòyáng,
where they were executed.
43. On the Dīng Wèi day,
Bǎoyì Jiedushi Shǐ Wáng Tán was appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of the Eastern Route Campaign Headquarters for Lùzhōu.
44. Liú Shǒuguāng reported that he had sent his son, the Central Army Cavalry Commander Jìwēi, to pacify the officials and people of Cāngzhōu.
On the Wù Shēn day,
Jìwēi was appointed as the Acting Military Governor of Yìchāng.
45. On the Xīn Hài day,
the Shìzhōng Hán Jiàn was dismissed from his post and made Tàibǎo,
while the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Yáng Shè was dismissed and returned to his original post.
The Tàicháng Qīng Zhào Guāngféng was appointed as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and the Hànlín Fèngzhǐ and Vice Minister of Works Dù Xiǎo was appointed as Vice Minister of Revenue,
both concurrently serving as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
(Liáng changed the title Hànlín Chéngzhǐ to Hànlín Fèngzhǐ
to avoid the taboo character "Chéng"
due to the temple name taboo.
However,
the character "Chéng"
and the character "Chéng"
have different pronunciations and meanings.)
(Dù Xiǎo was the son of Dù Ràngnéng.
Dù Ràngnéng died for the state; see Volume 259, the second year of the Jǐngfú era of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng.)
46. Huáinán sent an envoy, Zhāng Zhīyuǎn, to establish friendly relations with Fújiàn.
Zhāng Zhīyuǎn was arrogant and disrespectful,
so the King of Mǐn, Shěnzhī, executed him
and submitted his letter to the court.
(Note: The character "上" (shàng) is pronounced with the falling-rising tone.)
Shěnzhī was frugal and modest,
often wearing hemp shoes.
His official residence was humble and dilapidated,
and he never had it renovated.
He implemented lenient punishments and light taxes,
resulting in public and private prosperity,
and peace within his territory.
Every year, he sent tribute via the sea route from Dēngzhōu and Láizhōu,
with four or five out of ten ships sinking.
(To send tribute from Fújiàn to Dàliáng by land, one would travel via Qúzhōu and Xìnzhōu, then cross the river at the borders of Ráozhōu and Chízhōu,
cross the Huái River at Shūzhōu, Lúzhōu, and Shòuzhōu,
and then enter Liáng territory.
However, the areas from Xìnzhōu and Ráozhōu to Lúzhōu and Shòuzhōu were all under Yáng's control,
and since Zhū and Yáng were sworn enemies,
passage could not be granted.
Therefore, tribute was sent by sea.
The route went from the Fúzhōu Sea past the Wēnzhōu Sea,
then via the Tāizhōu Sea past Tiānmén Mountain into the Xiàngshān Sea of Míngzhōu,
past Cénjiāng,
skirting Liègǎng,
and heading northeast across the open sea to the shores of Dēngzhōu and Láizhōu.
The winds and waves were extremely perilous,
hence the high number of shipwrecks.)
47. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Jiǎ Zǐ day,
the Shu Director of Astrology Hú Xiùlín presented the Yǒngchāng Calendar,
which was put into use.
(Ōuyáng Xiū said: The Yǒngchāng Calendar was only used in that state;
it is now lost
and no longer seen.)
48. The Húzhōu Cìshǐ Gāo Lǐ was cruel and ruthless.
Once, he summoned the prefectural officials and asked:
"I want to kill all the common people.
Is that possible?"
An official replied:
"If so,
where will the taxes and levies come from?
You should select those who can be killed and kill them."
At the time, Gāo Lǐ had conscripted the people as soldiers.
When some complained of grievances,
Gāo Lǐ gathered all the militia at the Kāiyuán Temple
(Kāiyuán Temples still exist in various prefectures today,
as they were established during the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty)
and killed them upon entry.
More than half died.
Those outside realized what was happening
and started a fire in rebellion.
Gāo Lǐ closed the city gates and conducted a thorough search,
killing three thousand people in total.
The King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, wanted to execute him.
On the Wù Chén day,
Gāo Lǐ rebelled and surrendered Húzhōu to Huáinán.
(The Gāo Lǐ father and son, with their single prefecture,
were situated between the territories of Qián and Yáng,
and had long survived by attaching themselves to both sides.
Now that they exclusively attached themselves to Huáinán,
the troops of the Qián family would soon arrive.
The Jiǔ Yù Zhì states: Línhéng Town is in Rénhé County of Hángzhōu.
Note: Rénhé County was originally Qiántáng County.
In the early Tàipíng Xīngguó era of the Sòng dynasty, Qiántáng County was renamed Rénhé.
This was likely because the place was originally named Yìhé,
and to avoid the taboo of the Emperor Tàizōng's former princely title,
it was renamed Rénhé.)
49. In the eleventh month,
on the Jiǎ Wǔ day,
the Emperor performed a thanksgiving ceremony at the Yuánqiū Altar.
(A thanksgiving ceremony is an offering to Heaven to express gratitude for obtaining the empire.
According to Ōuyáng's history,
on this day,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
Xú Wútǎng commented: It is not called a ceremony at the southern suburb,
as the ritual was somewhat simpler compared to the southern suburb ceremony.)
On the Wù Xū day,
a general amnesty was declared.
The Prince of Yè, Luó Shàowēi, suffered from a wind-paralysis illness,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Wèi is an old and important garrison,
with many external troops.
I wish for a meritorious and senior minister to garrison it,
and I beg to retire and return home."
The Emperor heard this,
and, placing his hand on the table, was visibly moved.
Placing his hand on the table and being visibly moved
was not out of pity for Luó Shàowēi's illness.
Wèibó was a major garrison,
hereditary for one hundred and fifty years.
Suddenly, he was relinquishing the garrison and requesting a replacement,
which was beyond all expectations.
Joy overflowed within him,
and he unconsciously placed his hand on the table and showed emotion.
On the jǐhài day,
he appointed his son, Zhōuhàn, as Deputy Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng,
to administer the prefectural affairs.
He said to the envoy:
"Hurry back and tell your lord:
'Eat heartily for my sake!
If the unspeakable should occur,
(meaning death).
I am now having Zhōuhàn take charge of the military government,
still hoping that you will recover.'"
Examination of discrepancies says: The Biographies of Liáng Meritorious Officials states:
"Since the court's founding,
for major matters, envoys were always sent down to consult.
Shàowēi had strategic foresight,
and would also send swift letters offering advice and alternatives.
Sometimes, when their messages met midway,
their ideas coincided in five or six out of ten cases.
Tàizǔ sighed and said: 'Only one person exhausts his loyalty and strength.'"
It also says:
"He had three sons: the eldest, Tíngguī,
was Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries,
married Princess Ānyáng,
and also married Princess Jīnhuá,
but died early;
the second, Zhōuhàn,
was reinstated as General of Cloud-like Majesty,
served as Acting Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng,
soon became Acting Minister of Works,
and was formally appointed Military Commissioner of Wèibó,
also dying early;
the third was named Zhōujìng."
The Old History of the Five Dynasties also agrees.
The Veritable Records state:
"On the jǐhài day,
Luó Tíngguī, Director of the Bureau of Gates, was appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Wèibó,
to administer prefectural affairs,
and his name was changed to Zhōuhàn.
At that time, Prince Shàowēi of Yè's illness was worsening daily,
and, concerned about the aftermath,
he thus petitioned for this."
The Biography of Zhuāngzōng states:
"When Shàowēi died,
Wēn had his son Zhōuhàn succeed to the administration."
The Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng state:
"Shàowēi heavily increased taxes and levies,
emptying the government treasury to serve Wēn.
If there was the slightest transgression or offense,
Wēn would immediately send people to insult and humiliate him.
Shàowēi, feeling ashamed and humiliated,
regretted his plan of weakening himself,
and secretly gathered troops and purchased horses,
covertly harboring the intention to overthrow Wēn,
while bribing Wēn even more lavishly.
Wēn found his obsequious service strange,
and, suspecting he harbored treacherous plots but being unable to detect them,
bestowed upon Shàowēi several singing girls and concubines,
all of whom received his favor and affection.
Before half a year had passed,
Wēn summoned them back,
and through this learned of his secret affairs."
This is internally contradictory.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties also says:
"In the summer of the fourth year of Kāipíng,
an edict ordered Princess Jīnhuá to leave home and become a nun,
residing at the Xuánjìng Temple in Sòng Prefecture.
This was because Tàizǔ extended favor to the Luó family,
allowing her to maintain her widow's chastity to the end."

To let his wickedness fully ripen.

expanding it.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Shǔ's Menxià Shìláng and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Wáng Kǎi was dismissed and made Minister of War.
The Emperor's eldest son, Chēnwáng Yǒuyù, died early.
The next was his adopted son, Bówáng Yǒuwén.
Yǒuwén's original surname was Kāng,
and his given name was Qín.
He often remained in the eastern capital,
also serving as Jiànchāng Gōngshǐ.
The Emperor made his old residence in Dàliáng the Jiànchāng Palace.
His mother was a courtesan from Bózhōu,
and he served as Zuǒyòu Kòngquè Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
Next was Jūnwáng Yǒuzhēn,
who served as Dōngdū Mǎbù Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ.
初，
元貞张皇后严整多智，
帝敬惮之。
后殂，
张后殂于唐昭宗天祐元年。
诸子虽在外，
常征其妇入侍，
帝往往乱之。
友文妇王氏色美，
帝尤宠之，
虽未以友文为太子，
帝意常属之。
友珪心不平。
友珪尝有过，
帝挞之，
友珪益不自安。
帝疾甚，
命王氏召友文于东都，
欲与之诀，
且付以后事。
友珪妇张氏亦朝夕侍帝侧，
知之，
密告友珪曰：
“大家以传国宝付王氏怀往东都，
吾属死无日矣。”
夫妇相泣。
左右或说之曰：
“事急计生，
何不改图，
时不可失！”
古人有言曰：
“淫而不父，
必有子祸。”
岂不信哉！
说，
式芮翻。
六月，
丁丑朔，
帝命敬翔出友珪为莱州刺史，
即令之官。
已宣旨，
未行敕。
敬翔时为宣政使，
故使之行敕。
翔佐帝有年矣，
军国大谋无不预，
随事弥缝，
转帝凶暴之气以成，
功亦不为小。
寝疾弥留而出友珪于外，
使翔能为之谋，
则必有以处友珪，
而帝免剚刃之祸。
颠而不扶，
焉用彼相哉！
友珪益恐。
戊寅，
友珪易服微行入左龙虎军，
见统军韩勍，
以情告之。
勍亦见功臣宿将多以小过被诛，
惧不自保，
遂相与合谋。
臣子俱逆，
亦上之人有以致之也。
被，
皮义翻。
伏于禁中，
梁以侍卫亲军为控鹤军。
至寝殿，
侍疾者皆散走。
帝惊起，
问：
“反者为谁？”
友珪曰：
“非他人也。”
帝曰：
“我固疑此贼，
恨不早杀之。
汝悖逆如此，
天地岂容汝乎！”
友珪曰：
“老贼万段！”
友珪仆夫冯廷谔刺帝腹，
刃出于背。
友珪自以败毡裹之，
瘗于寝殿，
年六十一。
瘗，
于计翻。
遣供奉官丁昭浦驰诣东都，
命均王友贞杀友文。
己卯，
矫诏称：
“博王友文谋逆，
遣兵突入殿中，
赖郢王友珪忠孝，
将兵诛之，
保全朕躬。
然疾因震惊，
弥致危殆，
宜令友珪权主军国之务。”
韩勍为友珪谋，
多出府库金帛赐诸军及百官以取悦。
辛巳，
丁昭溥还，
闻友文已死，
乃发丧，
宣遗制，
友珪即皇帝位。
时朝廷新有内难，
中外人情恟恟。
许州军士更相告变，
匡国节度使韩建皆不之省，
亦不为备；
丙申，
马步都指挥使张厚作乱，
杀建，
考异曰：庄宗实录，
九月建遇害。
今从薛史。
甲辰，
以厚为陈州刺史。
七月，
丁未，
大赦。
27天雄节度使罗周翰幼弱，
军府事皆决于牙内都指挥使潘晏；
北面都招讨使、宣义节度使杨师厚军于魏州，
久欲图之，
惮太祖威严，
不敢发。
至是，
师厚馆于铜台驿，
因铜雀台以名驿。
然铜雀台在邺，
不在魏州。
执而杀之，
引兵入牙城，
据位视事。
壬子，
制以师厚为天雄节度使，
考异曰：梁功臣列传杨师厚传云：
“太祖初弃天下，
郡府乘间为乱甚众。
魏之衙内都指挥使潘晏与大将臧延范、赵训将谋反变；
有密告者，
师厚布兵擒捕，
斩之。
七月除魏博节度使。”
薛史师厚传略同。
今从庄宗列传朱友珪传及庄宗实录。
唐僖宗文德元年，
罗弘信得魏博，
传子至孙而亡。
28以侍卫诸军使韩勍领匡国节度使。
韩勍以同逆领节。
29甲寅，
加吴越王镠尚父。
30甲子，
以均王友贞为开封尹、东都留守。
31蜀太子元坦更名元膺。
宗懿更名元坦，
见上卷开平四年。
按欧史，
蜀主建时得铜牌子于什仿县，
有文二十余字，
建以为符谶，
因取之以名诸子，
故又更名元膺。
更，
工衡翻。
32丙寅，
废建昌宫使，
以河南尹张宗奭为国计使，
凡天下金谷旧隶建昌宫者悉主之。
梁祖受禅，
以博王友文领建昌宫使，
专领金谷。
友珪既杀友文，
故废之而置国计使。
33八月，
龙骧军三千人戍怀州者，
戍怀州所以备晋人自上党下太行以窥洛阳。
所过剽掠；
戊子，
遣东京马步军都指挥使霍彦威、左耀武指挥使杜晏球讨之，
庚寅，
击破乱军，
执其都将刘重遇于鄢陵，
甲午，
斩之。
为友贞以龙骧军起义诛友珪张本。
34 After Yǐngwáng Zhū Yǒuguī usurped the throne,
many of the veteran generals were indignant.
Although he bestowed excessive favors and courtesies upon them,
they remained displeased in the end.
When the envoy announcing the mourning arrived at Hézhōng,
Hùguó Jiedushi, Jìwáng Zhū Yǒuqiān, wept and said:
"The late emperor spent decades establishing the foundation of our state.
The recent incident that arose within the palace,
its reputation is exceedingly foul.
I, occupying a position as a frontier military governor,
feel deeply ashamed in my heart."
Zhū Yǒuqiān was originally Zhū Jiǎn, a Yájiàng officer in Shǎnzhōu.
At the end of the Táng, he attached himself to Zhū Wēn,
who bestowed upon him the name Yǒuqiān,
ranking him among his own sons.
Therefore, he used this to denounce Yǒuguī's crime of regicide and rebellion.
Judging by ancient laws,
when a minister kills his sovereign,
or a son kills his father,
all those in office may kill them without pardon.
Thus, regarding Yǒuguī's crime,
all who are ministers or sons of Liáng are entitled to execute him.
Yǒuguī defended himself with an imperial edict,
and also summoned Yǒuqiān.
Yǒuqiān said to the envoy:
"Who is it that has been established?
The late emperor's passing was not according to proper principle.
I shall go to Luòyáng to demand accountability,
what summons is there to heed!"
On Wùxū,
[Yǒuguī] appointed the commander of the Imperial Guard armies, Hán Qíng, as the Western Front Campaign Pacification Commissioner,
to oversee the various armies in attacking him.
Yǒuqiān attached Hézhōng to Jìn to seek rescue.
In the ninth month,
on Dīngwèi,
[Yǒuguī] appointed Gǎnhuà Jiedushi Kāng Huáizhēn as the Hézhōng Capital Pacification Commissioner,
and further appointed Hán Qíng as his deputy.
35 Yǒuguī, regarding the Minister of War and Administrator of the Chóngzhèng Academy, Jìng Xiáng,
a trusted confidant of Tàizǔ,
feared he might act against him,
and wanted to relieve him of his inner court position.
Inner court position,
refers to the Administrator of the Chóngzhèng Academy.
On Gēngwǔ,
he appointed Xiáng as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì;
on Rénshēn,
he appointed the Minister of Revenue Lǐ Zhèn to serve as Commissioner of the Chóngzhèng Academy.
Xiáng often claimed illness and did not participate in affairs.
Jìng Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn were both meritorious ministers who assisted the founding of the previous dynasty.
Lǐ Zhèn succeeded Jìng Xiáng in leading the Chóngzhèng Academy Commission,
thus Zhèn shared in Yǒuguī's wickedness.
Although Jìng Xiáng claimed illness and did not participate in affairs,
if judged by the ancient principle of a minister living and dying with his sovereign,
he too could not escape death.
36 Kāng Huáizhēn and others joined forces with Zhōngwǔ Jiedushi Niú Cúnjié, combining fifty thousand troops to camp west of Hézhōng city,
attacking it fiercely.
The Prince of Jìn dispatched his generals Lǐ Cúnshěn, Lǐ Sìgōng, and Lǐ Sì'ēn to lead troops to rescue them,
defeating the Liáng troops at Húbì.
Sì'ēn
was originally a son of the Luò family.
According to the "Biographies of Adopted Sons" in the Oūshǐ,
Sì'ēn's original surname was Luò,
and he was from the Tǔyùhún tribe.
37 When Wú Wǔzhōngwáng fell ill,
Zhōu Yǐn requested to summon Liú Wēi.
The event is recorded in the 265th scroll of the Táng Tiānyòu second year.
This incurred the suspicion of the military headquarters.
The military headquarters,
refers to the Guǎnglíng military headquarters.
Shuài,
is pronounced as suǒ lèi fān.
Xú Wēn was about to take action against him.
Wēi's advisor Huáng Nè persuaded Wēi, saying:
"Although you have been deeply slandered,
in truth, you have committed no offense.
If you go by light boat to have an audience,
then all suspicions will vanish."
Wēi complied.
Táo Yǎ, hearing of Lǐ Yù's defeat,
also became fearful,
and went together with Wēi to Guǎnglíng.
Wēn treated them with great respect,
according to the etiquette used in serving Wǔzhōngwáng,
generously bestowing official titles and ranks.
Yǎ and the others were pleased and submitted,
and from then on, everyone respected Wēn.
Nè
was from Sūzhōu.
Wēn, along with Wēi and Yǎ, led the generals and officials in requesting from Lǐ Yǎn,
to issue an imperial decree appointing the succeeding Prince of Wú, Yáng Lóngyǎn, as Grand Preceptor and Prince of Wú.
Lóngyǎn's succession as Prince of Wú
was an appointment made by Lǐ Màozhēn under imperial decree.
Yáng Xíngmì, because Lǐ Yǎn came as an envoy, honored him by accepting his imperial decree.
Xú Wēn and others, following this precedent, requested from Yǎn.
Shuài,
is read as shuài.
The Huáinán Xíngjūn Sīmǎ remained as before.
Wēn sent Wēi and Yǎ back to their garrisons.
Liú Wēi garrisoned Hóngzhōu,
Táo Yǎ garrisoned Shèzhōu.
Xú Wēn served Wēi and Yǎ as he had served Yáng Xíngmì.
To honor them and not dare forget the old ways,
he could force himself to act against his feelings to do this;
as for sending Wēi and Yǎ back to their garrisons,
not only did contemporaries admire him for it,
but Wēi and Yǎ were also convinced in their hearts.
Since ancient times,
the capacity of heroes has naturally differed,
but in following their capacity to handle the affairs of their time, it is the same.
Those skilled in observing history should not overlook this!
38 On Xīnsì,
Shǔ changed the name of Jiànnán Dōngchuān to Wǔdé Jūn.
39 Zhū Yǒuqiān again urgently appealed to Jìn for help.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Prince of Jìn personally led his army westward from Zélù,
not southward from Tàiyuán through Fén and Jìn.
Jiàng,
is pronounced jí liàng fān.
Sòng Bái said: Xiè County,
an old Hàn county,
was changed to Běixiè County in the Later Wèi.
According to this, the previous Xiè County was within the boundaries of Línjìn County.
In the Suí, the 16th year of the Kāihuáng era, Xiè County was established here.
In the 2nd year of the Dàyè era, it was abolished.
In the 9th year, Yúxiāng County was moved from the old Suíhuà city to the site of the abolished county.
In the Táng, the 1st year of the Wǔdé era, Yúxiāng County was changed to Xiè County,
and Yúxiāng County was separately established within the boundaries of Púzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Xiè is 95 lǐ east of Púzhōu,
Yúxiāng is 60 lǐ east of Púzhōu.
Xiè,
is pronounced hù mǎi fān.
Examination of discrepancies: The Zhuāngzōng Tónghuāng 4th year Veritable Records, Zhuāngzōng Biographies, Xuēshǐ, and Táng Yúlù's biography of Zhū Yǒuqiān all state
"encountered the Biàn army at Píngyáng,
and greatly defeated them."
Now following the Zhuāngzōng Tiānyòu 9th year Veritable Records.
They beheaded a thousand,
pursued them to the Báijìng Ridge and then returned.
Báijìng Ridge is east of Ānyì County in Hézhōng.
They retreated to defend Shǎnzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Hézhōng is 238 lǐ south to Shǎnzhōu.
Shǎn,
is pronounced shī rǎn fān.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Yīshì County is 95 lǐ northeast of Hézhōng Prefecture.
They removed their military equipment,
went to the Prince of Jìn's tent,
and bowed to him as an uncle.
The Prince of Jìn held a banquet at night with music,
and Yǒuqiān became heavily intoxicated.
The Prince of Jìn had him stay overnight in the tent,
Yǒuqiān slept peacefully,
snoring naturally and at ease.
Zhū Yǒuqiān used this to show he entrusted his heart to the Prince of Jìn,
with no suspicion or estrangement between them.
Hān,
is pronounced xià dàn fān.
40 Yáng Shīhòu, having gained the troops of Wèibó,
and also serving as the overall Campaign Pacification Commissioner,
with many of the elite imperial guard troops under his command,
and able to mobilize the troops of various garrisons,
his power and influence were very great.
He looked down upon Yǐngwáng Yǒuguī,
and in handling matters, often acted arbitrarily without regard.
Yǒuguī was troubled by this,
and issued an edict summoning him,
saying
"there are military matters concerning the northern frontier,
which I wish to discuss with you in person."
As Shīhòu was about to depart,
his confidants all advised him:
"If you go, the outcome will be unpredictable."
Shīhòu said:
"I know his character,
even if I go,
what can he do to me!"
Then he led over ten thousand elite troops,
crossed the river and headed for Luòyáng.
Yǒuguī was greatly afraid.
On Dīnghài,
he arrived at the capital gate.
The outer city gate is called the capital gate.
He entered for an audience with over ten men,
Yǒuguī was pleased,
using sweet words and humble speech to delight him,
and bestowed upon him an immense sum.
On Guǐsì,
he sent him back.
41 In the eleventh month,
the Zhào general Wáng Démíng led thirty thousand troops to raid Wǔchéng.
Wǔchéng,
was the Hàn-era Dōngwǔchéng County,
which belonged to Bèizhōu in the Táng.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 50 lǐ east of the prefecture.
They attacked Zōngchéng,
and captured it.
On Guǐchǒu,
Yáng Shīhòu set an ambush at Tángdiàn,
intercepted and attacked them,
greatly defeating them,
beheading over five thousand.
On the Jia Yin day (42nd),
the Divine Martial, Primordially Sagacious, and Filial Emperor was buried at the Xuān Mausoleum.
The Xuān Mausoleum is located in Yīquē County, Hénán.
Wú's Deputy Military Commissioner of Huáinán, Chén Zhāng, and others led a naval force to attack Yuè Prefecture of Chǔ,
capturing Prefect Yuàn Méi.
In the first year of the Kāipíng era,
Chǔ captured Yuè Prefecture.
In the third year,
Yuàn Méi surrendered to Chǔ.
He was captured by Huáinán at this time.
Méi had surrendered to Chǔ from Jiāngxī,
and Chǔ had him guard Yuè Prefecture.
Zhāng and others advanced to attack Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìchāng sent his general Ní Kěfú to resist them.
Wú, fearing that Chǔ would send troops to rescue Jīngnán,
sent Fǔ Prefecture Prefect Liú Xìn to lead troops from the five prefectures of Jiāng, Fǔ, Yuán, Jí, and Xìn to station at Jí Prefecture,
to provide support for Zhāng.
Stationing at Jí Prefecture was to display a formidable posture,
as if intending to advance and attack Tán and Héng,
in order to tie down Chǔ's troops.
In the twelfth month,
on the Wù Yín day (44th),
Shǔ's Field Army Commander-in-Chief Wáng Zōngfén attacked Wén Prefecture of Qí,
capturing it.
The defending general Lǐ Jìkuí fled.
Wén Prefecture
is the ancient land of Yīnpíng.
General,
read as liàng;
same below.
In this year,
Xí Prefecture's military commander Liú Xùn killed the prefect,
surrendered the prefecture to Jìn,
and the Prince of Jìn appointed him as Prefect of Yíng Prefecture.
Xùn
was from Yǒnghé.
Yǒnghé County belongs to Xí Prefecture.
It was the land of Húzhé County in the Hàn,
and became Yǒnghé County in the Suí.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is one hundred lǐ west of the prefectural seat.
Qián Prefecture's Defense Commissioner Lǐ Yàntú died.
The people of the prefecture supported Tán Quánbō to administer the prefecture's affairs.
He sent an envoy to submit to the central authority.
An edict appointed Quánbō as the Bǎishèng Defense Commissioner and the Qián-Sháo Two Prefectures Military Commissioner and Route Opening Commissioner.
Qián Prefecture previously had a Bǎishèng Command.
Now this was used as the name for the military prefecture.
The "Route Opening Commissioner"
means he was commissioned to open up the roads,
connecting south to Jiāo and Guǎng.
Gāo Jìchāng sent out troops,
claiming to assist Liáng in attacking Jìn,
and attacked Xiāng Prefecture.
Shānnán Dōngdào Military Commissioner Kǒng Qíng defeated him.
From then on, the route for tribute was cut off.
Since Gāo Jìchāng became hostile with Kǒng Qíng,
the route to Liáng was severed,
and he no longer paid tribute.
Defeated,
read as bǔ mài.
He was from Yǎn Prefecture.
Emperor Shàng of Jūnwáng
(personal name Yǒuzhēn,
the third son of Tàizǔ.
Wáng Pǔ's Huìyào says: The fourth son of Tàizǔ,
his mother was Empress Yuánzhēn, née Zhāng.
Upon ascending the throne,
he changed his name to Zhèn,
and later changed it again to Huáng.
I note that Wáng Pǔ calling him the fourth son
includes counting the adopted son, Prince Bó Wáng Yǒuwén.
Third year of Qiánhuà
(Guǐ Yǒu, 913)
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Dīng Sì day (1st),
Jìn's Zhōu Déwēi captured Shùn Prefecture of Yān.
In the fourth year of Zhēnguàn of the Táng, the Turks were pacified,
and their tribes were used to establish the four prefectures of Shùn, Yòu, Huà, and Cháng.
In the sixth year,
Shùn Prefecture's administration was temporarily moved to the Wǔliǔ Garrison south of Yíng Prefecture.
Shěn Kuò said: Thirty lǐ northeast of Yōu Prefecture is the Wàngjīng Post Station.
Going east and slightly north for over ten lǐ, one exits the ancient Great Wall.
After another twenty lǐ, one reaches Zhōngdùn.
Crossing the Sūnhóu River and traveling another twenty lǐ, one reaches Shùn Prefecture.
The land north of it is flat and open,
with thick soil suitable for crops.
Going northeast another seventy lǐ, one reaches Tán Prefecture.
The Jīn's Jiāngyù Tú states: Shùn Prefecture is one hundred fifteen lǐ from Yānjīng.
The Xiōngnú Xūzhī states: Shùn Prefecture is ninety lǐ south of Yānjīng.
The recorded distances vary,
so both are preserved here.
Sòng Bái said: Yōu Prefecture is eighty lǐ northeast to Shùn Prefecture.
The Yuán dynasty's Shùn Prefecture administered Huáiróu and Mìyún counties,
belonging to Dàtóng
[Capital]
2. On the Guǐ Hài day (7th),
Prince Yìng Wáng Yǒuguì performed the ancestral temple rites.
On the Jiǎ Zǐ day (8th),
he performed the suburban sacrifice at the Yuánqiū altar,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Fènglì.
The Kǎoyì says: The Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn states
"on the seventh day".
The Shílù states
"on the Gēng Xū day,
Yǒuguì performed the suburban sacrifice at Yuánqiū,
and changed the era name."
Now we follow the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ.
3. Wú's Chén Zhāng attacked Jīngnán,
but failed to capture it and withdrew.
Jīngnán and Chǔ troops joined forces at the river mouth to intercept him.
The river mouth
is the mouth of the Jīng River.
Withdrew,
read as xuán,
or as usual.
Two hundred ships sailed side by side in a single column.
Passing by at night,
the troops of the two military provinces suddenly came out in pursuit,
but could not catch up.
4. Jìn's Zhōu Déwēi captured Yān's Ānyuǎn Army.
Jì Prefecture's general Chéng Xíngyán and others surrendered to Jìn.
5. Second month,
on the Rén Wǔ day (15th),
Shǔ proclaimed a general amnesty.
6. Prince Yìng Wáng Yǒuguì, having achieved his ambition,
quickly became dissolute and debauched.
Inside and outside, there was anger and resentment.
Although Yǒuguì tried to placate them with gold and silk,
none ultimately sided with him.
Imperial Son-in-Law Zhào Yán,
son of Zhào Chōu
(Zhào Chōu defended Chén Prefecture
and repelled Huáng Cháo with merit,
see the annals of Emperor Xīzōng of Táng).
Yán married Tàizǔ's daughter, Princess Chánglè.
He was Tàizǔ's nephew.
Yuán Xiàngxiān's father, Jìngchū,
married Tàizǔ's younger sister, the Grand Princess Wàn'ān.
Prince Jūn Wáng Yǒuzhēn secretly plotted with them to kill Yǒuguì.
Yán said:
"The success or failure of this matter
lies with the Pacification Commissioner, Lord Yáng.
Yáng Shīhòu held the office of Zhōngshū Lìng
and was the Northern Front Chief Pacification Commissioner,
hence the title.
If we gain his support, our task will be accomplished."
At that time, Liáng's main military forces were all under Yáng Shīhòu's control,
and his prestige and achievements commanded respect from the masses.
Therefore, they wanted to obtain his order to instruct the Imperial Guard.
"Prince Yìng usurped the throne by regicide and patricide.
The people's hopes rest upon Dàliáng (i.e., Yǒuzhēn).
If you, sir, assist in accomplishing this,
it would be an unparalleled achievement."
And they promised five hundred thousand strings of cash to reward the army upon success.
Shīhòu discussed it with his officers,
saying:
"When Prince Yìng committed regicide and patricide,
I could not immediately punish him.
Now the relationship between ruler and subject is already established.
To change plans without cause,
is that acceptable?"
Someone said:
"Prince Yìng personally killed his sovereign and father,
he is a villain.
Prince Jūn raises troops to avenge this wrong,
it is righteous.
Upholding righteousness to punish a villain,
what ruler-subject relationship is there!
If he one day defeats the villain,
how will you, sir, position yourself then?"
Shīhòu said:
"I almost made a mistaken plan."
He then sent his general Wáng Shùnxián to Luòyáng,
to secretly plot with Yuán Xiàngxiān.
He also sent the Pacification Commissioner's Infantry and Cavalry Deputy Commander, Qiáo native Zhū Hànbīn, to station troops at Huá Prefecture as an external response.
Qiáo
was a Hàn dynasty county,
attached to Bó Prefecture in the Táng.
He also secretly finalized the plan with Xiàngxiān.
Yǒuguī dealt with the deserters from the Dragon Soaring Army.
Last year, the Dragon Soaring Army had mutinied in Huáizhōu.
To deal with,
zhí zhī fān.
Those captured were executed along with their clans,
and this continued for over a year.
At that time, some troops of the Dragon Soaring Army were garrisoned in Dàliáng.
Yǒuguī summoned them,
and Prince Jūn took the opportunity to incite their anger, saying:
"The Son of Heaven, because the garrison troops in Huáizhōu rebelled,
is pursuing you all, intending to bury you all alive."

Textual analysis says: The Biographies of Zhuāngzōng, the Biography of Zhū Yǒuzhēn, and the Old History of the Five Dynasties and the New History of the Five Dynasties' Annals of the Last Emperor state:
"The Left and Right Dragon Soaring Armies were both garrisoned in Biàn,
Yǒuzhēn forged an edict from Yǒuguī,
ordering them to return to Luòxià."
The Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng states:
"Yǒuguī, suspicious, summoned them."
According to the Veritable Records of Liáng Tàizǔ:
"On Bǐngxū,
the Eastern Capital reported that the Dragon Soaring Army, in accordance with the edict summoning them to the Western Capital,
was unwilling to advance due to the army's mood."
In reality, it was Yǒuguī who summoned them,
not Yǒuzhēn forging an edict,
he merely incited anger by saying they would be buried alive.
They did not know what to do.
On Bǐngxū,
Prince Jūn memorialized that the Dragon Soaring Army was suspicious and fearful,
and unwilling to advance.
On Wùzǐ,
the officers of the Dragon Soaring Army met with Prince Jūn,
weeping and pleading for a path to survival.
The Prince said:
"The Late Emperor campaigned with you all for over thirty years,
building the royal enterprise.
Now, even the Late Emperor has been assassinated by others,
how can you all escape death!"
He then took out a portrait of Tàizǔ to show them and wept, saying:
"If you can go to Luòyáng yourselves to avenge this shame,
then you can turn calamity into fortune."
The troops all leaped for joy, shouting "Long live!",
and requested weapons.
The Prince provided them.
At dawn on Gēngyín,
Yuán Xiàngxiān and others led several thousand imperial guards to charge into the palace.
Yǒuguī heard of the mutiny,
and with his wife, Lady Zhāng, and Féng Tíng'è, hurried to the base of the northern wall tower,
intending to climb over the city wall.
Realizing he could not escape,
he ordered Tíng'è to first kill his wife,
then kill himself.
Tíng'è also slit his own throat.
The various armies, over a hundred thousand strong, plundered the capital city extensively.
Before the Biàn troops reached Luòyáng,
the various imperial guard armies had already killed Yǒuguī.
The Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Dù Xiǎo, and the Attendant Academician Lǐ Tǐng were both killed by the mutinous soldiers.
The Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi Yú Jīng, and the Xuānzhèngshǐ Lǐ Zhèn were injured.
By late afternoon, order was restored.
Xiàngxiān and Zhào Yán took the imperial seal to Dàliáng to welcome Prince Jūn.
The Prince said:
"Dàliáng is the place where our state founded its enterprise.
Liáng Tàizǔ, starting from the Xuānwǔ military governor, annexed the various towns."
He then ascended the throne at Dàliáng,
and reinstated the reign title as the third year of Qiánhuà.
He posthumously demoted Yǒuguī to commoner status,
and restored the official titles and ranks of Prince Bó Yǒuwén.
On Bǐngshēn,
Jìn's Lǐ Cúnhuī attacked Yān's Tánzhōu,
and the prefect Chén Què surrendered the city.
The Xiongnu Records: Tánzhōu is one hundred and sixty lǐ south to Yānjīng,
and one hundred and ninety lǐ southeast to Jìzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Tánzhōu
is the ancient land of Báitán.
Shǔ's Táng Dàoxí, having been dismissed and returned from Xīngyuán,
was reappointed as the Shūmìshǐ.
The Crown Prince Yuányīng presented a memorial at court detailing Dàoxí's faults and evils.
To detail,
is to enumerate separately.
At the court assembly, he enumerated and listed his faults and evils in the court hall,
hence called a court memorial.
The Shǔ ruler was displeased.
On Gēngzǐ,
he appointed Dàoxí as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In the third month,
on Jiǎchén, the first day of the month,
Jìn's Zhōu Déwēi captured Yān's Lú
[Lú]
On Dīngwèi,
the Emperor changed his name to Huáng;
after a long time,
he changed it again to Zhèn.
On Gēngxū,
Yáng Shīhòu was additionally appointed as Zhōngshūlìng,
enfeoffed as Prince of Yè,
granted an edict that did not use his personal name,
and all matters, great or small, had to be consulted with him before action.
The Emperor sent an envoy to appease and summon Zhū Yǒuqiān;
Yǒuqiān again pledged allegiance,
and used the Liáng reign title.
Last year, Zhū Yǒuqiān had attached himself to Jìn.
Now, although he again pledged allegiance,
in reality, he secretly attached himself to Jìn.
On Bǐngchén,
the Emperor's younger brother Yǒujìng was established as Prince Kāng.
On Yǐchǒu,
the Jìn general Liú Guāngjùn captured Gǔběikǒu.
East of Yànlè County in Tánzhōu, there were two garrison posts: Dōngjūn and Běikǒu.
Běikǒu
is the Chángchéngkǒu.
Shěn Kuò said: Fifty lǐ northeast of Tánzhōu is the Jīngōu Station.
From the station, heading slightly northeast,
the terrain alternates between plains and lowlands,
for over thirty lǐ to the midway station.
Past the station,
winding northward through a gorge,
crossing the Luánshuǐ,
for another thirty-odd lǐ,
hooking and turning to pass through a mountain gap,
this is the so-called Gǔběikǒu.
The Xiongnu Records: Hǔběikǒu is three hundred lǐ south to Yānjīng.
Fifteen lǐ north of Chāngpíng County in Yōuzhōu is the Jūndū Pass,
thirty-five lǐ northwest is the Nàkuǎn Pass,
which is the old Jūyōng Pass.
On Wùchén,
Dài Sīyuǎn, the Liúhòu of Bǎoyì, was appointed as military governor,
to guard Xíngzhōu.
The Táng Zhāoyì Army governed five prefectures: Lù, Zé, Xíng, Míng, and Cí.
At the end of the Táng, due to military conflicts,
Jìn obtained Lùzhōu,
and still used it as the Zhāoyì Army.
From Mèng Fānglì onward until Liáng,
the three prefectures of Xíng, Míng, and Cí were made the Zhāoyì Army,
thus there were two Zhāoyì Armies.
Now, Liáng changed the Xíng, Míng, Cí Zhāoyì Army to the Bǎoyì Army,
and changed the Shǎnzhōu Bǎoyì Army to the Zhènguó Army.
Textual analysis says: The Old History's Biography of Sīyuǎn states:
"During the Zhēnmíng period,
he was the Liúhòu of Xíngzhōu.
When Zhāng Wànjìn killed Liú Jìwēi,
he was ordered to guard it."
According to this, Wànjìn killed Jìwēi earlier.
Now, follow the Basic Annals.
16. The Lord of Yān, Liú Shǒuguāng, ordered his general Yuán Xíngqīn to lead seven thousand cavalry
to pasture horses north of the mountains,
and to recruit soldiers from the northern mountain regions to respond to the Khitan.
Liú Shǒuguāng sought aid from the Khitan,
hence he sent Yuán Xíngqīn to recruit troops north of the mountains to support them,
intending them as external reinforcements.
Lǐ Sìyuán of Jìn divided his forces to subdue the eight armies behind the mountains,
conquering them all.
The Prince of Jìn appointed his younger brother, Lǐ Cúnjǔ, as the governor of Xīnzhōu to oversee them.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Cúnjǔ's subsequent disorder due to arrogance and indolence.
Lǐ Sìyuán advanced to attack Wǔzhōu,
and Gāo Xíngguī surrendered the city.
Upon hearing this,
Yuán Xíngqīn led his troops to attack Xíngguī.
Xíngguī sent his younger brother, Xíngzhōu, as a hostage to the Jìn army to seek rescue.
Lǐ Sìyuán led his forces to rescue him,
and Xíngqīn lifted the siege and withdrew.
Sìyuán and Xíngzhōu pursued him to Guǎngbiān Army.
North of Huáiróng County in Guīzhōu was Guǎngbiān Army,
formerly known as Báiyún City.
Sòng Bái said: Guǎngbiān Army is located 130 lǐ north of Guīzhōu.
The brothers Gāo Xíngzhōu were originally from Diāokē Village in Guǎngbiān Army.
Xíngqīn, exhausted and out of options, surrendered.
Sìyuán admired his bravery and prowess,
and adopted him as his son.
Examination of discrepancies: The Zhuāngzōng Veritable Records
records "Xíngzhōu"
as
"Xíngwēn."
Zhāng Zhāo's Zhōu Tàizǔ Veritable Records states:
"When Yān City was in dire straits,
with soldiers deserting and scattering,
Liú Shǒuguāng summoned Yuán Xíngqīn.
The generals under Xíngqīn believed Shǒuguāng was certain to fall,
and that answering the summons would be pointless.
They thus requested Xíngqīn to become the Yān commander,
declaring himself military governor.
Xíngqīn had no alternative,
and said to the generals: 'Even as commander,
I must return to Yōuzhōu.'
The crowd agreed.
Xíngqīn, concerned that Xíngguī in Wǔzhōu
might pose a future threat,
had someone seize Xíngguī's son in Huáiróng,
binding him and taking him along.
Upon reaching Wǔzhōu,
Xíngqīn said to Xíngguī: 'The officers and soldiers have established me as military governor.
I will take you and your son along,
first secure the military headquarters,
then surrender to Tàiyuán.
If you refuse,
I will surely kill your son.'
Xíngguī replied: 'The king entrusted you with his personal troops,
I would rather die than comply.'
His son tearfully pleaded with Xíngguī.
Xíngguī said to him: 'Lord Yuán is plotting rebellion—
how can we follow him!
This is our farewell.'
Xíngguī defended the city for over a month.
When the city's food ran out,
the soldiers showed signs of starvation.
Xíngguī then gathered the residents and said: 'It is not that I do not cherish the families of the elders,
but unfortunately, the troops lack food.
You may behead me and surrender,
and peace will be restored immediately.'
Xíngguī had governed with benevolence,
and the people wept, saying: 'We are willing to contribute our private grain to supply the army
and defend the city to the death together.'
That night, they lowered his brother Xíngzhōu by rope to serve as a hostage to the Jìn army,
begging for troops to rescue them.
Zhōu Déwēi ordered Lǐ Sìběn, Lǐ Sìyuán, and Ān Jīnquán to rescue Wǔzhōu.
By the time they arrived,
Xíngqīn had already lifted the siege.
Sìyuán and Xíngguī pursued him to Guǎngbiān Army.
Xíngqīn led his cavalry to resist.
Xíngguī shouted to Xíngqīn: 'We both served the Liú family.
I defended the city for the Liú family,
yet you presumptuously declared yourself military governor.
Whose fault is that?
In today's matter,
there is no need to trouble the troops.
Let you and me contend to decide victory.'
Xíngqīn was fierce and brave,
excelling in horsemanship and archery beyond all others.
He replied, 'Agreed!'
Xíngzhōu's horse stumbled slightly,
about to fall,
when Sìyuán galloped to rescue him,
striking Xíngqīn with a whip, nearly knocking him off his horse.
Xíngqīn straightened himself and drew his bow to shoot Sìyuán,
hitting his thigh and piercing the saddle.
Sìyuán pulled out the arrow.
After eight engagements in total,
drawing his bow seven times,
his arrows struck Xíngqīn,
who still fought on fiercely, bloodied but unyielding.
That night,
Xíngqīn, in desperate straits,
firmly held Guǎngbiān Army,
surrounded by Jìn troops.
Sìyuán sent someone to tell him: 'We are both fighting generals—
no need for lengthy explanations.
The situation is clear.
Come quickly to meet,
and I will ensure your merit and fame.'
The next day,
Xíngqīn came out bound and surrendered.
Sìyuán poured wine for him to drink,
patted his back, and said: 'You are a true warrior, my son.'
He adopted him as a foster son.
In battle, capturing enemies alive,
he was always successful,
becoming renowned in the army."
The Zhuāngzōng Veritable Records, the Basic Annals of the Old History of the Five Dynasties and the biography of Yuán Xíngqīn, and the Míngzōng Veritable Records all state:
"Xíngqīn heard that Xíngguī had surrendered to Jìn,
and led troops to attack him."
Only the Zhōu Tàizǔ Veritable Records biography of Gāo Xíngzhōu says:
"Xíngqīn declared himself military governor,
and Xíngguī defended the city,
refusing to submit."
However, it is feared that by the time of Xíngzhōu's death,
long after Yān's fall,
Xíngzhōu's name and status were esteemed and prominent.
His disciples and old subordinates may have embellished the deeds of the brothers,
hence this account differs significantly from the others.
I now follow the majority of the texts.
Conquering it,
at the end of the Táng, Rúzhōu was established east of Guīzhōu,
governing one county, Jìnshān.
Xíngzhōu remained to serve Sìyuán,
often sharing command of the personal troops with Sìyuán's foster son, Cóngkē, and following him.
Cóngkē's mother, Lady Wèi,
was from Zhènzhōu.
She was first married to a man named Wáng,
giving birth to Cóngkē.
Sìyuán, while fighting in Héběi with the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng,
obtained Lady Wèi
and took her as a concubine.
Hence, Cóngkē became Sìyuán's son.
When he grew up,
he became known
for his bravery and strength,
and Sìyuán loved him.
This marks the beginning of Lǐ Cóngkē.
Examination of discrepancies: Zhāng Zhāo, at the beginning of the state, compiled the Veritable Records of the Deposed Emperor of Táng, stating:
"The Deposed Emperor's personal name was Cóngkē,
the eldest son of Emperor Míngzōng.
His mother was Empress Xuānxiàn, Lady Wèi,
from Píngshān in Zhènzhōu.
At the end of the Zhōnghé era,
while Míngzōng was campaigning in Shāndōng,
he garrisoned Píngshān
and obtained Empress Wèi.
The Emperor was born on the 23rd day of the first month of the first year of Guāngqǐ, outside the official residence.
Due to the Zhào people breaking their covenant,
warfare continued incessantly,
and communication was cut off.
The Emperor was about ten years old
before he could return to the family.
At that time, Míngzōng was a subordinate general,
broad-minded but incapable of managing a livelihood.
Empress Cáo was also lacking in planning,
so the means of livelihood
depended solely on Empress Xuānxiàn.
Empress Cáo had no children of her own,
yet managed the household and supported the family.
The Emperor, along with his subordinates Wáng Jiànlì and Huángfǔ Lì,
traveled back and forth in Dàiběi to supply provisions.
Empress Cáo pitied him,
treating him no differently from her own son."
The Old History of the Five Dynasties states:
"The Last Emperor's personal name was Cóngkē,
originally surnamed Wáng,
from Zhènzhōu.
His mother was Empress Xuānxiàn, Lady Wèi,
who gave birth to the Emperor in Píngshān in the first year of Guāngqǐ.
During the Jǐngfú era,
Míngzōng was a cavalry general under Wǔhuáng (Lǐ Kèyòng).
While campaigning, he reached Píngshān,
encountered Lady Wèi,
captured her,
and at that time, the Emperor was over ten years old.
Míngzōng raised him as his own son."
Liú Shù adopted the Deposed Emperor's record,
believing that after Míngzōng ascended the throne, he did not establish Cóngkē but intended to establish Cóngróng.
After Cóngróng's death,
he passed the throne to Cónghòu.
Therefore, everyone considered Cóngkē an adopted son.
Considering that Zhāng Zhāo served as a historian under Míngzōng,
and compiled the Deposed Emperor's record in a different era,
with nothing to conceal or avoid,
yet did not mention him as an adopted son,
the account seems credible.
However, Lǐ Kèyòng had not campaigned in Shāndōng before the first year of Guāngqǐ.
Moreover, if Cóngkē were truly Míngzōng's son,
Míngzōng would certainly not have passed him over to establish Cóngróng;
Cóngkē would also not have accepted it.
I now follow the Old History of the Five Dynasties.
17. The Wú expeditionary commander-in-chief Lǐ Tāo led twenty thousand troops out through Qiānqiū Ridge,
to attack Wúyuè's Yìjǐn Army.
From Hángzhōu, crossing Qiānqiū Ridge to the southeast leads to Hángzhōu's Lín'ān County.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties records:
In the second year of the Kāipíng era of the Liáng, Lín'ān County's Guǎngyì Township was renamed Yìjǐn Township.
The character 帥 (shuài) is read as 率 (shuài).
The character 衣 (yì) is pronounced yì.
Mù Prefecture Governor Fù Liǎo was appointed as the commander-in-chief for recovery operations,
leading the naval forces to attack Wú's Dōngzhōu in order to divide their military strength.
Dōngzhōu
refers to Dōngzhōu in Chángzhōu.
The character 璙 (liǎo) is pronounced liào,
also pronounced liǎo.
18. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Yuán Xiàngxiān was appointed to concurrently hold the title of military commissioner of Zhènnán.
The Zhènnán Army,
based in Hóngzhōu,
was at that time under Wú control.
This is what is referred to as a nominal military commissioner,
which existed during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms periods.
19. Jìn's Zhōu Déwēi advanced his army to press close to the southern gate of Yōuzhōu.
On the Rénchén day,
the Yān ruler Liú Shǒuguāng sent an envoy with a letter to Déwēi to request peace,
the language being extremely humble and pitiful.
Déwēi said:
"The Great Yān Emperor has not yet performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
why is he cowering like this!
Hàn's Zhào Wēn said: A great man should soar like a male,
how can he cower like a female.
Forming alliances and renewing friendly relations,
this is not something I have heard of."
He did not reply to the letter.
Shǒuguāng grew fearful,
and again sent someone to plead pitifully,
whereupon Déwēi reported the matter to the Prince of Jìn.
20. The path through Qiānqiū Ridge was dangerous and narrow.
Qián Chuánguàn had men cut down trees to block the retreat route of the Wú army and then attacked them,
the Wú army was greatly defeated,
and Lǐ Tāo along with over three thousand soldiers were captured and taken back.
21. On the Jǐhài day,
Jìn's Liú Guāngjùn captured Yān's Píngzhōu,
seizing Prefect Zhāng Zàijí.
In the fifth month,
Guāngjùn attacked Yíngzhōu,
and Prefect Yáng Jìng surrendered.
Sòng Bái said: From Píngzhōu to Yíngzhōu is six hundred and ninety li to the northeast.
22. On the Yǐsì day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed the Minister of War Wáng Kǎi as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Grand Councilor.
23. Yáng Shīhòu and Liú Shǒuqí led a hundred thousand troops from Biàn, Huá, Xú, Yǎn, Wèi, Bó, Xíng, and Míng prefectures to plunder extensively within Zhào territory.
Yáng Shīhòu, taking advantage of the conflict between Yān and Jìn,
exploited the vulnerability to plunder Zhào.
They headed towards Zhàozhōu,
while Shǒuqí entered from Bèizhōu heading towards Jìzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Bǎixiāng north to Zhàozhōu is over seventy li;
from Bèizhōu north to Jìzhōu is one hundred and twenty li.
The character 趣 (qū) is pronounced qù.
On the Gēngxū day,
Shīhòu reached Zhènzhōu,
the Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Zhàozhōu north to Zhènzhōu is ninety-five li.
and burned its border fortress.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Shīhòu withdrew his army from Jiǔmén to Xiàbó,
Shǒuqí led his troops to join Shīhòu in attacking Xiàbó,
and captured it.
Jìn generals Lǐ Cúnshěn and Shǐ Jiàntáng were garrisoning Zhàozhōu,
their troops were few,
and the Prince of Zhào urgently appealed to Zhōu Déwēi for help.
Déwēi sent cavalry commander Lǐ Shàohéng to join forces with Zhào general Wáng Démíng to resist the Liáng army together.
Shīhòu and Shǒuqí crossed the Yù River from Gōnggāo and proceeded eastward.
In the fourth year of the Dàyè era of Suí Emperor Yáng,
the Yǒngjì Canal was dug,
drawing water from the Qìn River south to the Huáng River,
and north to Zhuōjùn.
Later generations thus called it the Yù River.
and requested to move south of the river;
Shīhòu submitted a memorial to transfer Wànjìn to govern Qīngzhōu,
and appointed Shǒuqí as military commissioner of Shùnhuà.
Last year, Cāngzhōu's Yìchāng Army was renamed the Shùnhuà Army.
24. Wú sent Xuānzhōu deputy commander Huā Qián to lead troops to join Guǎngdé garrison commander Guō Xìn in stationing at Guǎngdé,
planning to invade Yìjǐn Army again.
Wúyuè's Qián Chuánguàn then attacked them.
25. In the sixth month,
on the first day, Rénshēn,
the Prince of Jìn sent Zhāng Chéngyè to Yōuzhōu,
to discuss military affairs with Zhōu Déwēi.
26. On the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed the Daoist priest Dù Guāngtíng as Golden and Purple Grand Master of the Palace, Left Grand Master of Remonstrance,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Cài,
and bestowed upon him the honorific title "Guǎngchéng Xiānshēng".
Guāngtíng was learned and skilled in writing,
the Shǔ ruler valued him highly,
and often consulted him on government affairs.
27. Wúyuè's Qián Chuánguàn captured Guǎngdé,
and took Huā Qián and Guō Xìn captive back.
28. On the Wùzǐ day,
Zhāng Wànjìn was appointed as military commissioner of Pínglú.
29. On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Yān ruler Liú Shǒuguāng sent an envoy to Zhāng Chéngyè,
requesting to surrender the city;
Chéngyè, considering him untrustworthy,
did not consent.
30. The Shǔ Crown Prince Yuányīng
had a snout-like mouth and protruding teeth,
his gaze was not straight,
yet he was alert, intelligent, well-read,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
but his nature was irritable, suspicious, and cruel.
The Shǔ ruler ordered Dù Guāngtíng to select pure and virtuous individuals to serve in the Eastern Palace,
Guāngtíng recommended the Confucian scholars Xǔ Jì and Xú Jiǎnfū,
but the Crown Prince never exchanged words with them.
Daily, he engaged in unrestrained amusement with musicians and petty entertainers,
and none of his subordinates dared to remonstrate.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Shǔ ruler planned to go on an outing on the Qīxī festival.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Crown Prince summoned the various princes and high officials to a banquet.
Prince Jí Zōnghàn, the Palace Commissioner Pān Qiào, and Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts Máo Wénxī from Gāoyáng did not attend.
The Crown Prince angrily said:
"If Prince Jí is not coming,
it must be due to Qiào and Wénxī sowing discord."
The commanders of the Dàchāng Army, Xú Yáo and Cháng Qiān,
had long been trusted by the Crown Prince.
During the drinking,
they repeatedly glanced at the Junior Guardian Táng Dàoxí,
Dàoxí grew fearful and stood up.
At dawn on the Dīngwèi day,
