Shǔ's new palace was completed,
located north of the old palace.
Tiānpíng Jiedushi and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, Lángyé Zhōngyì Wáng Wáng Tán,
recruited many bandits and robbers,
placing them under his command as personal troops.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
the bandits, taking advantage of Tán's unpreparedness,
suddenly entered the headquarters and killed Tán.
The deputy Jiedushi, Péi Yàn, led the provincial troops to attack and execute them,
and the military government thereby regained stability.
In the winter of the 27th year,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
the Shǔ general Wáng Zōngwǎn and others marched out of Dàsǎn Pass,
and inflicted a major defeat on the Qí army,
capturing and beheading tens of thousands,
subsequently capturing Bǎojī.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Wáng Zōngbō and others marched out of Gù Pass,
reaching Lǒng Prefecture.
Gù Pass,
refers to Dàzhèn Gù Pass.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Bǎoshèng Jiedushi and concurrently Shìzhōng Lǐ Jìjí, fearing the suspicion and jealousy of the King of Qí,
(The Qí established the Bǎoshèng Army in Lǒng Prefecture.)
abandoned Lǒng Prefecture and fled to the Shǔ army.
The Shǔ army advanced to attack Lǒng Prefecture,
appointing Jìjí as the Fourth Zhāotǎo of the Northwest Front Xíngyíng.
Liú Zhījùn joined forces with Wáng Zōngwǎn and others to besiege Fèngxiáng,
but the Qí army did not come out.
Heavy snow fell,
and the Shǔ ruler recalled the army.
He restored Lǐ Jìjí's original name, Sāng Hóngzhì.
Hóngzhì
was a man of Líyáng.
On the day Dīngyǒu of the 28th year,
Zhèng Xǔ, the Vice Minister of Rites, was appointed Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
Xǔ
was the grandnephew of Qǐ.
(Regarding Zhèng Qǐ, see Volume 259, the first year of Qiánníng of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng.)
Textual analysis notes: The Basic Annals of Emperor Mò of Liáng in the Old History of the Five Dynasties does not record the year and month when Xǔ first became Chancellor.
In the tenth month of this year, on the day Dīngyǒu,
it states that Zhèng Xǔ, Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Píngzhāng Shì, concurrently held the position of Minister of Justice and Píngzhāng Shì.
By the fourth year of Zhēnmíng, on the day Jǐyǒu of the fourth month,
it again states that Zhèng Xǔ, Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Píngzhāng Shì, concurrently held the position of Minister of Justice.
It is suspected that he became Chancellor in the second year of Zhēnmíng,
and transferred to Minister of Justice in the fourth year.
His biography states:
"He was successively promoted to Vice Minister of Rites,
and during the Zhēnmíng period, he was appointed Píngzhāng Shì."
The Basic Annals of Emperor Jūn in the Supplementary Records of Táng states:
"In the tenth month of the second year of Zhēnmíng, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Zhèng Xǔ, Vice Minister of Rites, was appointed Vice Minister of the Secretariat and Píngzhāng Shì."
We now follow this.
Furthermore, Gāo Ruòzhuō's Hòu Shǐ Bǔ states:
"Xǔ succeeded on his nineteenth attempt at the imperial examination,
his name was the nineteenth on the list,
and his rank was also the same;
from passing the examination to becoming Chancellor took exactly nineteen years."
Now, according to the record, Xǔ passed the examination in the third year of Guānghuà.
From the third year of Guānghuà to this year is only seventeen years,
which again does not match.
On the day Jǐhài of the 29th year,
Shǔ issued a general amnesty.
In the 30th year, the King of Jìn sent an envoy to Wú,
to coordinate military forces to attack Liáng.
In the eleventh month,
Wú appointed the Deputy Military Commissioner Xú Zhīxùn as the Dū Zhāotǎo Shǐ of the Huáiběi Xíngyíng,
and together with Zhū Jǐn and others, led troops towards Sòng and Bó to coordinate with Jìn.
After crossing the Huái River,
they issued proclamations to the prefectures and counties,
and advanced to besiege Yǐng Prefecture.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Shǔ issued a general amnesty,
changing the reign title of the following year to Tiānhàn,
and the state name to Dàhàn.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, hearing that the King of Jìn had pacified Héběi,
sent an envoy to establish friendly relations;
the King of Jìn also sent an envoy in return.
In this year,
Qìng Prefecture rebelled and submitted to Qí.
(Qìng Prefecture was originally Qí territory.
It seems that because last year Lǐ Bǎohéng submitted Bīnníng to Liáng,
it thus came under Liáng's control.)
An edict appointed the Left Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn Hè Huái as the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry of the Western Front Xíngyíng,
leading troops to suppress it.
He defeated the Qí army,
and captured Níng and Yǎn prefectures.
(Yǎn Prefecture
was established by Qí's Lǐ Màozhēn,
located between Níng and Qìng.
In the Sòng dynasty, Yǎn Prefecture was abolished and became Dìngpíng Town,
belonging to Bīn Prefecture.)
Textual analysis notes: The biography of Hè Huái in the Old History of the Five Dynasties states:
"In the second year of Zhēnmíng, Qìng Prefecture rebelled,
and was occupied by Lǐ Jìzhì.
The Emperor ordered the Left Lónghǔ Tǒngjūn Hè Huái to be the Commander of Cavalry and Infantry of the Western Front Xíngyíng and concurrently Military Supervisor of All Armies,
and together with Zhāng Yún, defeated thirty thousand troops from Jīng and Fèng,
capturing Níng and Yǎn prefectures."
This was not a minor event,
yet the Basic Annals of Emperor Mò and the biography of Lǐ Màozhēn do not mention it,
only Huái's biography records it.
We now rely on this.
The Hé dōng Supervisor Zhāng Chéngyè, having become powerful and influential,
his nephews Guàn and four others came from Tóng Prefecture to rely on him.
The King of Jìn, for Chéngyè's sake,
promoted and employed them all.
Chéngyè governed his household very strictly.
One of his nephews committed robbery,
killing a cattle merchant.
Chéngyè immediately executed him;
the King urgently sent someone to save him,
but it was already too late.
The King appointed Guàn as Prefect of Lín Prefecture.
Chéngyè said to Guàn:
"You were originally a commoner from Chēdù,
and became a bandit with Liú Kāidào.
(Liú Kāidào must refer to Liú Zhījùn.
Zhījùn was Liáng's Kāidào Zhǐhuī Shǐ,
and also once governed Tóng Prefecture.
Chē
is pronounced chē zhē.
If you do not reform now,
your death is not far off!"
From then on, wherever Guàn went, he did not dare to be greedy or cruel.
The Wúyuè Yánèi Xiānfēng Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ Qián Chuánxiàng took a wife from Mǐn,
and from then on, Mǐn and Wúyuè established friendly relations.
Mǐn cast lead coins,
which circulated together with copper coins.
37. Initially,
the people of Yān suffered under the cruelty of Liú Shǒuguāng,
and many soldiers defected to the Khitan.
When Shǒuguāng was besieged in Yōuzhōu,
(the events are recorded in the previous volume).
The Khitan grew increasingly powerful.
The Khitan king Ābǎojī declared himself emperor,
and his people called him the Heavenly King.
He made his wife, the Shùlǜ clan, empress,
and established a bureaucracy.
At this time,
he changed the era name to Shéncè.
(A note on discrepancies: The Comprehensive Chronology states:
"The old histories do not record the establishment of an era name by Bǎojī.
Now, among the Khitan, there exists a calendar
that records a continuous period of 120 years.
In the third year of the Jǐngyòu era, I, as an envoy to the north, went to Yōujì
and obtained this calendar.
Upon examining the sequence of years,
I found that it begins with the yǐhài year.
The following year first records the era name Shéncè,
and later there was also Tiānzàn.
According to the Biography of the Khitan in the History of the Five Dynasties,
the name Tiānxiǎn is only recorded from the time of Yēlǜ Déguāng onward.
I suspect that the earlier information was not transmitted at that time,
or perhaps the barbarians, ashamed that Bǎojī had no era name,
retroactively created one.
Bǎojī
was also called the Heavenly King among the barbarians.")
The Miscellaneous Records of the Barbarian Court states:
"Tàizǔ (Ābǎojī) in one campaign annexed the Xī state,
yet still established a Xī person as the Xī king as before,
appointing a Khitan to oversee the military.
He also destroyed Bóhǎi,
captured its king Dà Yīnzhuàn,
and established his eldest son as the King of Eastern Dān of Bóhǎi,
titled the Human King.
He himself took the title Heavenly King,
first establishing the era name Tiānzàn,
also called Shéncè,
and the state was called the Great Liáo.
He built a tower in the large tribe where he resided,
called the Western Tower,
now known as the Upper Capital.
He also built a tower at Mùyè Mountain to the south,
called the Southern Tower.
He built a tower a thousand lǐ to the east,
called the Eastern Tower.
He built a tower three hundred lǐ to the north,
called the Northern Tower.
Tàizǔ would often hunt and travel among these four towers throughout the four seasons.")
It also states:
"After Ābǎojī transformed his family into a state,
he began to designate the royal clan as the 'Héngzhàng' (Lateral Tent),
with the surname Shìlǐ Mòlǐ,
which, translated into Chinese, is called the Yēlǜ clan.
He bestowed the surname Xiāo upon the empress's clan.
The royal clan only intermarried with the empress's clan.
If the various tribes did not receive the command of the Northern Lord,
they were not allowed to intermarry with these two clans.")
The Ouyáng History states:
"Ābǎojī, following the strategy of his wife Shùlǜ,
sent someone to tell the chiefs of the various tribes: 'I have a salt pond,
which all the tribes consume from.
Yet, the tribes know the benefit of eating salt but do not recognize that the salt has an owner.
Is this acceptable?
You should come and reward me.'
The tribes agreed,
and together they held a drinking feast at the salt pond.
Ābǎojī had hidden soldiers nearby.
When the drinking was at its height, the ambush was sprung,
and all the tribal chiefs were killed.
Thus, he established himself
and did not step down again.")
Regarding Ābǎojī declaring himself emperor,
the previous histories do not record the exact year and month.
The Biography of the Khitan in the Biographies of Zhuāngzōng places it after Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne and Lǐ Cúnshěn defended Fànyáng.
The Veritable Records of Hàn Gāozǔ and the Táng Yúlù both state that Ābǎojī devised a plan to annex the various tribes
and then declared himself emperor,
placing it during the Qiánníng era, before Liú Rén'gōng was stationed in Yōuzhōu.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties places it at the end of the Tiānyòu era of Zhuāngzōng.
According to the Comprehensive Chronology,
the first year of Ābǎojī's Shéncè era corresponds to the bǐngzǐ year,
which is the 13th year of Tiānyòu of Zhuāngzōng,
and the 2nd year of Zhēnmíng of the Liáng dynasty.
This seems to contradict it being at the end of Tiānyòu or after Zhuāngzōng's accession.
The Biān Yí Lù records that in the second year of Kāipíng, in the fifth month, Tàizǔ (of Liáng) still addressed Ābǎojī in a document as 'Qīng' (a term for a subject),
and mentioned
"you serve our dynasty as a subject,
hoping the state will send an envoy to confer the title."
He certainly had not yet declared himself emperor then.
How could it be before Liú Rén'gōng was stationed in Yōuzhōu!
The Táng Yúlù completely copied the Khitan account from the Veritable Records of Hàn Gāozǔ to compose its biography,
which is highly inaccurate.
It is unknown in which year he actually declared himself emperor.
Now, because he changed the era name,
it is placed here.)
Empress Shùlǜ was brave, decisive, and resourceful.
When Ābǎojī led troops and commanded the masses,
Empress Shùlǜ often participated in his planning.
Ābǎojī once crossed the desert to attack the Dǎngxiàng,
(the Dǎngxiàng were west of the desert).
(Desert,
pronounced qī jì fān.)
(Dǎng,
pronounced dǐ lǎng fān.)
The two Shìwéi tribes, Huángtóu and Chòubó, took advantage of the emptiness to join forces and raid his territory.
(Huángtóu
was a powerful tribe of the Shìwéi;
Chòubó,
a Shìwéi tribe named after the place where they lived.)
She deployed troops and waited for their arrival,
launched a fierce attack,
and routed them completely.
From then on, her name shook all the barbarian tribes.
Empress Shùlǜ had a mother and a mother-in-law.
She sat on a couch while they received her bow,
saying:
"I only bow to Heaven,
not to people.")
The Prince of Jìn was then managing Héběi
and wished to ally with the Khitan for support.
He often treated Ābǎojī as an uncle
and Empress Shùlǜ as an aunt.
(Because the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng, had sworn brotherhood with Ābǎojī).)
In his final years, Liú Shǒuguāng was in decline and distress.
He sent his military advisor Hán Yánhuī to seek aid from the Khitan.
(A note on discrepancies: The Biography of Hán Yánhuī in the Veritable Records of Hàn Gāozǔ states:
"During the Tiānyòu era, Regional Commander Liú Shǒuguāng attacked Zhōngshān unsuccessfully.
Wishing to ally with the northern barbarians,
he sent Yánhuī on a mission to the barbarians.")
Liú Shù believed that after Liú Shǒuguāng occupied Yōuzhōu, he never attacked Dìngzhōu.
Only in the third year of Guānghuà of the Táng dynasty did the Biàn general Zhāng Cúnjìng capture Yíng and Mò,
attack Dìngzhōu,
and Liú Rén'gōng sent Shǒuguāng to rescue Dìngzhōu,
but he was defeated by Cúnjìng.
Perhaps it was at this time,
when Rén'gōng was still the commander of Yōu,
not Shǒuguāng.)
Considering that during the peak of power of Liú Rén'gōng and his son, they often bullied and oppressed the Khitan,
how would they be willing to send an envoy to form an alliance with them!
In the first year of Qiánhuà, Shǒuguāng attacked Yì and Dìng.
Wáng Chùzhí sought help from Jìn,
so the Prince of Jìn sent Zhōu Déwēi to attack him.
His sending Yánhuī to ally with the Khitan probably occurred at this time.
However, there is no clear evidence for this,
so it is only stated that he was in decline and distress,
and appended here.)
(The Khitan) made him herd horses in the wild.
Yánhuī
was from Yōuzhōu,
intelligent and strategic,
and quite literate.
Empress Shùlǜ said to the Khitan ruler:
"Yánhuī can maintain his integrity and not yield.
He is a worthy man of the present age.
Why humiliate him with herding duties!
He should be treated with respect and employed.")
The Khitan ruler summoned Yánhuī to speak with him,
was pleased with him,
and thus made him his chief advisor,
consulting him on all actions.
Yánhuī began teaching the Khitan to establish a headquarters and open a government office,
build city walls,
establish marketplaces and residential districts,
to settle the Han people,
ensuring each had a spouse,
and to cultivate wasteland.
As a result, the Han people each lived peacefully and pursued their livelihoods,
and fewer fled.
The Khitan's power subdued the various states,
and Yánhuī contributed to this.
Shortly thereafter,
Yánhuī fled to Jìnyáng.
The Prince of Jìn intended to place him in his own administration,
but the chief secretary, Wáng Jiān, resented him;
Yánhuī, feeling uneasy,
requested to return east to visit his mother.
He traveled from Jìnyáng back to Yōuzhōu,
going from west to east.
The character "省"
is pronounced xǐng.
He stopped at the home of his fellow villager, Wáng Démíng.
Wáng Démíng was the adopted son of Zhào Wáng Róng,
that is, the Yān man Zhāng Wénlǐ.
Yánhuī said:
"Now Héběi is entirely under Jìn's control,
I should go again to the Qìdān."
Démíng said:
"Having rebelled and now going back,
would that not be seeking death?"
This meant that since he had already betrayed the Qìdān and returned to the Central Plains,
now going again to the Qìdān,
he feared being killed.
The character "復"
is pronounced fù;
the same below.
"Since I left them,
it has been as if they lost their hands and eyes;
now if I go to them,
their hands and eyes will be whole again,
how would they be willing to harm me!"
After visiting his mother,
he then re-entered Qìdān territory.
When the Qìdān ruler heard of his arrival,
he was overjoyed,
as if he had descended from heaven.
Patting his back, he said:
"Where have you been all this time?"
Yánhuī replied:
"I missed my mother,
and wanted to ask for leave to return,
but feared you would not permit it,
so I left privately."
The Qìdān ruler treated him even more generously.
When he declared himself emperor,
he appointed Yánhuī as chancellor,
and he was repeatedly promoted until he reached the position of Zhōngshū Lìng.
The Ouyáng Shǐ's "Account of the Four Barbarians" says: Ābǎojī appointed Yánhuī as chancellor,
with the title Zhèngshì Lìng,
and the Qìdān called him
"Chóngwén Xiànggong."
The Prince of Jìn sent an envoy to the Qìdān,
and Yánhuī sent a letter to the Prince of Jìn,
explaining the reason for his departure to the north,
and saying:
"It is not that I do not long for a wise lord,
nor that I do not miss my homeland,
the reason I did not stay
was precisely because I feared Wáng Jiān's slander."
He entrusted his elderly mother to him,
and also said:
"As long as Yánhuī is here,
the Qìdān will certainly not go south to graze."
Jiǎ Yì's "Guò Qín Lùn": The Hú people did not dare to go south to graze their horses.
That the Qìdān did not penetrate deeply to raid
was due to Yánhuī's efforts.
However, during Zhuāngzōng's reign,
the Qìdān besieged Zhōu Déwēi,
and rescued Zhāng Wénlǐ,
how could they not have wanted to penetrate deeply to raid!
Jìn's military strength was at its peak then,
capable of breaking their momentum,
how could it have been Yánhuī's doing!
1 In spring,
the first month,
an edict ordered Xuānwǔ Jiedùshǐ Yuán Xiàngxiān to rescue Yǐngzhōu.
Upon his arrival,
the Wú army withdrew.
Last November, Wú besieged Yǐngzhōu.
2 In the second month,
on Jiǎshēn,
the Prince of Jìn attacked Líyáng,
Liú Xún resisted him,
and after several days,
he withdrew without success.
3 The Prince of Jìn's younger brother, Cúnjǔ, the defense commissioner of the Wēisài Army, was in Xīnzhōu.
Jìn established the Wēisài Army in Xīnzhōu,
which later became a military district.
Xīnzhōu administered only Yǒngxīng County.
Xuē Jūzhèng said: In the seventh month of the second year of Tóngguāng of Táng Zhuāngzōng,
Xīnzhōu was elevated to a Wēisài Army Jiedùshǐ,
with Guī, Rú, and Wǔ prefectures subordinate to it.
His maidservants interfered in governance.
The Prince of Jìn ordered him to recruit brave men from the tribes north of the mountains and the remnants of Liú Shǒuguāng's defeated troops to reinforce the southern campaign army;
he also levied horses from the people,
and some people had to sell ten oxen to exchange for one warhorse.
The deadlines were urgent,
and the border people lamented and complained.
Cúnjǔ gathered five hundred cavalry,
and personally led them to deliver them,
appointing Shòuzhōu Cìshǐ Lú Wénjìn as his deputy commander.
Shòuzhōu belonged to Wú,
Lú Wénjìn only held the title of Cìshǐ remotely.
Cúnjǔ also showed no care or compassion.
On Jiǎwǔ,
they reached Qígōu Pass.
The minor officer Gōng Yànzhāng plotted with the soldiers, saying:
"We hear the Prince of Jìn is locked in fierce combat with the Liáng people.
The character "確"
means firm.
In general, in battle,
one advances, retreats, disperses, or regroups according to the military situation;
but in fierce combat, the two sides are evenly matched,
fighting with full strength,
and only those who endure firmly and use their long skills can win.
The character "校"
is pronounced xiào.
We have left our parents, wives, and children,
fighting as guests for others,
traveling a thousand li to die,
and our commander shows no pity or compassion,
what can we do?"
The crowd said:
"Kill the commander.
The defense commissioner is the head of a prefecture,
hence called commander.
The character "使"
is pronounced shǐ.
The character "長"
is pronounced zhǎng.
We will occupy the city and defend ourselves,
what can they do to us!"
So they took up arms and raised a great clamor,
rushing to the guesthouse.
At dawn,
Cúnjǔ was still asleep and had not risen,
and they killed him on the spot.
Wénjìn could not control them,
and beating his chest, he wept over the corpse, saying:
"You slaves have killed the young master,
how can I face the Prince of Jìn again!"
He was then pushed forward by the crowd,
and they returned to Xīnzhōu.
The defending general, Yáng Quánzhāng, resisted them;
they also attacked Wǔzhōu,
but the northern Yànmén area's overall defense commander, Lǐ Sìgōng, attacked and defeated them.
Zhōu Déwēi also sent troops in pursuit,
and Wénjìn led his followers to flee to the Qìdān.
When the Prince of Jìn heard that Cúnjǔ's misconduct had caused the rebellion,
he executed several maidservants and staff members.
4. Initially,
seven hundred li north of Yōuzhōu was the Yú Pass.
The Yú Pass entered the boundaries of Yíngzhōu and the boundaries of Shíchéng County in Píngzhōu.
The Yīnyì of the Hànshū states: Yú,
pronounced as Yù,
is now read as Yú.
From the pass northeastward, following the sea, there is a road.
The narrowest parts of the road are only a few feet wide,
with chaotic mountains on both sides,
high and steep, impossible to cross.
Upon reaching Jìnniúkǒu,
"Bǐ"
should be
"Běi".
Local soldiers were recruited to guard it.
The Ōu Shǐ states: The Yú Pass faces the sea to the east,
with the Tù'ěr and Fùzhōu mountains to the north,
both extremely steep.
Northeast along the sea, there is a road,
so narrow it barely allows a cart to pass,
with cultivable land alongside.
During the Táng dynasty, the Eastern Xiáshí, Western Xiáshí, Lǜchóu, Mǐzhuān, Chángyáng, Huánghuā, Zǐméng, and Báiláng forts were established to secure it.
Sòng Bái said: Beneath the Yú Pass fort lies the Yú River, which flows into the great sea.
The pass faces the sea to the east,
with the Tù'ěr and Fùzhōu mountains to the north,
both extremely steep.
Following the coast northeast from the foot of the mountains,
the narrowest part allows only a single cart track.
It is surrounded by sea on three sides,
connected to the land pass to the north.
To the west, chaotic mountains extend to the Jìnniú barrier, with six passes in total.
The barrier garrisons are interconnected,
forming a natural limit against the Róng and Dí.
Not entering Jì,
Yōuzhōu annually supplied silk and floss to provide clothing for the soldiers.
Each year, after the early harvest,
the fields were cleared and the walls fortified to await the Qìdān.
When the Qìdān arrived,
they would close the gates and refuse battle,
waiting for them to leave.
Then, the bravest soldiers were selected to occupy the narrow passes and intercept them.
The Yōuzhōu Lúlóng military governor administered Jì County.
Zēng,
pronounced Cí Líng fān.
Kuàng,
pronounced Kǔ Bàng fān.
Ài,
pronounced Wū Xiè fān.
The local soldiers all had their own fields and gardens.
Those who fought bravely and achieved merit were rewarded with honors and gifts.
Xūn,
refers to ranks of merit.
When Zhōu Déwēi became the Lúlóng military governor,
he relied on his bravery and neglected border defenses,
thus losing the strategic advantage of the Yú Pass.
The Qìdān often grazed their livestock between Yíngzhōu and Píngzhōu.
The Jīnlǔ Jiéyào states: In the Yānshān region,
northwest of Yìzhōu is the Jīnpō Pass,
west of Chāngpíng County is the Jūyōng Pass,
in Shùnzhōu is the ancient Gǔběikǒu,
northeast of Jǐngzhōu is the Sōngtíng Pass,
east of Píngzhōu is the Yú Pass,
and east of the Yú Pass is the route taken by the Jīn people.
These passes are all naturally formed to separate the Fān and Hàn peoples.
A single man guarding them can hold off a hundred.
In our dynasty's campaign to recover Yān,
if these passes had been secured,
the Yānshān region could have been defended.
However, the lands within the passes,
Píng, Luán, and Yíngzhōu,
were lost to Ābǎojī after the Later Táng,
who renamed Píngzhōu as Liáoxīng Prefecture,
placing Yíng and Luánzhōu under its jurisdiction,
calling it the Píngzhōu Circuit.
By the beginning of the Later Jìn,
Yēlǜ Déguāng had also acquired Yānshān, Tán, Shùn, Jǐng, Jì, Zhuō, and Yìzhōu,
establishing Yānshān as Yānjīng,
governing six commanderies,
called the Yānjīng Circuit,
while Píngzhōu remained a separate circuit.
During the maritime negotiations to cede territory,
only the Yān and Yún circuits were mentioned.

*Shí Guó Jìnián Wú Shǐ*:
“On the *yǐmǎo* day of the sixth month,
Jǐn killed Zhīxùn,
then climbed over the city wall and killed himself.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Zhīgào entered Yángzhōu to replace Zhīxùn in governing.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
he executed Jǐn’s associates.”
The *Guǎngběn*:
“On the *wùwǔ* day,
Zhīgào’s close official Mǎ Rényù heard of Zhīxùn’s death,
crossed from Suànshān,
and reported to Zhīgào.
Zhīgào that same day led troops into Yángzhōu,
and pacified the officials and people.”
Considering that Yángzhōu and Rùnzhōu are extremely close,
how could Zhīgào have heard the news only four days later!
Now follow *Jiāngnán Lù*.
Note: Xú Zhīgào reluctantly went to Rùnzhōu to await developments,
originally a strategy of Sòng Qíqiū,
as recorded in the third year of the previous scroll.
He then proceeded to pacify the military government.
At that time, Xú Wēn’s sons were all weak,
so Wēn had Zhīgào replace Zhīxùn in governing Wú,
and sank Zhū Jǐn’s corpse in Léitáng, exterminating his clan.
When Jǐn killed Zhīxùn,
Mǐ Zhìchéng, military governor of Tàiníng, followed with a dozen horsemen to inquire about Jǐn’s whereabouts,
and upon hearing he was already dead,
returned.
The proclamation commissioner Lǐ Yǎn was impoverished and in dire straits,
residing in Hǎilíng;
Lǐ Yǎn had been sent to proclaim edicts in Huáinán,
see the 263rd scroll, second year of Tiānfù under Táng Zhāozōng.
Both were killed.
Yán Kěqiú, fearing Zhìchéng would not obey orders,
falsely claimed a great victory over Chǔ troops in Yuánzhōu,
and when all officers came to offer congratulations,
had strong men lie in ambush at the halberd gate,
captured Zhìchéng,
and beheaded him,
along with his sons.
On the 15th day, Rénxū,
the Prince of Jìn went from Wèizhōu to Yángliú to inspect the army.
He personally took a boat to measure the river's depth,
which was deep enough to submerge spears.
The Prince said to his generals:
"The Liáng army has no real will to fight;
they only wish to use the river to hinder and weary our troops.
We should wade across and attack them."
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Prince led his personal guard to cross first,
with the other armies following.
They lifted their armor and held their spears sideways,
forming ranks and advancing.
On that day, the water level had dropped,
and the depth only reached their knees.
Xiè Yànzhāng, the Military Commissioner of Kuāngguó and Commander of the Northern Front Battle Array, led his troops to the bank to resist them.
Previously, he was recorded as the Military Commissioner of Héyáng;
here he is recorded as the Military Commissioner of Kuāngguó.
This is likely because he was transferred from Héyáng to Kuāngguó.
The character "chén"
is read as "zhèn" (battle array).
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ" (to lead).
They then gradually retreated,
and the Liáng troops pursued them.
When they reached the middle of the river,
the Jìn troops beat drums, shouted, and advanced again.
Xiè Yànzhāng could not hold his ground,
and retreated slightly to climb onto the bank.
The Jìn troops seized the opportunity to press their advantage,
and the Liáng troops were utterly defeated,
with casualties beyond count.
When fighting from the bank against those wading in the water,
the side holding the higher ground gains the advantage.
When both sides fight in the water,
the braver side wins.
This is why Xiè Yànzhāng was defeated.
The character "shèng"
is pronounced "shēng".
Xiè Yànzhāng barely escaped with his life.
On that day,
the Jìn forces captured four camps along the river.
16. After Táng Wényǐ of Shǔ died,
Zhāng Gé, the Grand Tutor, Vice Director of the Chancellery, and Co-manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, felt inwardly uneasy.
(Zhāng Gé's association with Táng Wényǐ was mentioned in the third year of the previous reign.)
Yáng Bīn, the Minister of Rites, fearing the loss of his own influence,
said to Zhāng Gé:
"You have the great merit of supporting the establishment [of the heir].
(This refers to drafting the memorial that led the various ministers to request the establishment of Zōngyǎn.)
On the Gēngwǔ day,
Zhāng Gé was demoted to Prefect of Màozhōu,
and Yáng Bīn to Defender of Róngjīng.
Xǔ Jì, the Vice Minister of Personnel, and Pān Qiáo, the Vice Minister of Revenue, were both demoted for being part of Zhāng Gé's faction.
Zhāng Gé was soon further demoted to Registrar of Wéizhōu.
Yǔ Níngjì memorialized to have Zhāng Gé transferred to Héshuǐ Garrison.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Pújiāng County of Qióngzhōu has Héshuǐ Garrison.)
Wáng Zōngkǎn's wife, being of the same surname as Zhāng Gé,
wanted to save him.
She said to Chéng Yǎn's mother:
"Warn your son
not to seek revenge for others,
or else blame will be laid upon you another day."
Chéng Yǎn complied.
Yǔ Níngjì was angered
and used public affairs to charge Chéng Yǎn with a crime.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day, Rénshēn,
the ruler of Shǔ appointed Wáng Zōngbì, who also held the title of Director of the Secretariat, as Prince of Jùlù,
Zōngyáo as Prince of Línzī,
Zōngwǎn as Prince of Líntáo,
Zōngbō as Prince of Línyǐng,
and Zōngyì, Zōngkuí, and Zōng'àn, who also held the title of Palace Attendant, were all made Princes of Lángyé Commandery.
Since the Sima clan crossed the river south,
the region south of the Yangtze considered the Wáng clan of Lángyé to be the foremost among the distinguished families,
hence these three were all enfeoffed as Princes of Lángyé.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Wáng Zōngkǎn was made Prince of Lè'ān.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Yǔ Chuánsù, the Minister of War, was appointed Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Vice Director of the Secretariat, Co-manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
The ruler of Shǔ did not personally attend to government affairs;
all internal and external appointments and removals came from Wáng Zōngbì.
Zōngbì accepted bribes and acted with much partiality,
causing discontent and resentment among both superiors and subordinates.
Sòng Guāngsì was clever and adept at currying favor,
(meaning to cater and ingratiate himself.)
and Shǔ from this point began to decline.
When there is good governance, the state is strong;
when there is no governance, the state declines.
Decline is the precursor to ruin;
can one not be warned!
17. Wú's Xú Wēn went to court at Guǎnglíng,
(from Shēngzhōu.)
intending to carry out extensive executions.
Xú Zhīgào and Yán Kěqiú fully detailed Xú Zhīxùn's faults and misdeeds,
and the reasons that led to the disaster.
Xú Wēn's anger gradually subsided,
and he then ordered Zhū Jǐn's bones to be retrieved from Léitáng and buried.
(Xú Wēn, realizing the fault lay with his own son,
therefore buried Zhū Jǐn.)
Those involved were all punished;
only Diāo Yànnéng, who had repeatedly submitted remonstrances,
was rewarded by Xú Wēn.
On the Wùxū day,
Xú Zhīgào was appointed Deputy Military Commissioner of Huáinán, Deputy Commander of All Inner and Outer Cavalry and Infantry Armies, and Co-administrator of the Prefectural Government.
(Textual analysis note: According to the Shí Guó Jìnián,
on the sixth month, Yǐmǎo day,
Xú Zhīxùn was killed.
Forty-four days have passed until now,
so Wú's government affairs must have been handled by someone.
It seems Xú Zhīgào, upon arriving in Guǎnglíng, immediately took over Wú's administration from Xú Zhīxùn,
and only now received an official appointment.)
Xú Zhījiàn was put in charge of the affairs of the Ruànzhōu militia.
(Replacing Xú Zhīgào.)
He oversaw the main policies of the Wú court,
while all other routine administrative matters
were decided by Xú Zhīgào.
Xú Zhīgào completely reversed Xú Zhīxùn's ways.
He served the King of Wú with utmost respect,
treated scholar-officials with humility,
governed the masses with leniency,
and disciplined himself with frugality.
By order of the King of Wú,
he entirely remitted all overdue taxes from before the 13th year of the Tiānyòu era.
(After Liáng usurped Táng,
Huáinán still used the Tiānyòu reign title.
This year was the 15th year of Tiānyòu.
Xú Zhīgào remitted overdue taxes from before the 13th year of Tiānyòu.
Taxes overdue from after that year were to be collected.
This refers to the overdue rent from the 14th year of Tiānyòu.)
He accepted admonishing advice,
removed the cunning and crafty,
and put a stop to personal solicitations.
Consequently, the officials and people unanimously turned their hearts to him,
and even veteran generals and fierce warriors were all pleased and submitted.
Previously,
in Wú there was a poll tax,
and also a tax calculated per acre paid in cash.
Money was heavy (valuable) and goods were light (cheap),
causing the people great hardship.
Qí Qiū advised Xú Zhīgào,
believing that
"Money is not obtained from farming and sericulture.
Now forcing the people to pay taxes in cash
is teaching them to abandon the fundamental (agriculture) and pursue the secondary (commerce).
I request the abolition of the poll tax;
(Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎnfánlù states: The present poll tax is the same as the suàn tax of the Hàn dynasty.
Because it was calculated per person and paid in cash,
it was also called the kǒu fù.
In the fourth year of Hàn, the suàn fù was first established.
Rú Chún said: According to the Hàn Yí Zhù,
people aged fifteen and above up to fifty-six paid the fù tax in cash,
120 cash per person constituted one suàn,
used for manufacturing weapons, chariots, and horses.
By Emperor Wén's time,
the population was large and there were many adult males,
so they took Emperor Gāozǔ's original quota and reduced it by two-thirds annually,
meaning each person paid only 40 cash per year.
Jiǎ Juānzhī said: Emperor Wén laid aside arms and promoted culture;
the people's fù tax was 40 cash,
and adult males performed corvée labor once every three years.
Rú Chún said: The regular annual fù tax was 120 cash,
with corvée labor once a year.
In Emperor Wén's time, the population was large,
so the fù tax was set at 40 cash,
and corvée labor was performed once every three years.
This 'fù'
refers to the 120 cash from Emperor Gāozǔ's time,
which was reduced to 40 by this time.
This 'corvée labor'
refers to the ancient rule where one adult male did not perform more than three days of service per year.
People aged fifteen and above,
even if not yet considered adult males, also paid the poll tax,
which was the so-called people's fù tax of 40 cash.
Once they became adult males,
they were originally supposed to perform three days of service per year,
but by this time it was reduced to performing only one year's service every three years.
The Táng system: Upon becoming an adult male, one entered corvée service;
if not serving, a commutation fee was collected per day.
The poll tax of later ages originated from this.)
The character "shuì"
is pronounced "shuō".
For silk and satin, a bolt worth 1,000 cash should be taxed as 3,000."
(Meaning, goods worth 1,000 cash were assessed for a tax quota of 3,000.)
"If this is done,
the state treasury will lose revenue amounting to hundreds of millions of cash annually."
Qí Qiū said:
"How can there be a case where the people are wealthy and the state is poor!"
Xú Zhīgào followed his advice.
As a result, all the uncultivated land in the Jiāng-Huái region was opened up,
(uncultivated land refers to empty, unplowed land.)
and the state became rich and powerful.
Zhīgào wanted to promote Qíqiū, but Xú Wēn disliked him.
Sòng Qíqiū plotted for Xú Zhīgào to seize power from the Xú family.
If Wēn had known about this,
it would have been more than just dislike.
Qíqiū’s character
was frivolous, narrow-minded, and irritable;
Wēn disliked him for this reason.
"Dislike"
is pronounced wù.
Diànzhí
means having him serve on duty in the Wú palace.
Jūn pànguān
refers to the marching judge.
They often stayed until midnight,
speaking in private—
dismissing attendants to have secret talks with Qíqiū.
A waterside pavilion is open on all sides,
with no fear of eavesdroppers at the wall.
Midnight
means the middle of the night.
"Dismiss"
is pronounced bǐng.
They removed all screens,
placed only a large stove,
sat facing each other,
did not speak,
but wrote characters in the ashes with iron chopsticks,
then erased them with a spoon.
Removing the screens
was to prevent attendants from hiding and secretly watching.
"Remove"
is pronounced qù.
No one could know what they discussed.
18 Qiánzhōu was strategically secure and fortified.
The Wú army attacked it
but could not capture it for a long time.
In February of this year,
Wú attacked Qiánzhōu.
Wáng Qí fell ill,
and Wú appointed Liú Xìn, the Zhènnán military governor, as the Qiánzhōu campaign commander.
Not long after,
Qí died.
Tán Quánbō sought aid from Wúyuè, Mǐn, and Chǔ.
The King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, appointed his commander Fú Qiú as the southwestern front relief commander,
leading twenty thousand troops to attack Xìnzhōu.
The commander
was an official position established by Wúyuè.
Mǐn troops stationed at Yúdū to rescue them.
Yúdū
was an ancient Hàn dynasty county,
under Qiánzhōu in the Táng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, it was 170 lǐ south of the prefecture.
They engaged in battle
but were unsuccessful;
the Wúyuè army besieged the city.
The prefect, Zhōu Běn,
opened the gates and set up empty curtains inside,

Suspecting an ambush,
by midnight,
the Wúyuè forces lifted the siege and withdrew.
Wú appointed Chén Zhāng, former prefect of Shūzhōu, as the southeastern front relief commander,
leading troops to invade Sūzhōu and Húzhōu,
to divert Wúyuè’s forces from rescuing Qiánzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Tīngzhōu was 480 lǐ north of Qiánzhōu.
They moved troops to station at Tīngzhōu,
showing intent to rescue Qiánzhōu.
The Wú people declined due to the difficulties at Qiánzhōu.
19 The Prince of Jìn planned a large-scale invasion.
Zhōu Déwēi led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry from Yōuzhōu,
Lǐ Cúnshěn led ten thousand infantry and cavalry from Cāngjǐng,
Lǐ Sìyuán led ten thousand infantry and cavalry from Xíngmíng,
Wáng Chùzhí sent a general leading ten thousand infantry and cavalry from Yìdìng,

In August,
combining the armies of Hédōng and Wèibó,
they held a grand review at Wèizhōu.
Nothing is more difficult than commanding large numbers of troops.
In this campaign,
the Jìn forces were initially defeated,
Zhōu Déwēi and his son died,
and the Prince of Jìn only succeeded after great peril.
"Yù"
is pronounced yù.
20 All the princes of Shǔ held military commands.
Péng Wáng Zōngdǐng said to his brothers:
"For royal princes to command troops
is the root of disaster and turmoil.
Now the ruler is young and the ministers strong,
conflicts are about to arise.
Training soldiers and repairing armor
are not suitable for us."
He thus firmly declined the military command,
and the Shǔ ruler permitted it.
He merely built a study and planted pines and bamboos for his own enjoyment.
History records that Wáng Zōngdǐng sought self-preservation but offered no support to the state.
21 Tàiníng military governor Zhāng Wànjìn
was reckless and fond of turmoil.
At that time, favored officials were in power
and often demanded bribes from Wànjìn.
Hearing that the Jìn army was about to march,
on Jǐyǒu,
Wànjìn sent an envoy to submit to Jìn,
and requested aid.
Liú Xún, the Tuánliànshǐ of Bózhōu, was appointed as Yǎnzhōu pacification commissioner,
leading troops to attack him.
Examination of discrepancies: The Zhuāngzōng Shílù states:
"On Jǐyǒu, eighth month of the fifteenth year of Tiānyòu,
Zhāng Wànjìn submitted."
The Mòdì Jì in the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ states:
"On Guǐwèi, third month of the fifth year of Zhēnmíng,
Zhāng Shǒujìn was stripped of titles and ranks,
and Liú Xún was appointed commissioner;
in the tenth month, Yǎnzhōu was captured,
and Shǒujìn’s clan was exterminated."
The biography of Wànjìn states:
"He rebelled in the seventh month of the fourth year of Zhēnmíng,
and in the winter of the fifth year,
his city was taken."
The biography of Liú Xún states:
"In the fifth year,
Wànjìn rebelled,
and in winter,
his city was taken."
The biography of Wànjìn in the Zhuāngzōng Shílù states:
"Liú Xún besieged it for years,
then slaughtered the city."
The Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn states:
"In the eighth month of the fifteenth year of Tiānyòu,
Wànjìn submitted to us."
Since Jūnwáng had no Shílù,
the annals and biographies often differ,
making it hard to rely on them.
Here, the Zhuāngzōng Shílù Lièzhuàn is taken as definitive.
22 On Jiǎzǐ,
Shǔ’s Shùndé Empress passed away.
She was née Zhōu,
the principal wife of Shǔ ruler Jiàn.
23 On Yǐchǒu,
the Shǔ ruler appointed palace attendants Wáng Tíngshào, Ōuyáng Huǎng, Lǐ Zhōulù, Zhū Guāngbǎo, Sòng Chéngyùn, Tián Lǔchái, etc., as generals and military commanders.
"Zhū Guāngbǎo"
should be
"Sòng Guāngbǎo."
"Yùn"
is pronounced yùn.
They were arrogant, unrestrained, greedy, and cruel,
becoming a major problem for Shǔ.
Zhōu Xiáng strongly admonished,
but he was not heeded.
Zhōu Xiáng rose with Shǔ ruler Jiàn from military origins,
having experienced many events.
At night,
taking advantage of the wind, they set fire,
burning hundreds of neighboring military barracks.
The next morning,
they summoned craftsmen to enlarge their residences;
the Shǔ ruler did not even inquire.
Guāngbǎo
was a cousin of Guāngsì.
24 The Prince of Jìn went from Wèizhōu to Yángliú,
led troops to raid Yùnzhōu and Púzhōu before returning,
advanced along the river,
and encamped at Májiā Dù.
Hè Huái and Xiè Yànzhāng led Liáng troops to camp at Xíngtái Village north of Púzhōu,
maintaining a standoff without engaging.
Whenever it is said they maintained a standoff without engaging,
it means their strength was insufficient to overcome each other,
and each awaited an opportunity to exploit the other’s situation.
The Prince of Jìn liked to personally lead light cavalry to challenge the enemy camp,
finding himself in danger and distress several times,
but was saved by Lǐ Shàoróng’s fierce fighting and protection.
He narrowly escaped.
The Prince of Zhào, Wáng Róng, and Wáng Chùzhí both sent envoys with letters saying:
"The lives of the common people depend on you,
the restoration of our dynasty depends on you."
"Our dynasty"
refers to the Táng.
"Dynasty"
is pronounced cháo.
The Prince laughed and said to the envoys:
"To pacify the world,
how can it be achieved without a hundred battles!
How can one stay deep within curtains and rooms to grow fat!"
The Prince of Jìn said this
referring to Wáng Róng.
However, Wáng Róng’s aim was to preserve his ancestors’ legacy and indulge himself;
the Prince of Jìn aimed to destroy Liáng and avenge his shame.
After Liáng was destroyed,
Zhuāngzōng became complacent,
galloping and hunting,
thinking that not staying behind curtains to grow fat was right,
not realizing that staying behind curtains would bring disaster.
One day,
the King was about to leave the camp,
when the Capital Camp Commissioner Lǐ Cúnshěn grabbed his horse’s reins and tearfully admonished him:
"Your Majesty should value yourself for the sake of the realm.
Leading the charge and breaking through enemy formations
is the duty of generals and soldiers.
The Capital Camp Commissioner
is the officer in overall charge of all camp affairs,
a temporary appointment title of the time.
Wèi,
read as yúwèi fān;
the following wáng wèi zhī is the same.
Chén,
read as zhèn.
It is not the business of Your Majesty."
The King, because of this, pulled on the reins and turned back.
Another day,
waiting until Lǐ Cúnshěn was not present,
he whipped his horse and rushed out,
turning to say to his attendants:
"That old man spoils my fun!"
The King led several hundred cavalrymen to the Liáng camp,
Xiè Yànzhāng had five thousand elite troops lying in ambush beneath the embankment;
the King led a dozen or so cavalrymen across the embankment,
the ambushing troops sprang out,
surrounding the King in several tens of layers,
the King fought fiercely within,
the cavalrymen who arrived later attacked from the outside,
and he barely managed to get out.
Just then, Lǐ Cúnshěn arrived with reinforcements,
the Liáng troops then retreated,
and the King finally considered Lǐ Cúnshěn’s words to be loyal.
The historian says the Jìn King was brave but reckless,
repeatedly facing danger,
his survival was due to luck.
However, the reason he faced danger twice and survived twice
was entirely due to the strength of Lǐ Cúnshěn’s reinforcements.
To say
"that old man spoils my fun"
was that acceptable?
25 Wú’s Liú Xìn sent his general Zhāng Xuān and others, leading three thousand troops at night to attack Chǔ general Zhāng Kěqiú at Gǔtíng,
and defeated him;
he also sent Liáng Quán and others
to attack Wúyuè and Mǐn troops,
the two states, hearing that the Chǔ troops were defeated,
both withdrew and returned.
Qiánzhōu’s situation was now isolated.
Quán,
read as qiě yuán fān.
26 Méishān barbarians raided Shàozhōu,
Méishān barbarians lived within the boundaries of Shàozhōu.
In the fifth year of the Xīníng era of Sòng, Xīnhuà County was established,
located two hundred and fifty lǐ northeast of Shàozhōu.
27 In the ninth month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Shǔ’s Internal Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner Sòng Guāngsì yielded the position of Judge of the Six Armies to concurrently Secretariat Director Wáng Zōngbì,
the Shǔ ruler approved it.
28 Wú’s Liú Xìn attacked Qiánzhōu day and night with great urgency,
beheading several thousand,
but could not capture it;
he sent someone to persuade Tán Quánbō,
taking hostages and accepting bribes before returning.
Xú Wēn was greatly angered,
and caned Liú Xìn’s envoy.
Liú Xìn’s son, Liú Yīngyǎn, commanded the personal guard troops,

saying:
"Your father occupies the upstream territory,
commanding an army ten times larger,

Guǎnglíng lies at the lower reaches of the river,
thus Liú Xìn occupies the upstream territory.
At that time, Huáinán’s troops attacking Qián were ten times those of the Qián people.
This is rebellion!
You may take these troops and go,

He also sent Shēngzhōu Yá’nèi Commanding Officer Zhū Jǐngyú to go with him,
saying:
"Tán Quánbō’s defending soldiers are all farmers,

hearing that a large army is coming again,
they will certainly all flee,
what Tán Quánbō is defending is an empty city,
if you go, you will certainly capture it."
The historian says Xú Wēn was both able to control his generals,
and able to assess the enemy.
29 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Shǔ buried the Shénwǔ Shèngwén Xiàodé Mínghuì Emperor at Yǒnglíng,
temple name Gāozǔ.
30 Yuè ruler Liú Yán performed the southern suburban sacrifice,
granted a great amnesty,
and changed the state’s name to Hàn.
31 Liú Xìn, hearing Xú Wēn’s words,
was greatly afraid,
and led his troops back to attack Qiánzhōu.
As soon as the vanguard arrived,
the Qián troops all collapsed,
exactly as Xú Wēn had predicted.
They pursued and captured him.
In the first year of the Guāngqǐ era of Táng Emperor Xīzōng,
Tán Quánbō supported Lú Guāngchóu in occupying Qiánzhōu,
passing through two surnames in between,
until Tán Quánbō himself took it and perished.
He held the title of Bǎishèng Military Commissioner.
Previously,
Wúyuè King Qián Liú often went to pay tribute via Qiánzhōu,
but by this time the route was cut off,
Wúyuè used to pay tribute via the Qiánzhōu route,
see the second year of the previous volume for details.
Now that Qiánzhōu had come under Wú control,
the route was cut off.
Xiān,
read as xī jiàn fān.
They reached Dàliáng.
This is the water route for Mǐn and Yuè to pay tribute to Dàliáng.
However, Wúyuè certainly embarked from Xǔpǔ or Dìnghǎi,

"Hè Huái has come with all his forces,

Liú had been in the army since youth,

Textual Analysis says: The Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng states:
"In the fifteenth year of Tiānyòu,
Hè Děi was stationed at Xíngtáilǐ north of Púzhōu.
In the twelfth month,
on the xīnyǒu day,
the Emperor encamped at Línpú.
The enemy also abandoned their camp and followed us.
On the guǐhài day,
we encamped at Húliǔ.
The next day,
battle was joined,
and Wáng Yànzhāng fled in defeat to Púyáng.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
we attacked Púyáng,
and captured it in one assault."
According to the Táng Geographical Treatise,
Púzhōu is also called Púyáng Commandery,
with its seat at Juànchéng,
having the two counties of Púyáng and Línpú.
According to the Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng, then Xíngtáilǐ was east of Línpú,
and Húliǔ was east of Púyáng.
What Yànzhāng defended,
and what Zhuāngzōng captured,
was Púyáng County,
not Púzhōu.
Yet the Biographies of Zhuāngzōng and the Biography of Yán Bǎo in the Old History of the Five Dynasties both say that Yànzhāng's cavalry had already entered Púzhōu,
with only infantry arrayed below the mountain,
and by evening all had thoughts of returning.
This treats Púyáng as Púzhōu.
The Biography of Lǐ Sìzhāo,
has Sìzhāo saying:
"The enemy has no camp fortifications,
is far from Línpú,
the day is already late,
all have thoughts of returning.
If we just harass them with elite cavalry,
not letting them eat in the evening,
and pursue and attack after dusk,
we will certainly defeat them.
If we withdraw our troops and dismantle our camp,
and the enemy enters Línpú,
waiting until they are reorganized and come again,
then victory or defeat is undecided."
This also treats Púyáng as Línpú.
According to the Liáng Annals in the Old History,
in an edict of the fourth month of the fifth year of Zhēnmíng,
exempting tax levies in Púzhōu,
shows that Púzhōu still belonged to Liáng.
The Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng,
in the twelfth month of the sixteenth year of Tiānyòu,
records the capture of Púyáng,
and issuing an instruction to the people of Cáo and Pú,
urging them to submit,
shows that Púzhōu did not yet belong to Jìn.
Also, Hè Děi was stationed west of Tǔshān,
the Jìn army was east of him,
Yànzhāng had already entered Púyáng to the west,
how could Děi then go further east back to Línpú!
I suspect that in Bǎo's biography 'Púzhōu' and in Sìzhāo's biography 'Línpú' should both be 'Púyáng',
an error due to the historians' embellishment.
Also, the Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng,
last year in the twelfth month,
says Jìn had already captured Púyáng,
and here again says they attacked and captured Púyáng.
According to the Liáng Annals in the Old History,
last year in the twelfth month the Jìn people attacked and captured Púyáng;
this year in the twelfth month it again says the Jìn people captured Púyáng;
the Táng Annals record the capture of Púyáng last winter,
and this year in the fourth month pursuing and attacking Hè Děi as far as Púyáng,
with no event of capturing Púyáng in the twelfth month.
The Biography of Hè Děi,
in the fourth year of Zhēnmíng, says he led a large army and camped at Xíngtáicūn,
was defeated in battle in the twelfth month,
withdrew his army to Xíngtái in the fourth month,
and soon died.
If it is not a repetition in the Veritable Records and the Liáng Annals,
then it must be that although Táng obtained Púyáng last winter,
they abandoned it and did not hold it,
and captured it again this winter.
He appointed the Tiānpíng military governor Dài Sīyuǎn to replace him as the Northern Front Recruitment Commissioner,
stationing him on the river to resist the Jìn.

'Interrogating with a written list' means

the Prince removed Jiànjí from his military post,
appointing him Prefect of Dàizhōu instead.
(The historian remarks that the Prince of Jin was unable to trust and employ worthy generals.
Lǐ Jiànjí, because of this, harbored resentment and died.)
4. Hàn's Yáng Dòngqián requested the establishment of schools,
the opening of the imperial examinations,
and the setting up of a system for selecting officials.
The ruler of Hàn, Liú Yán, followed his advice.
5. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Lǐ Qí, the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
Qí
was the younger brother of Lǐ Tǐng.
(Lǐ Tǐng first appears in the third year of Tiānfù of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng and died during the time when Liáng executed Zhū Yǒuguì.)
Relying on the influence of Zhào Yán and Zhāng Hànjié,
he was quite involved in accepting bribes.
Xiāo Qǐng served as chancellor alongside Qí.
Qǐng was cautious and secretive, and he covertly watched for Qí's faults.
After a long time,
there was someone seeking an official post through a provisional appointment.
Qí changed the provisional appointment to a regular one.
Qǐng reported this.
(The Ouyáng History says: An official privately connected to Qí was supposed to receive a probationary post.
Qí changed the probationary post to a regular one.
This was exposed by Qǐng.)
The intention was to exile Qí to a distant place.
Zhào and Zhāng intervened on his behalf.
He was merely dismissed and made Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
(Textual analysis notes: The Old History of the Five Dynasties only records the month and day Qí became chancellor,
not the year and month he was dismissed.
Therefore, it is mentioned here to conclude the matter.)
6. The military governor of Hézhōng, Prince of Jì Zhū Yǒuqiān, attacked and seized Tóngzhōu with his troops,
expelling the military governor of Zhōngwǔ, Chéng Quánhuī.
Quánhuī fled to Dàiliáng.
Yǒuqiān made his son, Lìngdé, the acting military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
He submitted a memorial requesting the symbols of authority (the ceremonial axe and banner).
The Emperor was angry
and did not grant it.
Later, fearing Yǒuqiān's resentment,
on the day Jǐyǒu,
he appointed Yǒuqiān to concurrently hold the post of military governor of Zhōngwǔ.
By the time the edict was issued,
Yǒuqiān had already requested the symbols of authority from the Prince of Jin.
(Zhū Yǒuqiān from this point on submitted to Jìn.)
(Textual analysis notes: The Biography of Zhuāngzōng states,
"The Emperor ordered his advisor Wáng Zhèngyán to send the ceremonial banner and confer it upon him."
The Biographies in the Veritable Records of Zhuāngzōng and the Biography of Yǒuqiān in the Old History of the Five Dynasties both say
"Yǒuqiān made Lìngdé the commander,
requested the symbols of authority,
but it was not granted."
The Basic Annals of Emperor Mò of the Old History of the Five Dynasties, under the sixth year of Zhēnmíng, states,
"[He] captured Tóngzhōu,
made Lìngdé the acting military governor,
submitted a memorial requesting the ceremonial banner,
but it was not approved."
However,
"in the fourth year of Zhēnmíng, sixth month, day Jiǎchén,
Zhū Lìngdé, Prefect of Shèzhōu, was made acting military governor of Zhōngwǔ."
It is likely that Tóngzhōu was already captured in the fourth year.)
7. The King of Wú, Xuān (Yáng Lóngyǎn), was dignified, sincere, respectful, and cautious.
Xú Wēn and his sons monopolized power.
The King never showed any sign of dissatisfaction in his words or expression.
Because of this, Wēn felt at ease.
After the establishment of the state and the adoption of imperial rituals,
(see the previous year in the previous volume.)
he often indulged in heavy drinking and ate little,
and consequently fell ill.
In the fifth month,
Wēn came to court from Jīnlíng,
to discuss who should be the successor.
Someone, hoping to curry favor with Wēn, said:
"The First Ruler of Shǔ said to the Martial Marquis: 'My heir is untalented.
You should take the throne yourself.'"
(See Volume 69, the third year of Huángchū of Emperor Wén of Wèi.)
Wēn said, "If I truly had the intention to take it for myself,
it would have been back when I executed Zhāng Hào,
(The execution of Zhāng Hào is recorded in Volume 269, the second year of Kāipíng.)
I would have ensured the Yáng family had no sons.
Even if they had a daughter, I would have set her up.
Anyone who dares to speak recklessly again will be executed!"
He then, in the King's name, welcomed the Duke of Dānyáng, Yáng Pǔ, to supervise the state.
(Textual analysis notes: The Records of Wú and the History of the Nine States place
the statement "even if they had a daughter, I would have set her up"
at the time of executing Zhāng Hào.
Here we follow the Old History of the Five Dynasties.)
The Annals of the Ten States says:
"The King was seriously ill.
The Grand Chancellor Wēn came to court
to discuss establishing a successor.
The Vice Director of the Chancellery, Yán Kěqiú, said that none of the King's sons were talented,
citing the incident where the First Ruler of Shǔ entrusted Zhūgě Liàng with his final instructions.
Wēn informed Xú Zhīgào.
Zhīgào said, 'Kěqiú is very knowledgeable,
but his words are not necessarily sincere.
He is probably just going along with your wishes, sir.'
Wēn said, 'If I wanted to take it for myself,
it wouldn't have been just today.
During the rebellion of Zhāng Hào,
the successor king was young and weak,
and power was in my hands.
Taking it would have been easier than turning over my hand.
But I recall when Tàizǔ was critically ill,
he wanted to pass the throne to Liú Wēi.
I alone strenuously objected.
Tàizǔ wept
and entrusted the future affairs to me.
How could I forget that!'
He then, together with the Commissioner of the Palace Attendants, Wáng Lìngmóu, decided on a plan.
In the name of Lóngyǎn,
they welcomed the Duke of Dānyáng, Yáng Pǔ, to supervise the state.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Lóngyǎn died.
In the sixth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Pǔ ascended the throne."
(It is unlikely that Yán Kěqiú would have made such a statement.
Here we follow the Old History of the Five Dynasties.)
(Passing over Yáng Méng and establishing Pǔ was because Méng was disliked by Xú Wēn.)
On the day Jǐchǒu,
King Xuān passed away.
He was twenty-four years old.
On the day Wùshēn,
Pǔ ascended the throne as King of Wú.
Pǔ
was the fourth son of Yáng Xíngmì.
8. On the day Dīngsì,

Shǔ appointed the Minister over the Masses and Vice Director of the Chancellery, Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery, Zhōu Xiáng, as Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
and concurrently Military Governor of Yǒngpíng.
(At the end of the Táng, the Yǒngpíng Army was established in Qióngzhōu.
According to the Geographical Treatise in the Ouyáng History,
Shǔ made Yǎzhōu the seat of the Yǒngpíng military command.)
9. The Emperor appointed Liú Xún, the military governor of Tàiníng, as the Commissioner for Pacification of the Hézhōng Circuit,
commanding Yǐn Hào, the military governor of Gǎnhuà; Wēn Zhāotú, the military governor of Jìngshèng; and Duàn Níng, the Commissioner of the Palace Buildings, to attack Tóngzhōu.
10. In the intercalary month,
on the first day, Gēngshēn,
the ruler of Shǔ built an ancestral temple for Gāozǔ (Wáng Jiàn) at Wànlǐ Bridge.
(The origin of the 'original temple' dates back to Hàn.
Yuán
means 'again'.
After the main ancestral temple was already established, a second temple built was called the 'original temple'.
Wànlǐ Bridge is in Chéngdū.
The Universal Geography says: In the past, Fèi Yī was sent as an envoy to Wú.
Zhūgě Liàng saw him off at this bridge
and said:
"The journey of ten thousand lǐ
begins here."
Hence the bridge was named.)
He offered common delicacies,
(referring to flavors he was usually fond of.)
(The Record of Rites, Suburban Sacrifices says: In the Dì and Cháng sacrifices,
one dares not use common delicacies but values variety,
which is the principle for interacting with the spirits.)
Xiè,
(pronounced xiè).
The official Dù Shìqiáo considered this improper.
(Huáyáng County was originally established in the seventeenth year of Zhēnguān of Táng as Shǔ County,
located within the walls of Yìzhōu,
sharing governance with Chéngdū.
It was renamed Huáyáng County in the first year of Qiányuán.)
Huá,
(pronounced huà).
The ruler wanted to execute him.
The Empress Dowager considered it unacceptable.
He was instead stripped of his office and exiled to Lízhōu.
Shìqiáo, filled with indignation,
drowned himself.
11. Liú Xún and others besieged Tóngzhōu.
Zhū Yǒuqiān sought aid from Jìn.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Prince of Jin sent Lǐ Cúnshěn, Lǐ Sìzhāo, Lǐ Jiànjí, and Lǐ Cúnzhì, the Prefect of Cízhōu, to lead troops to rescue him.
On the 12th day of the Yǐmǎo month,
the ruler of Shǔ issued an edict for a northern tour.
He appointed Hán Zhāo, the Minister of Rites and concurrently the Governor of Chéngdū, as Grand Academician of the Wénsī Hall,
placing his rank above that of the Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts.
Zhāo possessed no literary talent,
but through flattery and cunning, he gained favor,
moving freely in and out of the palace.
He requested from the ruler of Shǔ the prefectures of Tōng, Qú, Bā, and Jí to sell them off to fund the construction of his residence.
The ruler of Shǔ granted his request.
Those with insight knew that Shǔ was about to perish.
In the eighth month,
on the Wùchén day,
the ruler of Shǔ departed from Chéngdū,
clad in golden armor,
wearing a pearl-adorned cap,
and carrying a bow and arrows as he marched.
Banners, flags, soldiers, and armor
stretched for over a hundred lǐ.
Duàn Róng, the magistrate of Luò, submitted a memorial:
Luò
was an ancient county of Hàn,
under Táng, it belonged to Hàn Prefecture,
serving as the prefectural seat.
"Shàng"
is pronounced "shí zhǎng fān."
"It is not advisable to venture far from the capital.
You should entrust a senior minister with the task of leading the campaign."
His advice was not heeded.
In the ninth month,
they encamped at Ānyuǎn City.
Generally, when troops stay one night, it is called "xìn";
staying beyond one night is called "cì."
On the 13th, Lǐ Cúnshěn and others arrived at Hézhōng,
crossing the river that very day.
They crossed the river from Hézhōng to rescue Tóng Prefecture.
In every battle, they pursued relentlessly without pause.
Cúnshěn selected two hundred elite armored soldiers,
mingled them with Hézhōng troops,
and directly pressed against Liú Xún's fortifications.
Xún dispatched a thousand cavalry to pursue them;
upon learning that the Jìn forces had arrived,
he was greatly alarmed.
At that time, Xún's troops had gone out to pursue the Hézhōng soldiers,
but the Jìn cavalry counterattacked them,
capturing fifty of Liáng's cavalrymen.
When the Liáng forces realized they were facing the Jìn army,
they were greatly shocked.
The Jìn army encamped at Cháoyì.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: Cháoyì is located thirty-five lǐ east of Tóng Prefecture.
Hézhōng had long served Liáng.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng,
Zhū Quánzhōng subjugated Wáng Kē,
and Hézhōng subsequently served Liáng.
As various armies converged in large numbers,
the prices of fodder and grain soared.
Yǒuqiān's sons advised Yǒuqiān
to submit to Liáng,
in order to make their troops withdraw.
Yǒuqiān replied:
"In the past, the Prince of Jìn personally came to my aid in a crisis,
fighting through the night by torchlight.
This refers to the battle against Kāng Huáizhēn and others.
The event is recorded in the 268th scroll, in the second year of Qiánhuà.
It refers to the confrontation at the river.
He shared his provisions and supplies with me.
How could I betray him!"
The Jìn forces divided their troops to attack Huá Prefecture,
destroying its outer walls.
Lǐ Cúnshěn and others held their positions for several weeks,
then advanced to press against Liú Xún's camp.
Xún and others led their entire force out to engage in battle,
but suffered a major defeat.
They gathered their remaining troops and retreated to defend Luówén Fort.
The "Xuē Shǐ" states: Xún retreated with his remaining troops to defend Luówén Fort in Huá Prefecture.
Cúnshěn said to Lǐ Sìzhāo:
"A cornered beast will fight desperately.
It would be better to leave them a path of retreat,
and then attack them."
He then sent men to pasture horses at Shāyuàn.
Xún and others fled under cover of darkness.
They were pursued to the Wèi River,
where they were defeated again,
suffering heavy casualties and losses.
Liú Xún's military strategies
involved intricate planning at every step,
earning him fame at the time.
Yet, in the battle at Tóng Prefecture,
when he encountered Lǐ Cúnshěn,
he was toyed with
like an infant in the palm of someone's hand.
Why was this?
It was due to "niè"!
"Niè" refers to a bird that has been wounded.
Upon hearing the twang of a bowstring, it will soar high to escape,
but if its strength is insufficient, it will fall.
Thus, even an empty bow can bring it down.
Liú Xún had previously been defeated by Jìn troops.
Upon seeing the Jìn forces approach,
his morale was crushed and his courage vanished.
How could he possibly stand against them as an enemy!
He led his troops to seize territory as far as Xiàguī,
paid homage at the imperial tombs of the Táng emperors,
wept before them, and then returned.
The Táng imperial tombs are located in Fèngxiān County, Tóng Prefecture.
"Huán"
is pronounced "cóng xuān fān,"
or also as the usual pronunciation.
The Hézhōng troops advanced to attack Chóng Prefecture.
Wēn Zhāotú, the Military Commissioner of Jìngshèng, was greatly frightened.
In the first year,
Wēn Tāo surrendered with the Yìshèng Army,
Yào Prefecture was renamed Chóng Prefecture,
Yìshèng was changed to Jìngshèng,
and Tāo was granted his current name.
"What you possess are merely the two counties of Huáyuán and Měiyuán.
At the end of the Táng, Wēn Tāo became a bandit,
occupying Huáyuán County.
Lǐ Màozhēn established Huáyuán as Mào Prefecture,
with Tāo as its Prefect.
It was later renamed Yào Prefecture.
He also established Měiyuán County as Dǐng Prefecture,
forming the Yìshèng Army,
and appointed Tāo as its Military Commissioner.
Upon surrendering to Liáng,
Yào Prefecture was renamed Chóng Prefecture,
Dǐng Prefecture was renamed Yù Prefecture,
and Yìshèng was changed to Jìngshèng.
Thus, what he possessed originally were just two Táng counties.
In reality, he is merely a garrison commander.
Compared to a powerful province,
how can they be mentioned in the same breath?
Do you, sir, desire this?"
Zhāotú replied:
"Indeed."
Wéi said:
"I shall devise a plan for you, sir."
He then instructed Zhāotú to submit a petition requesting a transfer to another command.
The Emperor appointed Huá Wēnqí, the Defensive Commissioner of Rǔ Prefecture, to temporarily act as the Jìngshèng Military Commissioner-in-waiting.
On the 14th, in winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
the ruler of Shǔ went to the Wǔdìng Army,
and after a few days,
returned to Ānyuǎn.
On the 15th, in the eleventh month,
on the first day, Wùzǐ,
the ruler of Shǔ appointed Wáng Zōngchóu, who also served as Palace Attendant, as Military Commissioner of Shānnán, Northwest Front Commander-in-Chief, and Field Army Pacification Commissioner.

He appointed Wáng Zōngyù, Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng and concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat, Wáng Zōngyàn, Commander of the Yǒngníng Army, and Wáng Zōngxìn, Commander of the Left Shényǒng Army, as three Deputy Commanders to assist him.
They led troops to attack Qí,
exiting through the old pass,
and encamping at Xiányí.
"Bì" means
to construct fortifications to station troops.
Xiányí should be located within the boundaries of Yuán County, Lǒng Prefecture.
Liángyuán County belonged to Jīng Prefecture.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: It is located sixty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
On the Dīngyǒu day,
Wáng Zōngchóu attacked Lǒng Prefecture.
The Prince of Qí personally led fifteen thousand men to station at Yáng.
Yáng County belonged to Lǒng Prefecture.
The "Jiǔyù Zhì" states: It is located sixty-seven lǐ east of the prefecture,
fifty-five lǐ east of Fèngxiáng.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Shǔ general Chén Yànwēi exited Sǎnguān,
and defeated the Qí troops at Jiànkuò Ridge.
Dù Yòu said: Qí Mountain is present-day Qíshān County;
the mountain has two peaks,
hence it is commonly called Jiànkuò Ridge.
"Bài"
is pronounced "bǔ mài fān."
"Kuò"
is pronounced "gǔ huó fān."
He then led his troops back.
Zōngyù stationed at Tài
Prefecture,
Zōngchóu stationed at Shàngguī,
and Zōngyàn and Zōngxìn stationed at Wēiwǔ Fortress.
On the Gēngxū day,
the ruler of Shǔ departed from Ānyuǎn City.
In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
he arrived at Lìzhōu.
Lín Sī'è, the Tuánliànshǐ of Lángzhōu, came to pay court,
requesting that the ruler visit his administrative seat.
The ruler consented.
Lángzhōng
was the administrative seat of Lín Sī'è.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: From Lìzhōu southeast to Lángzhōu is 240 lǐ.
On the Guǐhài day,
he sailed down the river,
sailing on the Jiālíng River.
Huà,
is the same as zhòu (day).
Gě,
is pronounced gǔ wǒ fān.
The people of Chǔ call large ships gě.
The prefectures and counties provided supplies,
and the people began to feel sorrow and resentment.
This summarizes the prefectures and counties through which the ruler of Shǔ passed,
not specifically referring only to Lángzhōu.
On the Rénshēn day,
he arrived at Lángzhōu.
A commoner of the prefecture, Hé Kāng, had a daughter of great beauty
who was about to be married.
The ruler of Shǔ took her,
and bestowed one hundred bolts of silk upon her husband's family.
The husband died from overwhelming grief.
The Lǐjì states: "A feudal lord does not lower himself to fish for beauty."
The commentary says: This means he does not take from within his own state.
Taking from within the state is considered lowering oneself to fish for beauty.
For a ruler of a state to take from within,
is like catching fish:
whatever enters the net is taken,
showing no discrimination.
Wáng Yǎn seized another man's wife;
his "fishing" was even worse!
On the Guǐwèi day,
he arrived at Zǐzhōu.
16. Zhào Wáng Róng, relying on his family's generations-long governance of Chéngdé,
and having won the hearts of the people of Zhào,
having grown up in wealth and honor,
elegant and at ease,
built mansions, gardens, and ponds,
achieving the utmost splendor of the time.
He often engaged in amusement and excursions,
not personally attending to government affairs.
All matters were left to his subordinates to complete.
He remained deep within his mansion,
and power shifted to those around him.
The Xíngjūn Sīmǎ Lǐ Ăi and the eunuch Lǐ Hóngguī wielded authority both inside and outside the court;
outside was Lǐ Ăi,
inside was Lǐ Hóngguī.
Initially,
Liú Rén'gōng sent his officer Zhāng Wénlǐ to accompany his son Liú Shǒuwén to garrison Cāngzhōu.
When Shǒuwén went to Yōuzhōu to visit his father,
Wénlǐ seized the city behind his back and rebelled.
The people of Cāng attacked him,
and he fled to Zhènzhōu.
This recounts events from the end of the Táng,
narrating the origin of Zhāng Wénlǐ.
Shěng (visit),
is pronounced xī jǐng fān.
He claimed to understand military affairs,
and Zhào Wáng Róng found him remarkable,
adopting him as a son,
changing his name to Dé Míng,
and entrusting all military matters to him.
Dé Míng led the camp troops to follow the Jìn Wáng;
this matter began in the first year of Qiánhuà of Tàizǔ, in scroll 267.
He sent the Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ Fú Xí to replace him and return,
appointing him as Fángchéngshǐ.
In his later years, Róng was fond of Buddhism and seeking immortality.
He devoted himself to lecturing on Buddhist scriptures,
receiving talismans and registers,
extensively holding fasting ceremonies,
and compounding elixirs.
He lavishly decorated lodgings on the Western Hills,
and often went there for excursions.
The Western Hills of Zhènzhōu are called Fángshān,
on which there is a temple to the Queen Mother of the West.
Róng, wishing to seek immortality,
therefore frequently went there for excursions.
He would stay for several months before returning.
The generals, officers, and soldiers accompanying him often numbered no less than ten thousand.
The coming and going, with provisions and lodgings,
caused suffering for both the army and the people.
In this month,
returning from the Western Hills,
he stayed overnight at Gǔyíng Village.
Shí Xīméng urged the king to go elsewhere again;
Lǐ Hóngguī said to the king:
"The Jìn Wáng fights bloody battles along the river,
sometimes south of the river,
sometimes north of the river,
hence 'along the river.'
He personally braves arrows and stones,
yet you, king, exclusively use funds meant for the army on unnecessary expenses.
Moreover, these are difficult times,
and people's hearts are hard to fathom.
You, king, have long left your mansion empty,
traveling far on excursions.
What if some treacherous person stages a revolt,
closes the gates and resists?
What will you do then?"
The king was about to return,
but Xīméng secretly said to the king:
"Hóngguī wildly creates suspicion and discord,
uttering disrespectful words to coerce and threaten you, king.
He only wishes to boast and show off externally,
enhancing his own authority and influence."
The king then stayed,
and for two nights showed no intention of returning.
The poem "Jiǔ Yù" says: "For you, two nights."
The Máo commentary states: Two nights is called xìn.
This differs from the meaning in the Zuǒzhuàn
"an army traveling one night is called xìn"
— the meanings are different.
Donning armor and drawing blades,
they went before the tent and said to the king:
"The soldiers have been exposed for too long;
we wish to follow you, king, back!"
Hóngguī then stepped forward and said:
"Shí Xīméng incessantly urges you, king, to go on excursions,
and I have heard he intends to secretly plot regicide and rebellion.
I request he be executed to appease the masses."
The king did not listen.
The officer soldiers then raised a great clamor,
cut off Xīméng's head,
and presented it before him.
The king was both angry and afraid,
and hurriedly returned to his mansion.
That evening,
he sent his eldest son, the Deputy Ambassador Zhāozuò, and Wáng Dé Míng to lead troops and surround the residences of Hóngguī and Lǐ Ăi,
executing their clans,
implicating several dozen families.
He also killed Sū Hànhéng,
arrested his faction,
thoroughly investigated the evidence of rebellion,
causing great fear among the personal army.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Wénlǐ inciting the soldiers to kill Wáng Róng.
Zhì (investigate),
is pronounced zhí zhī fān;
same below.
17. The city walls of Jīnlíng in Wú were completed.
Chén Yànqiān presented the account books of expenses.
Xú Wēn said:
"Since I have entrusted you, sir,
I will not audit the accounts."
He burned them all.
18. Initially,
Mǐn Wáng Shěnzhī, acting under imperial authority, conferred upon his nephew, the Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu, Yán Bīn, the additional title of Pínglú Jiédùshǐ.
Yán Bīn governed Quánzhōu for seventeen years,
and the officials and people were at peace.
When a white deer and purple fungus were obtained,
the monk Hào Yuán considered them omens of a king.
Yán Bīn thus became arrogant and unrestrained,
secretly sending envoys by sea to offer tribute,
requesting to be made Jiédùshǐ of Quánzhōu.
When the matter was discovered,
Shěnzhī executed Hào Yuán and his faction,
and demoted Yán Bīn, sending him back to his private residence.
19. Hàn Zhǔ Yán sent an envoy to establish friendly relations with Shǔ.
20. Wúyuè Wáng Liú sent an envoy to seek a marriage for his son Chuán Xiù from Chǔ.
Chǔ Wáng Yīn agreed.
The first year of Lóngdé
(Xīnsì, 921)
The era name was changed in the fifth month of this year.
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
the ruler of Shǔ returned to Chéngdū.
Last year in the seventh month, the ruler of Shǔ set out on an inspection tour;
he only returned now.
2. Initially,
when the ruler of Shǔ was crown prince,
Gāozǔ arranged his marriage to the daughter of the Bīngbù Shàngshū Gāo Zhīyán.
She was not favored,
(Wáng Jiàn, the ruler of Shǔ, was given the temple name Gāozǔ).
and was especially neglected and treated coldly.
At this point, she was sent back to her family.
Zhīyán was shocked, fell down,
and died without eating.
The Wéi consort
was the granddaughter of Xú Gēng.
She was exceptionally beautiful.
When the ruler of Shǔ visited the Xú family,
he saw her and was pleased.
The Empress Dowager then took her into the rear palace.
The ruler of Shǔ did not wish to marry someone from his maternal clan,
