Chùzhí was troubled by this.
Since Xīnzhōu bordered the Qìdān,
he secretly sent someone to tell Yù
(Xīnzhōu
was a remote border area,
connecting to the Qìdān in the north.
"To tell" (语)
is pronounced "yù".)
to have them invade the frontier,
aiming to relieve the siege of Zhènzhōu.
Although Wáng Yù might not be able to relieve the siege of Zhènzhōu,
he could still serve as a guide for the Qìdān to invade Jìn.
Yù did not listen.
Yù had always resented Dū usurping his family's inheritance.
He then demanded from Chùzhí to be made the heir,
and Chùzhí agreed.
The people of the military headquarters all opposed summoning the Qìdān.
Dū also feared Yù would seize his position.
He secretly plotted with the clerk Hé Zhāoxùn to seize Chùzhí.
It happened that Chùzhí was feasting with Zhāng Wénlǐ east of the city.
According to this, Zhāng Wénlǐ was under attack at the time;
how could he come to Dìngzhōu to feast with Wáng Chùzhí?
The one feasting with Chùzhí must have been an envoy of Wénlǐ.
After "Wénlǐ"
there should be
"envoy"
[Chapter note: The twelve-line edition has
"envoy"
; the eleven-line edition is the same;
the Kǒng edition is the same;
Zhāng's collation is the same.
Dū had several hundred soldiers of the new army lie in ambush at the headquarters residence.
They raised a great clamor and seized him,
saying:
"The officers and soldiers do not wish to summon the Qìdān to the city.
We request the Commissioner to retire to the Western Residence."
They then imprisoned him along with his wives and concubines in the Western Residence.
Generally, in official residences, the eastern side is superior.
The Western Residence refers to a place for peaceful retirement.
At the end of the Táng, Wáng Chùcún commanded Yìwǔ.
Brothers succeeded one another,
but by this time, it was ruined.
Dū made himself the acting military governor,
and fully reported the situation to the Jìn King.
The Jìn King accordingly replaced Chùzhí with Dū.
This sets the background for Wáng Dū again summoning the Qìdān to Zhōngshān during the reign of Táng Míngzōng.
17. Wú’s Xú Wēn advised the King of Wú to perform the suburban sacrifice to the south.
Someone said:
“The ritual music is not yet prepared;
moreover, when Táng performed the suburban sacrifice to the south,
its cost was enormous,
and we cannot manage it now.”
Xú Wēn said:
“How can there be a king who does not serve Heaven!
I have heard that in serving Heaven, sincerity is valued;
what use is great expense!
Whenever Táng performed the suburban sacrifice,
they opened the southern gate,
and poured a hundred hú of grease onto its pivot.
Pouring grease onto the pivot
was to make it slippery and easy to turn,
and also to make the gate silent.
How is that worth emulating!”
The historian says that although Xú Wēn was not learned,
he understood the intention of the former kings in establishing rituals.
On the jiǎzǐ day
the King of Wú performed the suburban sacrifice to the south,
with Tàizǔ as the associate.
The King of Wú honored his
[father].
On the yǐchǒu day,
there was a great amnesty;
Xú Zhīgào was promoted to tóng píngzhāngshì,
and given charge of the Jiāngzhōu observation commissioner.
Soon after, Jiāngzhōu was made the Fènghuà Army,
and Xú Zhīgào was given charge as its military governor.
Xú Zhīgào rose from tuánliàn to observation commissioner,
and soon from liánchē to establishing a military governorship.
Xú Wēn heard that the Shòuzhōu tuánliàn commissioner Cuī Tàichū was harsh and exacting, losing the people’s hearts,
and wanted to summon him.
Xú Zhīgào said:
“Shòuzhōu is a major frontier town;
summoning him might cause a revolt;
it would be better to have him come to court,
and then detain him.”
Xú Wēn angrily said:
“If we cannot control one Cuī Tàichū,
what can we do about others!”
The historian says Xú Wēn’s authority and strategy surpassed Zhīgào’s.
18. In the eleventh month,
the King of Jìn sent Lǐ Cúnshěn and Lǐ Sìyuán to guard Déshèng,
and personally led troops to attack Zhènzhōu.
Zhāng Chùjǐn sent his younger brother Chùqí and his advisor Qí Jiǎn to apologize and submit,
but the King of Jìn did not accept,
attacking with all his elite forces;
after ten days, he had not taken it.
The King of Jìn only knew how to fight decisive battles in the wild, with victory or defeat determined in a breath,
and did not know the difficulty of attacking a city.
He hurried to Dìngzhōu,
wanting to seek aid from Wáng Chùzhí.
The Jìn troops pursued him to Xíngtáng,
and killed him.
Xíngtáng,
the Hàn dynasty’s Nánxíngtáng County,
belonged to Zhènzhōu in Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì says: it is fifty-five lǐ north of the prefecture.
19. The Khitan ruler, having already promised Lú Wénjìn to send troops,
Zhāng Wénlǐ, through Lú Wénjìn, sought aid from the Khitan.
This matter is seen above.
“In Zhènzhōu, beautiful women are like clouds,
gold and silk are like mountains;
if the Heavenly King goes quickly,
they will all be your possessions;
if not,
they will be taken by the King of Jìn.”
The Khitan ruler thought this reasonable,
and mobilized all his available forces to go south.
The historian says the Khitan were lured by profit to come,
without having any intention to seize the Central Plains.
“I have the wealth of sheep and horses at Xīlóu,
its pleasures are inexhaustible;
why must we toil our armies, going far out to take risks and seek profit!
I have heard that the King of Jìn in warfare
is unmatched in the world;
if by chance there is danger and defeat,
how could we ever regret it enough!”
The Khitan ruler did not listen.
In the twelfth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
they attacked Yōuzhōu,
and Lǐ Shàohóng defended the city walls and held out.
In the fifth year of Zhēnmíng,
the King of Jìn had ordered Lǐ Shàohóng to oversee the military and administrative affairs of Yōuzhōu.
They besieged Zhuōzhōu,
and after ten days captured it,
seizing the prefect Lǐ Sìbì,
and advanced to attack Dìngzhōu.
From Yōuzhōu southwest to Zhuōzhōu is one hundred twenty lǐ,
from Zhuōzhōu to Dìngzhōu is two hundred eighty lǐ.
The King of Jìn personally led five thousand of his own troops from Zhènzhōu to rescue it,
and sent the Shénwǔ capital commandant Wáng Sītóng to lead troops and garrison south of Lángshān to resist them.
Lángshān is two hundred lǐ northwest of Dìngzhōu,
and eighty lǐ northeast to Yìzhōu.
20. Gāo Jìchāng sent the capital commandant Ní Kěfú with ten thousand soldiers to repair the outer walls of Jiānglíng.
Jìchāng went to inspect,
reprimanded him for the slow progress of the work,
and caned him.
Jìchāng’s daughter was the wife of Kěfú’s son Zhījìn.
Jìchāng said to his daughter:
“Go back and tell your father-in-law: I only wanted to awe the masses and get things done.”
He gave her several hundred taels of white silver.
21. This year,
Hàn appointed the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Ní Shǔ as tóng píngzhāngshì.
22. The Chén and Xù barbarians invaded Chǔ,
and the Chǔ Níngyuǎn deputy military governor Yáo Yànzhāng attacked and pacified them.
In the first year of Tàizǔ’s Qiánhuà era,
Yáo Yànzhāng had already abandoned Róngzhōu and returned to Tánzhōu,
while still holding the title of Níngyuǎn deputy military governor as before.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the rénwǔ day, the first day of the month,
Wáng Dū visited Wáng Chùzhí at the western residence,
and Chùzhí struck his chest with a clenched fist,
saying:
“Treacherous villain,
how have I wronged you!”
Since there were no weapons,
he tried to bite his nose,
but Dù pulled back his sleeve and escaped.
Not long after,
Chùzhí died of worry and indignation.
2 On the jiǎwǔ day,
the Prince of Jìn arrived south of Xīnchéng.
According to Wèi Shōu's *Treatise on Geography*,
Xīnchéng was located in Wújí County,
which at that time belonged to Qízhōu.
Xīnlè,
was the ancient state of the Xiānyúzi.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Xīnshì County,
which was renamed Xīnlè during the Suí dynasty,
and belonged to Dìngzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is located fifty *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Xīnlè County
was established in the 16th year of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty.
The name Xīnlè
originates from the time of Emperor Chéng of Hàn, when Féng Zhāoyí, the mother of the Filial Prince of Zhōngshān, accompanied the prince to his fiefdom.
A palace was built in Lèlǐ,
located in the western countryside,
and was called Xīlè Chéng (Western Lè City).
Later, through linguistic corruption,
the pronunciation of
"Xī" (west)
became
"Xīn" (new),
hence the name Xīnlè (New Lè).
The officers and soldiers all turned pale with fear,
and some soldiers deserted.
The commanding generals executed them but could not stop the desertions.
The various generals all said:
"The barbarians have come with their entire nation's force;
we are outnumbered and cannot match them.
Furthermore, we have heard that the Liáng bandits are invading internally.
It would be appropriate to withdraw our troops to Wèizhōu to save our foundation,
or perhaps we should lift the siege of Zhènzhōu
and enter Jǐngxíng to the west to avoid them."
The Prince of Jìn hesitated and had not yet decided.
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"The Khitan were lured by Wáng Yù,
and came fundamentally for profit and wealth;
they are not capable of rescuing Zhènzhōu from its dire straits.
Your Highness has recently defeated the Liáng troops;
in the 5th year of Zhēnmíng, you defeated Hè Huái at Húliǔ,
and also defeated Wáng Zàn at Qīchéng,
and this year defeated Dài Sīyuǎn at Déshèng.
When the Khitan hear of Your Highness's arrival,
their hearts will be dismayed and their morale depleted.

5. Yán Bǎo, the military governor of Tiānpíng and concurrently palace attendant of Jìn, built fortifications to besiege Zhènzhōu.
He diverted the waters of the Hūtuó River to encircle it.
Communication inside and outside was cut off.
The food in the city was exhausted.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
they sent out over five hundred men to seek food.
Bǎo allowed them to exit,
intending to ambush and capture them.
These men then attacked the long siege lines.
(The text "these men"
collectively refers to the over five hundred Zhènzhōu soldiers.)
Bǎo's forces were unprepared.
Suddenly, several thousand more men arrived.
Before the various armies could assemble,
the Zhènzhōu men broke through the long siege lines and emerged.
They set fires and attacked Bǎo's camp.
Bǎo could not resist,
and retreated to defend Zhàozhōu.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Zhènzhōu is 190 lǐ south to Zhàozhōu.)
They seized his fodder and grain,
which lasted for several days.
When the Prince of Jìn heard of this,
he appointed Lǐ Sìzhāo, the military governor of Zhāoyì and concurrently secretariat director, as the northern front pacification commissioner,
to replace Bǎo.
6. In summer,
in the fourth month,
the daughter of Shǔ military commissioner Wáng Chénggāng was about to be married.
The ruler of Shǔ took her into his palace.
Chénggāng pleaded for her return.
The ruler of Shǔ was angered,
and exiled him to Màozhōu.
The daughter, hearing her father had been punished,
committed suicide.
(The ruler of Shǔ took Hé Kāng's daughter,
and her husband died because of it;
he took Wáng Chénggāng's daughter,
then Chénggāng was punished because of it,
and the daughter killed herself because of it. The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn* repeatedly records this to serve as a warning.)
7. On the jiǎxū day,
Zhāng Chùjǐn sent a thousand soldiers to welcome grain supplies at Jiǔmén.
Lǐ Sìzhāo set an ambush at the old camp.
(The old camp
was Yán Bǎo's camp.)
They killed or captured almost all of them.
Five remaining men hid among the ruins of a wall.
Sìzhāo circled his horse and shot at them.
A Zhènzhōu soldier shot an arrow that hit him in the head.
Sìzhāo's quiver was empty of arrows.
He pulled the arrow from his head and shot it back,
killing the man with one shot.
As dusk fell,
he returned to camp.
The wound bled incessantly,
and he died that night.
When the Prince of Jìn heard of it,
he abstained from wine and meat for several days.
(The term "abstained"
means to refrain from consuming.)
The official Rèn Yuán
was sent to oversee the various armies attacking Zhènzhōu.
His orders were consistent,
and the Zhènzhōu people did not know of Sìzhāo's death.
(Yuán
was from Sānyuán.
The history remarks on Rèn Yuán's talent.)
The Prince of Jìn appointed Lǐ Cúnjìn, the commander of the Tiānxióng infantry and cavalry and military governor of Zhènwǔ, as the northern front pacification commissioner.
He ordered Sìzhāo's sons to escort the coffin back to Jìnyáng for burial.
His son Jìnéng disobeyed the order,
leading several thousand of his father's personal troops,
and from the field camp escorted the coffin back to Lùzhōu.
The Prince of Jìn sent his maternal brother Cúnwò galloping after them to explain the order.
The brothers were both indignant,
and wanted to kill Cúnwò.
(Lǐ Sìzhāo defended Lùzhōu to the death,
nurtured the wounded and crippled,
restored the military administration,
and had considerable merit and service.
He died on the battlefield.
The Prince of Jìn ordered them to escort the coffin back to Jìnyáng for burial,
but there was no command to honor the dead or comfort the living.
This is why the brothers were both indignant.)
(Cúnwò
was the Prince of Jìn's brother by the same mother.)
Sìzhāo had seven sons: Jìchóu, Jìtāo, Jìdá, Jìzhōng, Jìnéng, Jìxí, Jìyuǎn.
Jìchóu was the prefect of Zézhōu,
and should have inherited the title,
but he was inherently weak.
Jìtāo was vicious and cunning.
He imprisoned Jìchóu in a separate room,
and deceitfully had soldiers force him to become the acting military governor.
Jìtāo pretended to decline,
and reported the matter to the Prince of Jìn.
The Prince of Jìn, as military affairs were pressing,
(with Zhènzhōu not yet taken,
and Liáng troops again attacking and harassing the Hé region,
military affairs were indeed pressing.
"Pressing"
means intense.)
changed the name of the Zhāoyì Army to Ānyì,
and appointed Jìtāo as acting military governor.
(This sets the stage for Lǐ Jìtāo's later rebellion against Jìn and allegiance to Liáng.)
(The *Kǎoyì* states: Note that Lùzhōu was originally called the Zhāoyì Army.
Now, appointing Jìtāo as Ānyì acting military governor,
was likely because the Prince of Jìn changed the name to avoid his father's taboo name.
When Jìtāo later surrendered to Liáng,
Liáng also appointed him as military governor of Kuāngyì.
People today still refer to Zézhōu as Ānyì.)
8. Yán Bǎo, ashamed and resentful
(because of the defeat at Zhènzhōu),
died on the jiǎxū day.
9. The ruler of Hàn, Liú Yán, following an astrologer's advice,
traveled to Méikǒu Town to avoid disaster.
The place was near the western border of Mǐn.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chéngxiāng County in Méizhōu has Méikǒu Town,
bordering Tīngzhōu of Mǐn.
"Near"
is pronounced jìn.)
Before he had gone several tens of lǐ,
scouts reported his location,
and Yán fled, barely escaping.
10. In the fifth month,
on the yǐyǒu day,
Jìn's Lǐ Cúnjìn arrived at Zhènzhōu,
and camped at the Dōngyuán Crossing.
(Zhēndìng was originally Dōngyuán.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn renamed it Zhēndìng.
The ferry crossing still bore the name Dōngyuán.)
11. Jìn's prefect of Wèizhōu, Lǐ Cúnrú,
originally surnamed Yáng,
named Pó'ér,
had gained the Prince of Jìn's favor as an actor.
He was quite strong,
and the Prince of Jìn bestowed him a surname and given name,
appointing him prefect.
He focused solely on extortion and levies.
The city defense soldiers were all taxed a monthly fee and allowed to return home.
(He levied a monthly fee from them and exempted them from defense duties.)
The estate commissioner Duàn Níng and the infantry commander Zhāng Lǎng led troops to cross the river at night and attack him.
At dawn they scaled the walls,
captured Cúnrú,
and thus captured Wèizhōu.
Dài Sīyuǎn, together with Níng, also captured Qímén, Gòngchéng, and Xīnxiāng.
(Gòngchéng and Xīnxiāng counties both belonged to Wèizhōu.
The *Old Tángshū* Geography Treatise states: In Suí, land was taken from Jí and Huòjiā counties,
and Xīnxiāng County was established at the ancient Xīnlè city.
Gòngchéng County
was the Hàn Gòng County,
and became Gòngchéng County in Táng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Wèizhōu's seat was at Jí County.
In the sixth year of Xīníng, Xīnxiāng County was abolished and made a town,
belonging to Jí County.
Jí County also had Qímén Town.
Gòngchéng was 55 lǐ northwest of the prefectural seat.
"Gòng"
is pronounced gōng.)
The area south of Xiàngzhōu
all came under Liáng control.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Chánzhōu is 240 lǐ west to Wèizhōu.
Xiàngzhōu is 150 lǐ south to Wèizhōu.)
The Liáng army's morale revived.
The Emperor appointed Zhāng Lǎng as prefect of Wèizhōu.
(Lǎng
was from Xúzhōu.)
12. In the ninth month,
on the first day, wùyín,
Zhāng Chùjǐn sent his brother Chùqiú to take advantage of Lǐ Cúnjìn's lack of preparedness,
leading seven thousand troops to suddenly arrive at the Dōngyuán Crossing.
At that time, Jìn's cavalry was also heading toward Zhènzhōu city,
and the two forces did not meet.
The Zhènzhōu troops reached the gate of Cúnjìn's camp.
Cúnjìn, in disarray, led over ten men to fight on a bridge.
The Zhènzhōu troops retreated.
Jìn cavalry cut off their rear,
attacking from both sides.
The Zhènzhōu troops were nearly annihilated,
but Cúnjìn also died in battle.
At that time,
Jìn's military was the strongest under heaven,
while Zhènzhōu was reputed to be timid.
The Prince of Jìn, upholding righteousness to punish rebellion,
should have taken it in one strike.
The people of Zhènzhōu forgot the century-long nurturing grace of the Wáng family,
and fought for the momentary lives of Zhāng Wénlǐ and his son.
Shǐ Jiàntáng fell first,
Yán Bǎo retreated defeated afterward,
Lǐ Sìzhāo and Lǐ Cúnjìn in succession returned with their corpses on carts: these four were all Jìn's valiant generals.
So then, was Zhènzhōu brave and Jìn timid?
No.
The people of Zhènzhōu bore the crime of regicide.
They knew that when the city fell, they would surely be executed together.
Therefore, they fought with all their might against Jìn.
Jìn, with its ever-victorious army, faced a populace resolved to die.
Although its troops were elite and generals brave,
they still perished and could not conquer.
Therefore, in ancient campaigns to punish crimes,
they dispersed the factions,
punishing only the chief culprit,
truly considering this situation.
In Zhènzhōu, provisions were exhausted and strength depleted.
Chǔ Jǐn sent an envoy to the mobile administration to request surrender.
Before a response arrived,
Cún Shěn’s troops reached the city walls.
On the night of the bǐngwǔ day,
a general in the city, Lǐ Zàifēng, acted as an inside agent,
secretly lowering ropes to let the Jìn soldiers in.
By dawn they had all ascended,
capturing Chǔ Jǐn, his brothers, family members, and his accomplices Gāo Méng, Lǐ Zhù, and Qí Jiǎn, and sending them to the mobile administration.
The people of Zhào requested and ate them,
and dismembered Zhāng Wénlǐ’s corpse in the marketplace.
A former attendant of the Prince of Zhào recovered the prince’s remains from the ashes.
The Prince of Jìn ordered a sacrifice and burial for him.
He appointed the Zhào general Fú Xí as military governor of Chéngdé,
Wū Zhèn as prefect of Zhàozhōu,
Zhào Rénzhēn as prefect of Shēnzhōu,
and Lǐ Zàifēng as prefect of Jìzhōu.
Zhèn
was from Xìndū.
Fú Xí did not dare accept the post of Chéngdé,
declining and saying:
“My former lord has no heir and remains unburied;
I should wear the coarsest mourning to bury him.
A minister wears the coarsest mourning for his lord.
(Mourning: cuī, pronounced cāng huí fān.)
After the burial,
I will proceed to the mobile administration.”
The people of Zhào requested that the Prince of Jìn concurrently hold the post of military governor of Chéngdé,
and he consented.
The Prince of Jìn carved out the two prefectures of Xiāng and Wèi to establish the Yìníng Army,
appointing Xí as its military governor.
Xí declined, saying:
“Wèibó is the seat of your hegemony;
it should not be divided.
I would rather obtain a commandery in Hénán,
and Xí will seize it himself.”
The world indeed has many who can speak but cannot act.
Fú Xí upheld principles without compromise,
yet ultimately could not seize a commandery in Hénán.
Therefore, a gentleman values keeping his word.
Lǐ Cúnshěn was additionally appointed concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
13 In the eleventh month,
on the wùyín day,
the Jìn Tèjìn and Héđōng military supervisor Zhāng Chéngyè died.
Lady Cáo Tàifūren went to his residence,
observed mourning for him,
according to the rites for sons and nephews.
Zhāng Chéngyè had pacified the troubles of Lǐ Kèníng and Cún Hào,
and for this reason Lady Cáo Tàifūren deeply felt indebted to him.
(For: wèi, pronounced yú wèi fān.)
She did not eat for several days.
She ordered Hé Zàn, the assistant to the Héđōng garrison commander, to temporarily take charge of the Héđōng military administration.
14 In the twelfth month,
the Prince of Jìn appointed Zhāng Xiàn, the observation judge of Wèibó from Jìnyáng, to concurrently serve as observation judge of Zhènjì,
temporarily overseeing the military administration of Zhènzhōu.
Taxes in Wèizhōu were largely in arrears.
The Prince of Jìn reprimanded the registrar Zhào Jìliáng from Jìyīn for this.
(Under the Táng system,
each prefecture had registrars, directors of works, directors of military affairs, directors of merit, and other functionaries,
known as pàn sī.
Jìyīn
was a Hàn commandery name.
The Suí established Jìyīn County,
which the Táng attached to Cáozhōu.
Jì
is pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.)
“When will Your Highness pacify Hénán?”
The prince angrily said:
“Your duty is to supervise taxation;
failing in your duty,
how dare you meddle in my military affairs!”
Jìliáng replied:
“Your Highness is planning conquests yet does not cherish the people.
Once the people’s hearts turn away,
I fear even Héběi will not be yours,
let alone Hénán!”
The prince was pleased,
and apologized to him.
From then on, he valued him,
often consulting him in planning and discussions.
15 This year,
the Qìdān changed their era name to Tiānzàn.
16 The Great Fēng King Gōng Yì
was cruel by nature.
The naval commander Wáng Jiàn killed him,
proclaimed himself king,
and again called himself King of Gāolì,
making Kāizhōu the eastern capital,
and Píngrǎng the western capital.
Jiàn was frugal, simple, and generous,
and the people of the country were content.
Xú Jīng’s Gāolì Tújīng says: Wáng Jiàn’s ancestors
were a great clan of Gāolì.
When the Gāo clan’s rule declined,
the people of the country, considering Jiàn worthy,
established him as ruler.
In the second year of Later Táng Chángxīng,
he claimed to temporarily administer state affairs,
requesting recognition from Míngzōng;
Míngzōng then appointed Jiàn as commissioner of the Dàyì Army,
enfeoffing him as King of Gāolì.
Note: Xú Jīng was an envoy to Gāolì during the Xuānhé period,
presenting the Tújīng,
but his records are sketchy.
Relying on the country’s oral traditions,
he thus stated that Jiàn obtained the state after the Gāo clan,
not knowing that Jiàn actually killed Gōng Yì to gain the state.
For details, see the textual analysis in the fifth year of Zhēnmíng.
Diǎn Guǎngmíng punctuation, Niè Chóngqí proofread.
